prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts; analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 1, Section II — Texts and Human Experiences (20 marks). Allow about 45 minutes.

prompts.question: How does the composer of your prescribed text represent the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of its form? In your response, make reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks how emotion is represented, not which emotions appear. Strong responses name a feature of their text’s form and show the emotion it creates or reveals.

Each form has its own features. Prose fiction answers work with narration and point of view, poetry with imagery, sound and the line, drama with dialogue, staging and dramatic irony, nonfiction with the writer’s voice and selection of detail, and film and media with camera, sound and editing.
The best answers treat emotion as arising from human experience: they connect a feeling to the situation that produces it, and show how the text invites the reader or audience to share or judge it.
A sustained thesis about how the text represents emotion, developed through well-chosen references across the whole text, separates the top range from responses that analyse one scene well.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the emotions characters feel and retelling the events that cause them, without analysing the features that represent them.
Naming techniques without saying what each does to the reader’s or audience’s understanding of the emotion.
Discussing features that belong to another form, such as camera angles in a novel or stanzas in a documentary.
Writing about human experiences in general and losing the question’s focus on emotions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Analyses skilfully how the composer represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of their chosen form; Presents an insightful response supported by well-chosen textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a coherent and sustained response using language appropriate for audience, purpose and context
13-16 marks: Analyses how the composer represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of their chosen form; Presents a thoughtful response supported by textual references from the prescribed text; Writes an organised response using language appropriate for audience, purpose and context
9-12 marks: Explains how the composer represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of their chosen form; Presents a response supported by some textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a response using variable control of language appropriate for audience and purpose
5-8 marks: Expresses limited understanding of how the composer represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of their chosen form; Describes aspects of the prescribed text; Writes a response with minimal control of language
1-4 marks: Refers to the prescribed text in a minimal way; Attempts to compose a response

sampleAnswers.answer:
Anthony Doerr represents the emotions arising from human experiences mainly through the features of prose fiction: structure, imagery, symbol, point of view and dialogue. In All the Light We Cannot See he seldom names a feeling directly. Instead, he builds the reader's response through the order in which events are told, through the sensations that Marie-Laure LeBlanc relies on, and through objects that carry memory. Fear, grief, longing and guilt emerge from choices about how the story is shaped and how the characters speak.

Structure does much of this work. Doerr alternates short chapters between Werner Pfennig and Marie-Laure, and moves between their earlier lives from 1934 and the Battle of Saint-Malo in August 1944. Because the reader knows the bombing is coming while the characters are still hopeful, every memory of a better time is coloured by dread. This dramatic irony is strongest in Werner's promise to his sister Jutta. He tells her, “It's not forever, Jutta,” and he promises to “fly us west.” Doerr later brings the Allied aircraft that bomb Saint-Malo into the story, so the longing for flight becomes a source of loss.

Objects carry emotion too. Daniel builds a model of Paris and later of Saint-Malo so that his daughter can learn the streets by touch, and the care in that gift is expressed through an object. The model is also where the Sea of Flames is hidden, so the thing that shows love becomes a source of danger. When von Rumpel runs his fingers down the model, the emotion moves from tenderness to threat, and the reader feels that change through the object itself.

Because Marie-Laure is blind, Doerr registers her fear through touch and sound rather than sight. When she finds a stone hidden inside a miniature house, the prose slows to the feel of it: “The size of a pigeon's egg.” The room feels “flimsy, tenuous,” and the danger is imagined as a huge hand: “Giant fingertips seem about to punch through.” The metaphor makes the threat both enormous and indifferent. The reader feels helplessness through the body of a girl who cannot see what is coming, so the emotion arrives through sensation rather than through a label.

Werner's emotions are shown more through action than speech. After his squad kills the girl, his disillusion builds, and the reader sees it in the way he keeps his knowledge of Etienne's signal to himself. Frederick's protest works in a similar way. The narration gives his defiance a small and precise form: he says, “He is already finished, sir,” in a small voice. The reader feels pity and horror at once, because the words are quiet and the cruelty around them is loud.

Dialogue carries emotion that the narration cannot easily reach. Etienne explains that he thought a powerful enough broadcast would let his brother hear him. He wanted to bring his brother some peace and to protect him “as he had always protected me.” In that phrase grief, love and guilt sit together. The emotion comes from a human experience of loss and obligation, and the novel leaves it unresolved rather than giving Etienne a consoling answer.

Desperation is conveyed through repetition and the model of the city. Von Rumpel moves his fingers down a miniature street and asks whether it is “here or here or here”, a question that enacts his frantic search. He is cruel and greedy, but Doerr also presents a man who is ill and believes the diamond can save him, so his obsession is partly a fear of death. The repetition lets the reader hear his urgency without the narrator naming it.

The novel leaves several emotions unresolved. Daniel's fate is never discovered, so Marie-Laure lives with uncertainty. In the final section she is old and thinks about the people she has lost, her father above all. Doerr therefore represents emotion as something that lasts beyond the events that cause it. Through the features of prose fiction, fear, grief and longing remain with the reader after the last page. The reader is left with the same uncertainty as Marie-Laure, and the feeling lingers because the story does not close the gap.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how structure, sensation, dialogue and repetition carry fear, grief and longing, and it sustains that argument to the ending. The strongest move is linking the airplane promise to the later bombing as dramatic irony. The one move that would lift it further is to show how a second scene uses the same sensory technique.
sampleAnswers.prescribedText: All the Light We Cannot See

sampleAnswers.answer:
Doerr shows many emotions in All the Light We Cannot See. Marie-Laure feels fear when she hides in the attic during the bombing of Saint-Malo, and she is sad when her father disappears. Werner becomes disillusioned after his squad kills a girl. Etienne feels grief for his brother, and he broadcasts his brother's voice on the radio because he misses him. These emotions come from experiences of war and loss, which are human experiences that many readers will recognise.

Doerr uses the features of prose fiction to show these feelings. The chapters go between Werner and Marie-Laure, so the reader sees each character's feelings in turn. The chapters are short, and the story jumps between years, which creates tension. Werner's promise to Jutta also shows his hope, because he says he will fly away with her. Later, the aircraft that bomb Saint-Malo show that his hope has been turned around.

The model of Saint-Malo is also an important object. Daniel makes it so that his daughter can learn the streets, which shows how much he cares for her. Marie-Laure uses it to find her way around, and later the Sea of Flames is hidden inside it. An object that shows love also becomes a place of danger.

Madame Manec's illness and death also bring feeling into the story. Etienne and Marie-Laure are moved by her bravery, and their decision to fight the Germans is an emotional response to loss as well as a political one.

Doerr also uses dialogue. Etienne speaks about his brother, and von Rumpel speaks about the diamond. Von Rumpel is a cruel man who wants the diamond, but he also seems afraid, and he asks Marie-Laure questions about where it is. These scenes show emotion through what the characters say, which makes the feelings clear to the reader. The emotions are not hidden, but they are not explained at length either.

Overall, Doerr represents emotions through the features of prose fiction, and those emotions come from the human experiences in the novel. The reader feels fear, grief and longing because of the way the story is told.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains which emotions appear and where, but it names features of prose fiction without analysing their effect. Its strength is the accurate link between Etienne's broadcasts and his grief. The one move that would lift it is to take the alternating chapters and show how they change what the reader feels at one particular point.
sampleAnswers.prescribedText: All the Light We Cannot See

sampleAnswers.answer: In All the Light We Cannot See, Marie-Laure is blind and her father is taken away. Werner is in the army and he feels bad about the war. As a boy he fixes radios and he wants to fly away with his sister Jutta, so he has hope. Frederick is hurt at school because he will not do what the others do. The book is set in World War Two and the characters have sad and scary feelings. Madame Manec is kind to Marie-Laure and she helps the people in the town, and then she dies. Etienne is a man who lost his brother in the war, and he plays the radio. Von Rumpel wants a diamond and he is scary. Doerr writes about what happens to them, so the reader feels sorry for them. I think the book is good because it makes you feel sad.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes events in the novel and names emotions without showing how the text creates them. Its strength is a clear sense of the story's sad events. The one move that would lift it is to quote one short phrase and explain which feature of prose fiction makes its emotion felt.
sampleAnswers.prescribedText: All the Light We Cannot See

sampleAnswers.answer:
Amanda Lohrey represents the emotions that arise from human experiences in Vertigo mostly through the features of prose fiction: setting, a figure the couple come to call 'the boy', and a structure that holds back what the characters cannot say. The result is that grief is felt by the reader before it is named. The emotions in the novella are restlessness, grief, fear and a cautious hope, and each one is carried by a feature that makes it physical rather than stated.

The first emotion is restlessness. Luke and Anna are thirty-something and worn down by city life, and Lohrey gives this feeling a spatial form. The city offers them no relief, and the move to the coast is a change of landscape as much as a change of life. The reader understands their discontent through where they are and what they do, rather than through a direct account of their unhappiness. The coast then brings a different emotion. Surrounded by nature, they begin to feel rejuvenated, and the novella lets the setting carry that hope before anything threatens it. The hope is fragile, and the title shows why. Vertigo describes a bodily feeling of losing one's balance, so the emotion it names is disorientation rather than despair. Luke and Anna lose their footing when the place that was meant to steady them becomes a place of danger, and the reader is asked to feel that shift as they do.

Grief is represented through silence. The loss is one that neither of them can talk about, so the emotion appears in what they avoid saying. Lohrey does not explain the grief in full, and the reader must notice the gap between what the characters say and what they feel. The structure supports this. The reason for the boy's presence is held back until late, so the reader meets the couple's unspoken grief through unease rather than explanation, and the form makes the emotion something the reader has to work out. The silence also divides the couple from each other. They are kept apart by what they do not say, and the reader sees a loneliness inside the marriage as well as the loss that caused it.

The boy is the most important device for representing grief. Lohrey uses him to make the loss present without naming it, so the feeling he produces is a mix of tenderness and unease. A reader feels this as Luke and Anna do, and the figure works as a symbol that does not need to be explained.

The bushfire makes emotion physical. Its threat to the new home brings fear into the open, and the danger comes from the landscape the couple chose for safety. The emotional force of the scene comes from its immediacy. Fear is not described as a feeling but as a threat to the place they live, and the fire forces them to confront what they had tried to put behind them. The drought in the background adds to the sense of strain, so that the land seems to share the pressure the characters feel. The fear is also a fear of exposure. The fire removes the distance that let the couple keep their grief at arm's length, and it turns a buried emotion into a danger that cannot be avoided by moving on.

Lohrey represents emotion through the features of prose fiction rather than through statement. Setting carries restlessness and renewal, silence and structure carry grief, the boy carries the loss as a presence, and the fire carries fear and exposure. Together these features suggest that the emotions arising from human experiences return unexpectedly and cannot be closed off by moving away. The novella's emotional power lies in this indirectness, which asks the reader to feel the couple's grief and hope, slowly and at one remove, without ever being told what to feel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how Lohrey represents restlessness, grief, fear and hope through setting, silence, the boy and the fire, and it sustains that focus across the response. To lift it further, it could test one feature more closely against a specific moment in the novella, since most of its evidence stays at the level of the novella's broad shape.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Amanda Lohrey uses the features of prose fiction to present the emotions that come from human experiences in Vertigo. The couple feel restless at the start, and the novella then shows grief and fear. Lohrey does this mainly through setting and through a boy who appears in the story, and this creates a sense of unease for the reader.

At the beginning, Luke and Anna are restless and tired of city life. They move to a small village on the coast, and the coast is beautiful and full of nature. This makes them feel better, so the emotion at this point is hope. The setting is important because it changes the way the characters feel.

The loss the couple have experienced is the main cause of their grief. They do not talk about it, and this shows that they are finding it hard to deal with their feelings. Lohrey also includes a boy who appears in the story. He seems to be connected to their loss. This adds a sense of mystery and makes the reader feel uncertain about what is going on.

The bushfire is the most frightening event in the novella. It threatens their new home, so the couple feel scared. This is a good example of emotion because the fear is connected to the landscape they moved to. The fire shows that they cannot escape their feelings by moving away.

Overall, Lohrey uses setting, the boy and the bushfire to show emotions. The reader can see how the characters feel from these features, and the novella makes emotion seem important to the way people live.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the emotions and the features that carry them, but the analysis is thin and it relies on plot more than on form. Its strength is the link it draws between the bushfire and the fear the couple feel. To lift it, the answer should analyse how one feature, such as the boy, produces an emotion rather than stating that it does.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Vertigo, Amanda Lohrey writes about a couple called Luke and Anna who are sad because of a loss. They move from the city to the coast, where there is lots of nature, and they feel happier. Then a bushfire comes and they are scared. There is also a boy, and this is strange. The book uses setting and the boy to show how the couple feel. The couple are not talking about their loss, so the reader has to guess how they feel. The fire makes the characters scared and they have to think about what happened before. The novel shows emotions like sadness, happiness and fear. In the end, Lohrey shows that emotions are important in the story.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the couple, the coast, the fire and the boy in order, with little reference to the text and no clear claim about how emotion is represented. Its strength is that it links the setting to the couple's feelings. To lift it, the answer needs to name one device, say how it works, and connect it to one emotion.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Nineteen Eighty-Four, Orwell represents the emotions arising from human experiences mainly through the features of prose fiction rather than through direct statement. Close third-person narration places the reader inside Winston Smith's perceptions, so that fear, hatred, hope and grief are felt as sensations and half-formed thoughts. Orwell also uses the diary, the dream, setting, imagery and dialogue to show feeling that Winston cannot speak aloud. The result is a novel in which emotion is constantly controlled, as it is under the Party, and in which the reader sees both its intensity and its suppression.

Fear is established in the opening chapter through setting and restrained narration. Winston's “chin nuzzled into his breast” is a physical image of defensiveness, and the poster of Big Brother has eyes that “follow you about when you move”. The narrator adds that there is “no way of knowing” when one is watched. Orwell gives the reader this fear as the atmosphere of a room rather than as a statement, so the paranoia is felt before Winston names it. The poster is a feature of setting that works as a source of emotion, not merely as background.

Hatred is rendered through the narrator's comparisons. In the Two Minutes Hate the crowd grows wild, and in its second minute the Hate “rose to a frenzy”. Winston's own feeling is described with a cool simile: it could be switched “like the flame of a blowlamp” from one object to another. The image is mechanical, so the emotion seems an instrument the Party can aim rather than a natural passion. The reader feels disquiet at hatred shown from the inside, and the sentences expose manipulation without explicit comment from the narrator.

The diary is the novel's main vehicle for hope, and its form shows how fragile that hope is. Winston's pen “had slid voluptuously over the smooth paper” as he prints “DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER”, and the sensual verb shows a physical release of feeling. Later he writes that hope “lies in the proles”, and the line returns to him as “a mystical truth and a palpable absurdity”. The narration lets that judgement undercut Winston's hope even as it is expressed, so the emotion is at once sincere and self-deceiving. Orwell asks the reader to hold both.

Love is conveyed through a small object and a landscape. Julia's note, written “in a large unformed handwriting”, reads “I LOVE YOU”, and the plainness of the words produces a physical shock, with “the desire to stay alive” welling up in Winston. In the countryside Orwell uses setting as an emotional symbol. Winston recognises the place with a “curious, slow shock of recognition” and names it “the Golden Country—almost”, the landscape of a dream he has had repeatedly. The narration moves from the city to the pasture, and the reader feels the affair as a longing for a world the Party has taken away.

Grief appears in dream, which allows Orwell to present feeling Winston cannot rationalise. In the dream his mother is sitting “with his young sister in her arms”, and he knows that “the lives of his mother and his sister” have been “sacrificed to his own”. The logic of the dream is emotional rather than factual: its causes are unclear, but its guilt is exact. Orwell's use of dream as a structural feature lets the novel admit a grief that the Party's rational world cannot name, which gives the book an emotional depth beyond its surveillance plot.

Dialogue and free indirect narration carry fear and betrayal in the later sections. Parsons, arrested for “Thoughtcrime!”, speaks of his daughter's denunciation with “a sort of doleful pride”, and his mixture of pride and misery shows how far the Party has penetrated family life. When O'Brien tells Winston that “the worst thing in the world” is rats, the narrator records “a sort of premonitory tremor”. Winston's cry, “Do it to Julia!”, is repeated and frantic, and the repetition captures panic and shame in a single line. Emotion here is produced by rhythm and speech rather than by description.

The ending controls emotion through flatness. Winston's tears are “gin-scented”, he has “won the victory over himself”, and the narrative closes with “He loved Big Brother.” The sentence is either triumphant or hollow, and Orwell withholds the explanation that would settle which. The appendix, “The Principles of Newspeak”, follows in a cool, scholarly register, and its distance from feeling completes the theme. The Party's language has removed the capacity for emotion that the rest of the book has used to draw the reader in.

Throughout the prescribed text, Orwell's representation of emotion depends on the features of prose fiction working together. Narration, the diary, the dream, symbolic setting, simile and dialogue each make fear, hatred, hope, love and grief felt by the reader, and each is then undercut by the Party's world. The reader is asked to feel the emotions the Party seeks to destroy, and to recognise that Winston's final contentment is itself a loss.

Orwell represents emotions through features of prose fiction such as narration, setting and the diary. In Nineteen Eighty-Four the main emotions are fear, hatred and hope, and the novel shows them through Winston Smith's point of view. The reader sees the world through Winston, so his feelings become the reader's feelings.

Fear is shown from the start. Winston goes home on a cold day in April, and the telescreen watches him in his flat. The poster of Big Brother has eyes that seem to follow people, so the reader feels that they are being watched too. Winston is careful about what he does, and this shows how fear controls his behaviour.

Hatred is shown in the Two Minutes Hate. The crowd becomes very angry at Goldstein on the screen, and the Hate rises to a frenzy. Winston is also caught up in it, and the novel says his hatred can be switched to other targets. This shows that the Party can control emotions, which is one of the main ideas of the novel.

Hope is shown in Winston's diary. He writes “DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER” in capital letters, and later he writes that hope lies in the proles. This matters because it shows Winston is still hopeful even though he is in danger. The diary is a way of showing his inner thoughts directly to the reader.

Love is shown through Julia. She sends him a note saying “I LOVE YOU”, and this affects Winston a great deal. They go to the countryside, which Winston calls the Golden Country, and it is a happy place for them. Orwell describes the countryside in some detail, which helps the reader feel the happiness of the affair.

Grief is shown in a dream about Winston's mother and sister. The dream lets Winston think about things he cannot understand. He feels that his mother and sister were sacrificed for him, and the reader feels sad for him.

The ending shows Winston loving Big Brother. This is the most important emotion in the book because it shows that the Party has won. The emotion is flat, and the reader feels that something is wrong. The appendix on Newspeak is written in a different style and shows the Party's control of language.

Overall, Orwell uses features of prose fiction to show emotions. The reader feels fear, hatred, hope, love and grief, and sees that the Party controls all of them.

In the prescribed text, Parrett represents the emotions that arise from human experiences mainly through characterisation, setting and the placement of key information. Past the Shallows does not explain its feelings at length. Instead it gives three brothers who respond to the same violent household in different ways, places them on a coast where the sea is at once a source of pleasure and of danger, and holds its central loss until near the end. Through these features the novel produces fear, responsibility, anger, tenderness and grief, and the reader comes to feel them through the characters' circumstances rather than through direct statement.

The three brothers give the novel its emotional range, and each responds differently to the same cruelty. Joe, the eldest, escapes to his grandfather's house, so his response is flight rather than endurance. Miles, the middle brother, works alongside the father on the boat and looks after Harry at the same time, and Parrett shows responsibility as a weight that slowly wears him down. Harry, the youngest, is the most vulnerable, and he is the child at whom his father's anger is most often aimed. His fear of the water is the emotion the novel sustains most consistently, because it shapes where he goes, what he refuses to do and whom he trusts.

The father is the source of much of the fear and anger in the novel. He is an abalone fisherman and a violent alcoholic, and his brutality makes the household a place of constant danger. Parrett gives his cruelty a hidden cause by presenting him as a man who carries a devastating secret that is destroying him. This does not make him sympathetic in any simple way, but it means his rage is never only his own. It is the visible surface of something the boys cannot fully see. The emotions this produces are fear in Harry and a steady, anxious obligation in Miles, and both are shown through the way the boys behave around their father.

Setting carries emotion as strongly as character does. The sea on the south-east coast of Tasmania is where Joe and Miles both love to surf, and it is also the place of the father's work and of the danger that eventually takes Harry. The same water therefore holds opposing emotions, joy for the brothers who are at ease in it and terror for the one who is not. Parrett uses this doubleness to bind fear and happiness together in the landscape, so the coast cannot be read as a mere backdrop. The home is a place of fear, the boat a place of work and danger, and the water a place of both pleasure and loss.

Tenderness enters the novel through George Fuller and his dog, Jake. Harry finds in George a kind of company that he does not find at home, and the dog offers a companion who asks nothing of him. These relationships exist at the edge of the family's violence, so they show affection and relief in a way the household cannot. The friendship is a small counterweight to the father's cruelty, and it makes the later loss more painful, because the reader has seen how much Harry depends on it.

The emotional climax is structural as well as dramatic. Miles wakes in hospital, where Joe has come back to his bedside, and Joe tells him that Harry has drowned. The news is delivered by another character, and the emotion is carried by the bare fact of the sentence and by Miles's inability to take it in. Parrett places the strongest grief where the surviving brother has the least capacity to respond, so the reader feels the loss through his helplessness. A reader who has followed the brothers through the boat trip understands what those words cost.

The representation is most effective where emotion is held back. Parrett trusts the reader to infer grief from action, silence and the sudden shift of place, rather than from extended explanation of feeling. This restraint suits a household in which open feeling is dangerous, and it makes the emotion more forceful because the reader must work to recognise it. The risk is distance: restraint can turn loss into a fact of the plot rather than something the characters live through. Parrett largely avoids this by tying each emotion to a concrete situation, a boat, a house, a friendship or a hospital bed.

Through characterisation, setting and the placement of its central loss, Parrett represents emotion as something produced by one violent family working on three children in different ways. Fear, responsibility, anger, tenderness and grief are not separate displays in the novel. They arise from the same household and the same coast, and they carry the most force where the features of prose fiction work together: in the boys' bodies, in the sea and in the hospital room.

In Past the Shallows, Favel Parrett shows the emotions of her characters through the boys' lives with a cruel father and the sea where he works. The three brothers are Joe, Miles and Harry. Harry's fear is the clearest emotion, because he is frightened of the water and does not want to be on it. Miles shows responsibility because he has to work and care for his brother at the same time. Joe shows a different emotion because he escapes, which suggests he has his own feelings about leaving. Setting is also important. The coast is where Joe and Miles surf, so it is a place of enjoyment, but it is also where the father works and where the danger is. This means the sea holds different emotions for different characters. The father's violence is the main reason for these feelings, and it is the main source of fear in the household.

Parrett also uses George Fuller and his dog Jake to show tenderness. Harry goes to George's place and seems to feel better there, which contrasts with his home. This shows that not all the emotions in the novel are negative. The dog is a friend to Harry, and this friendship makes the reader feel warmth towards him.

The most emotional part of the novel is the hospital scene. Miles wakes up in hospital and Joe tells him that Harry has drowned. This is a sad moment, and Miles must deal with the grief of losing his brother. The reader can see that Miles is very upset because he has lost Harry. This scene shows grief strongly, and it comes after the boat trip, which makes it important for the reader.

Overall, Parrett uses characters, setting and the hospital scene to show emotions like fear, responsibility, tenderness and grief. These emotions come from the boys' lives with their father and from the sea. The novel shows these emotions clearly, so the reader understands how the characters feel.

Dobson rarely names an emotion and then explains it. In the prescribed text, the emotions arising from human experiences are carried by the features of poetry: imagery, structure, the position of a speaker and the repetition of a place. Cock Crow, Summer's End and Amy Caroline show this most clearly, with guilt, loss and regret present without being stated as the poem's argument. Over the Hill adds a contrasting emotion, calm, produced by the same means. The effect is a restraint that asks the reader to feel what the poem leaves unsaid.

Cock Crow is organised around a journey. The speaker moves along a road between a lit house and the town, and the repeated movement carries the feeling of a woman torn between household duty and personal freedom. The lit house is warm, yet it is also the place she is leaving. The title and the cock crow recall Peter's denial of Jesus, and this allusion makes the guilt larger than a single choice. The poem leaves it unclear whether she betrays her family or herself. The repetition of the road gives the sense of a mind returning to the same decision, and the dark trees closing in add fear. The strongest image is “My mother and my daughter slept”, which places the speaker between generations, so that her guilt feels both personal and inherited.

Summer's End expresses loss through season and structure. The poem is a diptych, and its second part, Picnic, returns the reader to an earlier moment, so the feeling of the first part, the end of summer, is complicated by memory. The opening words “After the summer season” make the end of the season feel like a turning point, and the reader senses the chill of change before any loss is named. The reader is left to feel the difference between the seasons without a line telling them how to feel. The emotion is bittersweet. The warmth of the fire and the memory of the child console the speaker, yet the pairing of present and past makes the loss of that warmth felt. Dobson therefore represents grief as a pattern that returns across seasons rather than as a single event.

In Amy Caroline, Dobson represents sorrow through restraint. The poem sets out a woman's life of hardship in a plain, list-like manner, and the emotional weight sits in the phrase “little money, many griefs”. The sorrow becomes more personal when the poem turns to the woman's own wishes. At twilight she plays “the songs learnt long ago” in the semi-dark, a private grief the household has never seen. The piano and the semi-dark do more emotional work than any adjective would, because they let the reader imagine the woman alone. The poem then records regret in a flat admission, “She was sorry”, followed by the jinker and horse she never owned. Because the feeling is quiet and cumulative rather than dramatic, the reader senses the cost of a life more strongly than a direct statement could convey.

Over the Hill shows calm rather than sorrow, and the features of poetry produce it. The tone is measured, and the imagery of western light and the evening sky softens the subject of a man near death. The setting also frames him against something larger than his fear. Dobson avoids the fear that the subject invites, so the reader feels respect rather than pity. The emotion is achieved, not given, and this suggests that Dobson represents feeling as a matter of how a person holds experience, not only of what the experience is.

Dobson represents emotion through the features of poetry rather than through declaration. Guilt is carried by allusion and repetition in Cock Crow, loss by the diptych structure of Summer's End, sorrow by the list and twilight of Amy Caroline, and calm by imagery in Over the Hill. Each poem asks the reader to supply the feeling it does not name, which is why these emotions feel earned rather than imposed. The poems offer little comfort and no neat resolution. They present emotions arising from human experiences as things that persist, and that persistence gives the representation its force.

Its strongest feature is the reading of the repeated road in Cock Crow as a device that carries guilt without naming it. To lift it, the conclusion could assess where the representation is less successful, such as whether the calm of Over the Hill is as convincing as the sorrow of Amy Caroline.

Slessor represents the emotions arising from human experiences mostly through the features of poetry rather than by stating what his speakers feel. In Beach Burial the emotion is a restrained pity mixed with bewilderment. In William Street, delight and disgust pull against each other, and in Out of Time wonder gives way to grief. In each poem the emotional force comes from imagery, sound, tone and structure. Read together, the three poems show that Slessor’s poetry makes feeling a product of its craft: the reader feels the emotion because the language is arranged to produce it.

Beach Burial places its grief in a grave scene on the sand, where men pulled from the surf are buried by soldiers who handle them with rough but careful hands. The emotion arises most strongly from the inscribed crosses, which read “Unknown Seaman”. Those two words hold grief and irony together: the men are identified only by what they are not, and the reader feels the loss of identity as well as of life. The sound of the poem supports this restraint. Critics have noted its use of assonance, echo and half-rhyme, which give the lines a soft, recurring music that slows the reader much as the burial slows the men. The poem’s emotion is therefore not a cry. It is the quiet, perplexed pity of people who cannot make sense of what they are doing, and the sound patterns make the reader share that bewilderment.

William Street produces its emotions through contrast and repetition. A refrain returns in each stanza, setting the speaker’s claim that the street is “lovely” against an unnamed “you” who finds it “ugly”. The repetition makes the feeling uncomfortable: the reader is asked to hold delight and disgust at once and to decide whose judgement is correct. The imagery is intense. Red, green and flashing neon lights reflect off the wet road like running fire, and a catalogue of smells, from smoke and frying onions to kerosene, fills the air. Pawnshop trousers hang in the windows like hanged men, and this image moves the mood from exhilaration towards dread and pity. By the last stanza the figures on the pavement are close to starvation, and the poem’s sympathy becomes plain. The emotion shifts with each quatrain, which is why the poem feels unsettled rather than simply admiring.

Out of Time moves through a sequence of emotions that its imagery and rhythm control. Its opening image of Time as a moving line of yachts is bright, sensuous and almost joyful, and the light lends the lines a sharp glow. The poem then reverses that feeling. The yachts become a funeral procession, the gulls fall and the body dies and decays, so wonder turns into grief and dread. The sound of the poem helps this change. Repeated consonants and unexpected stresses slow some lines and speed others, so the rhythm alternates between flow and pause, much as the speaker moves between being absorbed in the moment and being carried away by Time. The loss is felt in the lines themselves, which pause and falter as the mood darkens.

The three poems produce different emotional effects, and this variety is part of Slessor’s method. Beach Burial asks for pity that stays restrained, William Street asks for a divided response, and Out of Time asks for grief about mortality. What links them is that the features of poetry do the emotional work. Sound, image and structure shape the reader’s feelings, rather than the speaker announcing them. A reader who notices this can explain why the emotions are strong without assuming the poems simply report what the poet feels.

Slessor therefore represents emotion as something produced by craft. The feelings in these poems are not sentiment for its own sake. They come from the careful arrangement of images, rhythm and refrain, and each poem invites a reader to share an emotion that its speaker does not fully name. Beach Burial turns grief into a quiet bewilderment, William Street places the reader between admiration and disgust, and Out of Time moves from wonder to grief. That movement is the clearest sign of Slessor’s skill: the poems make the reader feel what they represent, rather than only observe it.

Jane Harrison represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the basic features of drama: setting, character, dialogue, conflict and the staging that connects the stage to the audience. In the prescribed text, Rainbow’s End, emotion is never only described. It is built out of the situation the women live in, and the audience feels the strain of that situation through what the characters say to one another and the pressure they are under.

The most basic feature is setting. The play takes place in a shanty on the flats of the Goulburn River in 1950s regional Victoria, and the family’s home becomes the emotional centre of the play. Because Nan Dear, Gladys and Dolly share a small house, the staging keeps each private feeling visible to the others. Fear, pride and frustration do not stay inside one character. They pass across the room and show in the reactions of the other women, so the audience reads one woman’s emotion in another’s response. The confined space also keeps the family’s hopes pressed against limits that come from outside the house, so the sense of constraint is present even in quiet moments.

Dialogue carries the widest emotional range, and Harrison uses the generational conflict among the women to produce it. Nan Dear is irascible, and her insistence on keeping the family out of sight produces a fear that is sharper because it is protective. The audience is asked to feel something close to sympathy for her, even when she frustrates Gladys. Her caution does not read as cowardice; it reads as the judgement of someone who knows what a community can take away. Each argument with Gladys is therefore a clash between two emotional responses to the same injustice: Nan’s fear of losing what little the family has, and Gladys’s anger at being told to accept less. Harrison lets the audience hold both reactions at once, which is why the emotion is complex rather than simply admirable.

Conflict gives hope and anger their fullest dramatic form, and Gladys is the character who carries it. She campaigns for better housing for her community, so the play places her in public demands for better housing. Her determination is pride and frustration at once, and the play keeps her persistence in view throughout. Because Gladys has little formal schooling, her confidence in these encounters is hard won, and the audience feels the effort behind each assertion. The audience sees the injustice in the characters’ reactions as well as in what they say.

Humour and romance give Harrison another emotional register. Dolly is bright and witty, and her relationship with Errol, the young salesman, brings lightness and hope into a play weighed down by housing and poverty. The romance is a feature of comedy used with a serious purpose. The audience enjoys the attraction, then recognises its danger: a relationship across the colour line draws the attention the family has tried to avoid. Errol’s interest and Dolly’s excitement sit beside the anxiety of the older women, so the tone moves quickly from delight to unease. Harrison uses this shift to show that the same human experience of love can produce hope and fear at once.

Harrison also shapes emotion through structure. The play moves in short scenes of naturalistic action, so the audience passes quickly between hardship, humour and confrontation, and no feeling is allowed to settle for long. Taken together, these features show that the emotions in the play are products of the conditions the characters live in rather than private moods. Fear, pride, anger, affection and hope all arise from living under a system the women did not design and cannot easily leave. By tying emotion to dialogue, conflict and a shared space, Harrison makes the audience respond as participants rather than observers. That is the work the features of drama do in the prescribed text, and it is why the play represents emotion so effectively.

Harrison represents emotion in Rainbow’s End through features of drama such as setting, dialogue and conflict. The play is set in a shanty by the Goulburn River in the 1950s, and the three women live in it together. Because they share the house, they see each other’s feelings, and the audience sees emotion in the way each character responds to the others. This is the first way the prescribed text makes emotion visible.

Dialogue is the main way the play shows emotion. Nan Dear does not want the family to be noticed, and she is worried about what might happen if they are. Gladys wants better housing and is angry about the way the family is treated. Dolly has hopes for her future. These different attitudes create tension between the characters, and this tension is an emotional experience for the audience. Their arguments show the fear and frustration that come from living with little money and few choices.

Conflict is another feature. Gladys campaigns for housing, and this brings her into contact with officials who do not help the family. The audience can see her frustration with the housing. This is an example of the human experience of injustice, and it makes the audience feel angry on her behalf. The emotion comes from the situation rather than from any single line of speech.

The romance between Dolly and Errol adds a different emotion. Errol is a salesman who falls in love with Dolly, and the audience sees her excitement about him. However, the relationship also causes worry because of the colour line, and the older women are anxious about what people will say. So the play mixes hope and fear. This shows that love can be an emotional experience that is complicated by the society the characters live in.

The play uses humour as well. Dolly is witty, and some scenes are light. This gives the audience a break from the tension and makes the serious moments stronger. The comedy is brief, and it reminds the audience that the family also finds warmth and pleasure in one another. In this way Harrison uses features of drama to create a range of emotions, from warmth to fear.

Overall, Harrison uses setting, dialogue, conflict and romance to represent emotion. The audience feels the fear, anger and hope of the characters because the play puts them in situations that matter to them. This is why the play is effective in representing emotion.

Miller represents the emotions of The Crucible mainly through the features of drama rather than through description. Fear, guilt, jealousy, grief and pride are not reported to the audience; they are built through setting, stage action, dramatic irony, the pacing of dialogue and the climaxes of the courtroom and the jail. Written in 1953 as an allegory for McCarthyism, the play turns a collective panic into personal emotions, each tied to a particular character in a particular room. The human experiences it presents are therefore felt as well as understood.

The first act establishes the method. Parris's house is a place of fear and self-interest, where a minister frets over his position while his daughter lies motionless. Miller builds dramatic irony as Abigail deceives the adults around her. The audience learns that the dancing was an attempt to curse Elizabeth Proctor while Parris and the others are still deciding whom to believe, and that knowledge makes every accusation more frightening. Abigail's threats to the girls who might talk, that she can make them wish they had "never seen the sun go down", are delivered as raw menace, and the audience feels the danger before any official acts.

Act Two moves the play into the Proctor home, where fear becomes domestic. The poppet Mary Warren brings home is an ordinary object, but Cheever finds a needle inside it, and the object becomes evidence that carries fear from the court into the household. Miller lets the prop do emotional work: the audience watches a family home become a place where a poppet can lead to an arrest. The arrest follows so directly from the needle that the atmosphere of the court seems to have reached inside the Proctors' door.

Dialogue carries guilt in the same act. John Proctor's outburst moves from accusation to confession: "I'll plead no more!" is followed by the admission that his spirit twists around "the single error of my life". The line shows shame turning into anger, and its repeated exclamations make the self-reproach urgent. Elizabeth's grief has a similar force. Proctor describes an "everlasting funeral" that marches round her heart, and the image turns the marriage into a mourning that has no end.

The courtroom in Act Three is the emotional climax, and Miller stages it through noise, interruption and public exposure. Danforth's assertion that "No uncorrupted man may fear this court" makes fear itself a sign of guilt, and the audience recognises the irony in a court that treats fear as proof. When Proctor confesses his affair, private shame becomes public spectacle. The stage then fills with screaming girls, and Mary Warren, threatened with hanging, recants and joins them. Miller shows fear overcoming conscience through action the audience can watch, rather than through explanation.

The final act is set in the jail, and its emotional force comes from confinement. Proctor signs a confession, then tears it up. Miller's stage direction, "With the cry of his whole soul", tells the actor how to deliver the speech that follows, so the audience hears the emotion before it fully understands the argument. His line "Because it is my name" is a cry of pride, but it is also the moment at which guilt becomes a defence of identity. The confined space makes each line feel urgent, because there is nowhere left for Proctor to retreat.

Elizabeth expresses emotion more quietly, and Miller gives her a different register. She tells John that she counted herself "so plain" and that her suspicion made the house cold: "It were a cold house I kept". Her regret is staged through dialogue rather than action, and it changes how the audience reads her earlier coldness. Her answer to Hale, "He have his goodness now", is a refusal, and its force lies in its restraint. The contrast between the screaming court of Act Three and this quiet acceptance is one of the play's most deliberate effects.

Taken together, these features show that Miller does not treat emotion as a theme to be named. Fear is heard in the girls' screams, guilt is shown in a torn confession, and grief is embedded in a marriage that has gone cold. Staging, dialogue and dramatic irony work together so that the audience feels the cost of each emotion as the characters do. That is why the play's emotional power outlasts the particular accusations of its plot.

Miller uses the features of drama to show the emotions of The Crucible. The play moves between different places, including Parris's house, the Proctor home, the court and the jail, and each place has a different emotional feel. In Act One the characters are afraid because the girls are suspected of witchcraft, and Abigail is the one who keeps everyone frightened. Parris is afraid that he will lose his position as minister. Miller lets the audience see that Abigail is lying, which creates dramatic irony, because the audience knows more than Parris does.

In Act Two, the poppet is an important object. Mary Warren gives it to Elizabeth, and a needle is found inside it. This makes the audience worried for Elizabeth, because the object is used as evidence against her. Miller uses a simple thing to show how fear can grow from a small detail. John becomes angry and tears up the arrest warrant, and Elizabeth calms him down and gives herself up. The emotion in the house moves from fear to anger and then to resignation.

The court in Act Three is where the emotion is strongest. Proctor says that Abigail has been lying and he confesses to the affair. This is a big moment, and the room is thrown into confusion. Danforth says that no uncorrupted man may fear this court, which shows his certainty about the court. Mary Warren then changes her story because she is threatened with hanging, and this shows fear overcoming honesty.

In Act Four the characters are in the jail. Proctor has to decide whether to confess. He signs the paper and then he tears it up, which shows his guilt and his pride. He says "Because it is my name", and this line shows how important his reputation is to him. Elizabeth also has emotions in this act. She says that her house was cold, and this shows that she feels guilty about how she treated him.

Overall, Miller uses setting, dialogue and dramatic irony to show emotions. These features help the audience feel the characters' emotions and understand the play's message about fear and reputation. The play is powerful because the emotions are shown in the events of the trials, not only described.

In the first act the girls are scared and Abigail tells lies, and Parris is also worried about his job. In the second act John and Elizabeth Proctor argue, and Mary Warren is scared and changes her story. Mary also brings home a doll. The doll has a needle in it and Elizabeth is arrested. The emotions are fear and sadness, and Miller uses the stage to show them to the audience, so the audience can see what the characters are feeling.

Shakespeare presents the emotions of The Merchant of Venice as things characters cannot fully explain, and the features of drama invite the audience to share that uncertainty. The play opens with Antonio saying, “I know not why I am so sad”, while his friends offer reasons that he rejects. Melancholy is represented as a state others try to diagnose and fail to understand. This sets up a pattern across the prescribed text: emotions arise from human experiences such as prejudice, humiliation, mercy and love, and each is revealed through staging, reported speech and song rather than direct statement.

Reported speech is one of drama's most effective tools for emotion. Solanio describes Shylock's cries in the street, quoting them as “My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!” The grief is real, but it reaches the audience through the account of a Venetian who treats it as a spectacle, so the emotion is both displayed and judged. Because we must reconstruct Shylock's loss from a hostile retelling, the scene turns his grief into a question about the listeners' cruelty rather than a simple expression of sorrow.

Asides allow the audience to hold feelings that characters conceal. When Shylock first sees Antonio, he remarks aside, “How like a fawning publican he looks!”, and vows to “feed fat the ancient grudge” he bears him. The men on stage cannot hear this hatred, but the audience does, so it understands Shylock's grievance before any bargain is struck. The public deal that follows is made in the shadow of that private speech, and its irony depends on the convention that the audience hears what the characters do not say aloud.

Shylock's humiliation is staged most fully in his defence of his humanity. He asks, “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, builds a list of the bodily and emotional features Jews share with Christians, and concludes that if Christians wrong him he will take revenge. The repeated questions give his rage a rhythm that mounts towards its close: “The villainy you teach me I will execute”. The emotion is not only anger but anger that the Christians have taught him, so his humiliation becomes a threat the audience can see is partly of their making.

The trial scene shows how quick exchanges and reversals produce emotional whiplash. Gratiano's repeated exclamations express a triumph the audience is invited to distrust. Portia's turn to “no jot of blood” removes Shylock's hope within a few lines, and his bitter reply, “the devil give him good of it”, turns despair into contempt. The emotional force comes from the speed of the exchange, with relief, elation and disbelief packed together. The audience knows Portia's identity and Shylock does not, so every appeal he makes is shaped by dramatic irony.

Portia's speech on mercy marks the play's highest emotional register. She begins, “The quality of mercy is not strain'd”, and describes it as falling “upon the place beneath”. The lyric imagery lifts compassion above the legal argument, yet it is addressed to a man who refuses it, and its pivot to law, “Therefore, Jew”, reminds us that the appeal to pity comes from a disguised woman. The emotion is persuasive and, in the light of the forced conversion that follows, uncomfortable.

Love is conveyed through music. A song is sung while Bassanio considers the caskets, asking, “Tell me where is fancy bred”, and answering that fancy is engendered in the eyes and “dies in the cradle where it lies”. The song gives his choice an emotional pressure the audience can feel, and it suggests that romantic feeling may be fragile. In the last act Lorenzo declares, “The man that hath no music in himself”, implying that music measures a person's feeling, and the moonlit exchanges that follow turn the lovers' passion into a shared, almost ritual register.

Jessica's shame is presented in private. After Launcelot leaves, she speaks alone and admits that she is “ashamed to be my father's child”. The soliloquy lets the audience hear her rejection of home directly rather than through the gossip of the Venetians, and the emotion is confessed before she acts on it.

Taken together, the features of drama make emotion in this play a matter of staging and perspective. Melancholy is left unexplained, grief is reported with mockery, hatred is confided in an aside, mercy is spoken in disguise, shame is confessed alone and love is set to music. The audience is not simply moved by these feelings. It is positioned to see how they are produced, displayed and judged, and that positioning is why the emotions of the prescribed text remain uneasy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it sustains an argument that emotion in the play is staged and perspectival, and each paragraph ties a named feature of drama, such as reported speech, asides, song or the courtroom's pace, to a specific emotion. The reading of Solanio's report and of Portia's mercy speech is precise. To lift it, the final paragraph could address the grief and humiliation Shylock is made to carry directly, rather than summarising the features.

Shakespeare shows many emotions in The Merchant of Venice, and the features of drama help to show them. At the start Antonio is sad and his friends try to find out why. He says he does not know why he is sad, and they think it is because of his ships. This shows that Antonio's sadness is a feeling that cannot easily be explained. The audience has to wait to see what kind of sadness it is, and this is one of the first ways the play makes emotion a matter of mystery.

Shylock also has strong emotions. When Solanio tells how Shylock cried in the street about his daughter and his ducats, the audience hears about his grief. Solanio is making fun of him, which shows that the Venetians do not care about his feelings. This is an example of how emotions can be shown through what other characters say about them.

Shylock's emotions are also shown in the trial, where he is angry. He says that Jews have eyes and hands like Christians and that they should be able to get revenge when they are wronged. This shows his anger and humiliation. He says the villainy he has learnt from the Christians, which tells the audience that he is angry because of how he is treated. The court scene is also fast, and Gratiano keeps calling Portia a learned judge, which shows that the Christians are pleased with the result.

Portia's speech about mercy is very famous. It is a speech about how mercy is better than justice, and the audience can feel this emotion. Portia is disguised as a male lawyer, so the audience knows something that Shylock does not. This is called dramatic irony and it makes the trial more emotional.

Jessica is also emotional. She feels ashamed of her father and says that her house is hell. She speaks alone at the end of a scene and says she is ashamed to be his child. Her feelings are private at this point, which makes them different from the anger Shylock shows in public. This shows how she feels about her family.

The song sung while Bassanio chooses a casket is about love. It says that love begins in the eyes and can die. This suggests that love can be fragile. At the end of the play, the lovers talk under the moon and Lorenzo says that a man with no music in himself cannot be trusted.

Overall, Shakespeare uses drama to show emotions through different techniques. The audience sees the emotions of the characters and can understand how they feel, which makes the play interesting to watch.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies emotions and some features of drama, such as the song and dramatic irony, but it tends to explain what happens rather than analyse how the staging produces the feeling. Its point about Solanio's mockery is a real strength. To lift it, use two or three exact quotations and state, for each, the emotion it produces and the device that produces it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Shakespeare shows emotions in The Merchant of Venice in different ways. Antonio is sad at the start and nobody knows why. Shylock is upset when his daughter runs away and takes his money, and some of the other characters laugh at him. Shylock also gets angry in the court and wants his bond. Jessica is ashamed of her father and runs away dressed as a boy, which shows her feelings about home. Portia makes a speech about mercy which is very emotional. At the end the lovers are happy and talk about music under the moon. Antonio is sad, Shylock is angry and the lovers are happy, and the words of each character show this. The features of drama, like the stage and the characters' words, help to show these emotions. Shakespeare uses drama well to show how people feel, and the audience can tell what each character feels from what they say.

Tim Winton represents emotion in The Boy Behind the Curtain as something to be examined, not merely felt. Through the features of nonfiction, especially the first-person retrospective voice, the linked essays and the citation of other texts, he lets a child’s fear, shame and wonder reach the page, and then has the adult narrator test what those feelings meant. The emotions arising from human experiences in the prescribed text are therefore shown in two registers at once: the immediacy of the moment and the judgement of a later life. The reader is moved, and is also invited to think.

Fear is the first emotion the collection renders with force. In Havoc: A Life in Accidents, Winton’s father, a police officer on a motorbike, is struck by a driver when Winton is about five, and the family’s stable life breaks apart. The dread is physical. The boy seeks out his father’s helmet. Later, at a roadside crash, the narrator recognises that his fear had echoed the dread of that first day. The retrospective voice does not simply report the feeling. It finds the pattern that links one fear to another, so the reader sees a childhood shaped by a single kind of dread.

The same dread returns in In the Shadow of the Hospital, where structure does much of the emotional work. The essay moves across decades, from a child who visits his father in hospital, to an adult who lives beside Fremantle Hospital for five years. The walk through the hospital to his father’s room is a “gauntlet of horrors”, and the hospital remained an image of horror. Feeling, in this essay, is stubborn. It outlasts reason, and the sequence of scenes lets the reader feel it accumulate over a lifetime.

Shame and humour are the subtler emotions, and they appear together in Betsy. The narrator’s grandfather drives an old Hillman Minx that the boy calls Betsy, and the boy is mortified to be seen in it. His friends laugh at their warped reflections in its rounded hubcaps, and the comedy is exact. But the comedy carries feeling, and the adult narrator does not let the child’s verdict stand. He admits that he judged the car too quickly, and he respects her durability, which is rare given what he calls “instant obsolescence”. A memoir allows the older self to revise what the younger one felt, and that revision is itself part of the emotional arc.

Joy and wonder receive a warmer treatment. In The Wait and the Flow, the thrill of riding a wave toward shore never gets old, and Winton keeps surfing until his skin hurts, accepting the pain for the happiness it brings. The essay presents delight as a choice made with full knowledge of its cost. Wonder is registered through the cultural references the book uses. At eight, Winton watches Kubrick’s 2001, which he describes as a “wormhole into the life of the imagination”, and the phrase shows how a film can turn a child’s attention toward a larger inner world.

The Demon Shark shows how feeling is shaped by what a person is shown. A childhood trailer for a documentary about a shark attack unsettles the boy, and by adulthood he has absorbed a public fear that owes more to media and politicians than to experience. The essay also draws on Peter Matthiessen’s account of a shark-filming expedition, and it includes his children’s question about why God made sharks. Its point is that bees kill more people each year yet provoke less fear. The emotion is represented as an inheritance, and the remedy it proposes is familiarity: people who spend time in the water tend to be less afraid of it.

Across these essays, the representation of emotion rests on three features: retrospection, which lets the adult correct the child; structure, which lets feeling accumulate across decades; and citation, which lets a private fear meet a wider record. The reader feels the father’s accident and the hospital corridors, and is also invited to ask whether the feelings were justified. In the prescribed text, then, emotion is a human experience that has been reflected on, not only lived through.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it shows how retrospection, structure and citation shape emotions arising from human experiences, and it follows fear and shame across several essays as the adult narrator revises them. Its strongest move is the contrast between the child's verdict on Betsy and the adult's admission that he judged too quickly. The move that would lift it is to examine the diction or sentence rhythm of one passage, such as the opening of In the Shadow of the Hospital, rather than summarising its sequence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Tim Winton shows emotions in The Boy Behind the Curtain through the way he tells his stories. Because he is writing about his own life, the feelings are his own, and he presents them as a memoir. The features of nonfiction, such as personal memory and a first-person voice, make the reader feel close to him and to the people in his life. The emotions arising from human experiences are personal and easy to recognise.

In the essay Havoc: A Life in Accidents, Winton describes his father being hurt in a motorbike accident. The narrator was scared, and this fear is important in the essay. Later, when the narrator is older, he recognises that he was frightened again at a roadside crash. This shows that fear can come back over time. The helmet his father wore makes the fear concrete.

The essay In the Shadow of the Hospital shows Winton afraid of hospitals again. He remembers visiting his father in hospital when he was a child. The walk through the hospital is frightening, and he calls it a “gauntlet of horrors”. As an adult he still feels uncomfortable in hospitals, even though he knows they are places of care. This shows that emotions can last a long time.

Winton also writes about shame in Betsy. He is embarrassed about his grandfather’s car, and his friends laugh at it. Later he thinks that he judged it too quickly. This is a good example of how memoir allows the author to look back and change his view of what he felt.

Joy appears in The Wait and the Flow, where Winton describes surfing and how happy it makes him. He says the thrill of catching a wave is worth the pain of his skin hurting. This shows the emotions are not always negative.

The Demon Shark shows that Winton thinks people fear sharks for the wrong reasons. He notes that bees kill more people each year but provoke less fear. He also says people who spend time in the water are less afraid. These points use evidence to argue against fear.

The features of nonfiction help Winton represent emotions in the book. The first-person voice makes the feelings personal, and the essays about different times in his life show how emotions change. Through these features the reader understands the human experiences in the book, and the prescribed text becomes a record of feeling.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies the emotions and names the essays, but it explains what Winton feels rather than analysing how the features of nonfiction produce the feeling, and it leans on brief references. Its strength is the observation that the memoir lets the adult revise the child's fear. The move that would lift it is to choose one passage and trace a specific technique, such as the concrete detail of the helmet, through to its emotional effect.

He is also frightened when he visits his father in hospital, and he feels afraid there. Later he feels uncomfortable in hospitals even as an adult. In another essay he is embarrassed about a car called Betsy because his friends make fun of it. He likes surfing and feels happy when he catches a wave, even though it hurts his skin. He also writes about sharks and says people are scared of them. These emotions are part of the human experiences in the book. Winton uses his own life to show these feelings, which is what nonfiction does, so the features of nonfiction help show the emotions.

Yousafzai and Lamb represent the emotions arising from human experiences mainly through the features of nonfiction that a memoir makes possible: a first-person voice, a retrospective view, a chronological shape and a documentary sense of place. The emotions are not announced in the abstract. They are built through particular experiences, from fear on the road to school to grief at the closure of girls' schools, and the reader feels them because the prescribed text places them inside one life. Christina Lamb's background as a journalist also sets Malala's experience within the wider history of Swat, which connects emotion to context rather than leaving it as private feeling.

First-person narration is the most important feature. Because the story is told by Malala, the fear of Taliban rule is felt from the inside. She writes about threats and violence as experienced by a girl who wants to go to school, and the reader is positioned to share her anxiety. The retrospective perspective adds a second emotional layer. The adult narrator looks back on her younger self with a mixture of pride and distance, so the frightened girl is presented with tenderness rather than with pity alone. The memoir thus represents fear as something lived through and understood, not simply reported.

The early sections on Swat use the documentary qualities of nonfiction to build emotion. The ban on girls' schooling, which took effect in Mingora in January 2009, is delivered as historical fact, but it carries the grief of a student watching her school and her classmates' futures close down. Her blog, written under the name Gul Makai for the BBC, gives the reader the immediacy of a diary, and the memoir shows the anxiety of writing while afraid. The mixture of public fact and private feeling allows the book to represent fear and resolve together, which is one of its central emotional arguments.

The attack on 9 October 2012 is the emotional centre of the memoir. The narration moves to a short, vivid account of the bus, the gunman and the shooting, and the prose becomes more immediate. Emotion here is represented through shock and disorientation as much as through reflection. A survivor can report what happened and also admit gaps in what she remembers, and this honesty doubles the emotional effect, since the reader feels both the violence of the event and the uncertainty of its aftermath. Nonfiction gives the account a credibility that makes this scene land with unusual force.

The later sections turn to grief, dependence and recovery. The account of waking in Birmingham, learning to walk again and facing an operation to repair her face gives emotion a bodily dimension. The memoir's description of her parents' distress shows love and fear in their most personal form. The inclusion of the family's own experience, including her mother's difficulty adjusting to life in England, widens the emotional range beyond Malala herself. The features of nonfiction allow the reader to feel the cost of the attack for everyone around her.

Hope is also represented, though not sentimentally. Malala's commitment to education is shown as an emotion as well as a cause: her love of learning, her attachment to her father's school and her wish to return to her studies. The closing sections move outward to education for all children, and the hope feels earned because the reader has already shared the fear and the recovery that precede it.

Christina Lamb's role also shapes how emotion is represented. Her journalistic habit of setting out facts, dates and places tempers the intensity of the personal narrative, so that emotion does not become melodrama. The reader sees the Taliban's rule as a political system and as a set of human experiences, with fear as a response to real events. This restraint is not coldness. It allows anger, sorrow and admiration to register with more force because the authors do not ask for them directly.

Overall, Yousafzai and Lamb represent emotion through features of nonfiction that bind feeling to experience: first-person narration, retrospective reflection, documentary context, and an honest account of injury and recovery. Fear, grief, love and hope are not explained to the reader but felt through particular scenes. The prescribed text is most powerful where it lets the reader watch a frightened girl become a determined one, without pretending that the change was easy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how first-person narration, retrospection and documentary context produce fear, grief and hope, tying each feature to a particular scene. The strongest move is the account of the bus attack and the uncertainty of memory it admits. To lift it further, support the point about documentary context with a closely worded passage from the memoir.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Yousafzai and Lamb represent emotion through the features of nonfiction. The memoir is written in the first person, so the reader sees events through Malala's eyes. This is why the fear of living under the Taliban comes across so strongly. The book describes the ban on girls' schools, and the reader can feel how frustrating and sad this is.

Another feature is the retrospective voice. Malala looks back on her younger self, which lets her show how she felt at the time and how she understands those feelings now. She is not afraid all the time, and this makes her seem more real to the reader. The reader can also see the love of her family, particularly her father, who supports her education and her right to go to school.

The attack on the bus is the most emotional part of the book. The reader learns about the gunman and the shooting, and the shock is clear. The memoir then moves to the hospital in Birmingham, where Malala has to learn to walk again. This shows the physical side of her suffering and her determination to recover, and it makes the reader sympathise with her.

The family's feelings also matter. Her parents are worried about her, and her mother finds life in a new country hard. These experiences show that the attack affected everyone around her, not only Malala. The emotions are therefore spread across the whole family.

The authors also use the prescribed text to show hope. Malala wants to return to school and is committed to education for all children. This hope shows her character and ends the memoir on a positive note. Overall, the authors represent emotions well through these features, and the reader is able to share Malala's fear, sadness and hope.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it names first-person narration and reflection as features of nonfiction and identifies several emotions, but it explains rather than analyses how each feature produces its effect. The first-person point is the strongest, and the answer would move up by testing it against one specific scene, such as the bus attack, and naming the emotion that the feature creates there.

sampleAnswers.answer: Yousafzai and Lamb write a memoir about Malala's life in Swat and her recovery in Birmingham. The book is nonfiction, so it uses real events and tells the reader what happened. Malala was scared of the Taliban and sad that girls could not go to school. When she was shot on the bus, the reader feels shocked. After this her family was worried about her and she had to recover in hospital. The book uses first-person writing, so we know what Malala thinks and feels. The main emotions in the book are fear, sadness and hope. These make the reader feel sorry for her and want her to succeed. The story is told in order, from her childhood in Swat to her time in England, which helps us understand her feelings. So the authors represent emotions through the features of nonfiction, because the story is real and told by Malala herself.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it lists emotions and identifies the book as first-person nonfiction, but it describes events rather than analysing how the authors represent emotion. The lift would come from choosing one feature, such as the first-person narration, and showing how it makes the reader feel the fear of the bus attack.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In the prescribed text, Stephen Daldry represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of film, and rarely through what characters say. Billy Elliot seldom tells the audience what a character feels. Instead, emotion is attached to a space, an object, a sound or a silence, and each of these carries a cost. Shock, anger, grief and joy each have a feature that makes them visible and makes them weigh on the people in the story.

The gym is the film's central space. Billy's father sends him there to learn boxing, but the ballet class meets in the gym because the usual basement studio has become a soup kitchen for the striking miners. The mise-en-scene therefore places two ideas of discipline in one room: the boxing that stands for the family's expectations of masculinity, and the ballet that stands for Billy's own wish.
