sampleAnswers.answer:
The exploration of human experience in The Merchant of Venice invites the audience to reconsider deception, though not in the way its opening suggests. At first deceit seems the property of an outsider. Shylock presents his bond as kindness, insisting “This is kind I offer”, and he proposes the forfeit “in a merry sport”. Bassanio suspects the bond at once, while Antonio accepts it. The play then shows that its Christian characters deceive themselves, one another and the audience just as readily. How far the play asks us to reconsider deception depends on who deceives, why, and at what cost.

Bassanio names the danger in the sharpest phrase of the scene: “fair terms and a villain's mind”. Antonio dismisses the warning, certain that his ships will “come home a month before the day”. His confidence is a self-deception the audience can see coming. When Shylock justifies interest by citing Jacob's flocks, Antonio retorts, “The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose”, and then, “O, what a goodly outside falsehood hath!” These lines accuse Shylock of hiding villainy beneath religion, yet the play's Christians will later speak of mercy while attaching conditions that make it coercive.

The Belmont caskets extend this suspicion to the whole society. Bassanio, who comes after the gold and silver caskets have caught the wrong suitors, chooses the plain lead and concludes that “The world is still deceived with ornament”. He widens the claim to law and religion, where a plea “so tainted and corrupt” can be made acceptable by “a gracious voice”. In this speech deception is not a Jewish trait but a common practice of the age, and the line “The seeming truth which cunning times put on” asks which Venetian is not implicated.

Portia's disguise is the play's most deliberate deception, and the question is whether its ends excuse it. She enters the court as Balthazar, a doctor of law, while Nerissa poses as a clerk, and she wins by a technicality: the bond grants a pound of flesh but “no jot of blood”. Gratiano's cry, “O upright judge!”, voices the Christians' triumph. The audience knows Portia's identity and Shylock does not, so the trial runs on dramatic irony, and the audience is asked to admire the wit while noticing that the law turns against the man who holds it. The sentence then requires that Shylock “presently become a Christian”. The mercy the play praises is therefore conditional, and Portia's great speech, “The quality of mercy is not strain'd”, is itself delivered in disguise, which makes the praise of mercy a performance as much as an appeal.

Shylock's reply is what most directly reconsiders the question. Defending his humanity, he asks, “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, lists the senses and passions Jews share with Christians, and argues that wrong demands revenge. His climax is that “The villainy you teach me I will execute”. Deception here is taught and returned. The play does not excuse Shylock's cruelty, but a reader who condemns his bond as deceit must ask whether the Christian example he learns from is any more honest, and why the Christians' own deceits end in marriage and laughter.

Jessica's deception of her father is treated with more sympathy, which exposes a double standard in the play. Her verdict on her father's household is “Our house is hell”, and she leaves in boy's clothes, carrying away his ducats and jewels. She knows the disguise is shameful, admitting, “I am much ashamed of my exchange”. In the final act, however, she recalls Lorenzo's “many vows of faith” and adds that they were “ne'er a true one”. The vows that justified her flight may themselves be deceptions, so the audience must weigh a daughter's escape from cruelty against the faithlessness of the romance that rewards it.

The final ring test is the play's last exercise in deception. Portia feigns anger that Bassanio has given away her ring, and Bassanio admits the loss rather than lie, saying that if he could “add a lie unto a fault” he would deny it. Portia replies that “void is your false heart of truth”. The accusation is part of her own staged trick, so the most accomplished deceiver in the play calls the honest man false. The reversal shows how readily deception is assigned to others, and it asks whether Portia's disguise belongs in the same category as the fault she imputes to Bassanio.

The play therefore invites a substantial reconsideration of deception, though not a complete one. It refuses to make deceit the trait of one religion or one outsider. Commerce, law, love and religion are each built on appearances, and the audience is asked to judge a deception by its motive and its cost rather than by its form. The comedy of the final act, in which the rings return and the lovers are reconciled, does not erase the cruelty of the trial. That unresolved tension is what makes the play's view of deception more complicated than its opening suggests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates how far the play invites reconsideration, sustains a thesis across the paragraphs and supports each claim with precise references to the bond, the caskets, the trial and the ring test. The strongest move is linking Shylock's taught villainy to the Christians' own deceptions. To lift it, the final paragraph could weigh more carefully where the play itself rewards deception, such as Portia's disguise or Jessica's flight.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Merchant of Venice shows deception in several places, and the question asks whether this changes how the audience understands it. At the start Shylock makes a bond with Antonio and calls it a merry sport. If Antonio cannot repay the money, Shylock may take a pound of his flesh. Bassanio can see that the terms are fair in appearance but wicked. Antonio does not think the bond will be enforced because he expects his ships to come home, so he does not see the danger he is in. This shows that appearances can mislead, and it suggests that Shylock is not the only person who deceives.

At Belmont the caskets also test deception. The gold and silver caskets look more valuable than the lead, but they hold the wrong answers, and Bassanio chooses the plain lead. He says that the world is still deceived with ornament. This means that things which look good are not always good. The play then links this idea to law and religion, so that a person can seem good when he is not.

Portia disguises herself as Balthazar, a lawyer, and saves Antonio. She says the bond gives Shylock a pound of flesh but no jot of blood, so he cannot take any blood, and this trick works. Shylock loses his case. The Duke pardons his life, and Antonio asks that he become a Christian. Portia also makes a speech about mercy, which the audience may think is the moral point of the trial. Mercy is shown as better than justice, so the trial appears to end well.

Shylock argues that Jews have eyes and hands like Christians. He says that if Christians wrong Jews, they will take revenge, and that the villainy he has been taught he will carry out. This shows that deception can be learned. Jessica also deceives her father by running away with Lorenzo and taking his money. She feels ashamed of her disguise but still does it.

At the end, Portia tests Bassanio about the ring. She pretends to be angry that he gave it away. Bassanio tells her the truth, that he gave it to the lawyer. Portia then calls him false, even though she has been deceiving him. This shows that deception appears in many forms in the play, from the trial to the romance.

Overall, the play invites the audience to reconsider deception because many characters use false appearances. Some of their deceptions are presented as clever or necessary, and the reader must decide whether they are acceptable. The play's view of deception is therefore more complicated than the opening suggests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the play's deceptions in sequence and gives some relevant references, but it tends to retell the plot rather than argue about it. Its best point is that Portia accuses the honest Bassanio of falseness while deceiving him. To lift it, use precise quotations and make each paragraph test a single claim about whether a deception is justified.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Merchant of Venice has a lot of deception in it. Shylock makes a bond with Antonio, and if Antonio does not pay the money back Shylock can take a pound of his flesh. Antonio thinks the bond is kind but Bassanio is not sure about it. Antonio is worried about his ships and Shylock is angry about his money, so both of them have reasons to hide what they feel. Bassanio goes to Belmont to choose a casket to marry Portia and he picks the lead one because the others look better. Portia dresses up as a lawyer and wins the case for Antonio, and Shylock has to become a Christian. Jessica also runs away from her father and takes his money. Shylock is treated badly by the Christians but he is cruel too. At the end Portia tests Bassanio with a ring and everyone is happy. This shows that deception is a big part of the play, and people should think about whether it is right or wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the bond, the caskets and the trial in order, with no quotations and little sense of how the play handles deception. Its closing question about right and wrong is a real attempt at the topic. To lift it, choose one deception, quote the words that reveal it, and explain what the play asks the audience to think about it.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in The Boy Behind the Curtain invite you to reconsider your understanding of independence?
markerNotes: The stem asks how far the book invites reconsideration, so the strongest answers take a position on the extent and qualify it, rather than listing what Winton is independent of.

The brake scene in Havoc: A Life in Accidents is the best evidence that a child's competence can be borrowed from a parent. Answers that see the father's teaching in it are stronger than those that read it only as bravery.
Twice on Sundays and The Wait and the Flow show independence as a choice made within a community. This lets strong answers avoid reading the book as a celebration of the lone individual.
Winton's adult revision of his verdict on Betsy is the book reconsidering its own judgements. An answer that finds this in the text has the reconsideration the question asks for.
commonStudentErrors: Treating independence only as being alone or self-sufficient, and never testing that idea against the church, family or surfing episodes.
Retelling the father's accident in Havoc: A Life in Accidents without asking what the brake scene shows about where Winton's competence comes from.
Presenting Winton's leaving of the church as simple heroism and ignoring the essay's ambivalence about the community he leaves.
Quoting remembered lines as exact wording instead of describing the scene and the technique precisely.

sampleAnswers.answer:
To a considerable extent, The Boy Behind the Curtain invites the reader to reconsider independence. The ordinary meaning of the word is self-reliance: standing alone, making one’s own choices and needing nobody. Tim Winton’s linked essays keep returning to people who are shaped by others. They inherit their competence from a father, a congregation and a sport, and they find that independence has to be practised again and again. The book does not abandon the value of independent judgement. It shows that judgement is formed in relationships and tested by experience, and that an independent mind is one willing to revise its own verdicts. The exploration of human experience in the collection therefore offers a different idea of independence, one that does not depend on the absence of other people.

The first challenge to a simple idea of independence comes in Havoc: A Life in Accidents. When Winton is about five, his father, a police officer on a motorbike, is struck by a driver and nearly killed. Winton takes on more responsibility at home. He understands what is happening while his mother struggles, and he helps her. Years later the essay shows where his capacity to act in a crisis comes from. At a roadside crash, his father kneels beside a motionless rider, drags the bike off the road and has his son keep pumping the brake so that the ambulance can spot the lights. The boy is given a real job, but the competence was taught to him. As an adult, Winton has a child press a brake at a crash, as his father once taught him. Independence, in this essay, is a skill handed down rather than a self-made virtue.

Twice on Sundays shows independence as a social act. The family’s church sets them apart, and the policeman father has enough standing in the neighbourhood that children who would rather be at the beach partly come to his Sunday school. The church gives the boy his love of language and story. When he questions scripture and the elders, he is called “obtuse”, a “stumbling-block” and a “wayward son”. He leaves slowly and quietly. The decision is his own, but it is not a clean break. He still values the liturgy, is unsure what kind of believer he is. Independence here means judging for oneself without cutting off the people who taught one to judge.

In The Wait and the Flow, the solitary pursuit of surfing turns out to be communal. Winton first rides a wave at about five, pushed out by his cousins, and his skill grows inside a network of people. When surf culture in the 1980s becomes marked by aggression and machismo, he takes up snorkelling and diving instead. He misses the water and returns only after moving to a smaller town, where he finds a gentler group of surfers. The sport teaches patience, which the essay links to writing: a writer must be ready when an idea arrives and then follow it through. Independence, read this way, is not control. It is readiness, and the freedom to choose one’s company.

The book’s most pointed act of reconsideration concerns its own verdicts. In Betsy, the narrator’s grandfather drives an old Hillman Minx that the boy calls Betsy, and the boy is ashamed to be seen in a car that offers no glamour at all. His friends laugh at their warped reflections in its hubcaps. Years later, though, the adult admits that he judged the car too quickly. She outlasted several eras, and her durability, set against what he calls “instant obsolescence”, is something he now respects. That is the reconsideration the question asks for, performed within the text itself.

Dependence is the book’s counterweight, and the essay In the Shadow of the Hospital makes it physical. At eighteen, Winton wakes in a hospital bed with glass in his hair and no memory of the crash, and he learns that being a patient is much worse than visiting one. As a child he had walked through the hospital to his father’s room, a walk he calls a “gauntlet of horrors”. Later in the essay his father shows him a new pacemaker. Winton reflects that a few decades earlier his father probably would not have survived, but instead went home the day after the procedure. Modern care makes that survival possible, and it reminds the reader that independence has always depended on other people.

To a considerable extent, then, the book unsettles independence as self-sufficiency and replaces it with something harder to achieve. The Winton of these essays is taught, supported and sometimes frightened, yet he still judges for himself and returns to a question when experience changes his mind. The reader comes away less certain that independence is a possession, and more aware that it is a practice that needs other people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it takes a clear position on how far the book invites reconsideration of independence and sustains it through the Havoc, church, surfing and Betsy essays. Its strongest move is turning the boy's borrowed brake-pressing into evidence that competence is inherited. To lift it further, the surfing paragraph could test the idea of community more directly against Winton's own choices.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Boy Behind the Curtain makes the reader think about independence in a different way from the usual meaning. Independence usually means being able to do things alone and not needing other people. Winton’s book shows that a person’s independence is shaped by family, church and events they cannot control.

In the essay Havoc: A Life in Accidents, Winton’s father is hit by a car when Winton is young. The father is a police officer and was riding a motorbike. He nearly dies and comes home changed. Winton takes on more responsibility at home, and this makes him grow up faster than other children. The reader can see that independence can be forced on a child by hard events rather than chosen.

Later in the same essay, Winton and his father come across a crash on the road. His father tells him to keep pressing the brake so the ambulance can find them. Winton does this, which shows he has learned something from his father. The reader might think this is independence, but it comes from his father’s teaching, so it is not entirely his own.

The essay Twice on Sundays is about Winton’s family church. The family goes to church twice on Sundays, and they gather the neighbourhood children for Sunday school. The children do not really want to go, but some go partly because Winton’s father is a police officer. Winton grows up in this church and learns about the Bible and stories. When he gets older he starts to question the church, and the church members call him names. He leaves the church. This is a sign of independence because he made his own choice to leave. However, he still likes some parts of the church, so he is not completely separate from it.

The Wait and the Flow is about surfing. Winton started surfing when he was five, with help from his cousins. Surfing involves waiting for waves, which is a kind of patience. He stopped surfing for a while because the surf culture became unpleasant, but he came back when he found friendlier surfers. This shows that independence can be connected to a group of people.

Winton also writes about Betsy, his grandfather’s old car. He was embarrassed by it as a child, but later he judged it too quickly. This shows that he changed his mind as an adult. So the book suggests that views can change over time, and that thinking independently includes reconsidering your opinions.

Overall, the book makes the reader reconsider independence. It is not only about being alone. Winton shows that independence depends on family, community and experience, and that it can also mean changing your mind.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how family, church and surfing shape independence, but it mostly describes the essays and does not analyse how the writing makes the reader reconsider. Its strength is the link between the borrowed brake-pressing and the idea that independence is inherited. The move that would lift it is to analyse one essay in depth, showing how a specific technique, such as the adult's correction in Betsy, changes what the reader thinks.

sampleAnswers.answer: In The Boy Behind the Curtain, Tim Winton writes about his life. In one essay his father has a bad accident on a motorbike, and Winton has to help his mother, so he grows up quickly. As an adult, he finds a crashed car on a road and gets a child to press the brake. Winton also goes to church with his family and later he leaves it because he questions what they believe. He likes surfing, and he started when he was five with his cousins. In another essay he is embarrassed by an old car called Betsy, but at the end he says he was wrong about it. In the hospital essay he ends up as a patient himself after a crash. The book makes the reader think about independence, because Winton has to act alone at times but still depends on his family and other people. So the book shows that independence is not just being alone, and that Winton needs other people even when he is on his own.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes events from several essays with little reference to the question or to the text's language. Its strength is the basic point that Winton relies on family and community. The move that would lift it is to take one episode, quote a phrase from it and explain what it shows about independence.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in I am Malala invite you to reconsider your understanding of strength?
markerNotes: The stem asks for an evaluation of the extent to which the memoir reconsiders strength, so the strongest answers take a position and then test it. Saying the book 'shows strength' without judging how far it changes a reader's view stays in the 9-12 row.

Strong answers treat the Taliban's power as a version of strength to be tested, not as the default meaning. The attack on the bus is most useful when read as the Taliban's own display of force, and then questioned.

The best evidence is the pseudonym and the fear the memoir admits. Answers that link these two points show that courage in this text is acting while afraid, which is the reconsideration the question asks for.

Top answers recognise the limits of the reconsideration. The memoir still centres one exceptional girl, and a sophisticated answer says so rather than claiming the book wholly overturns the heroic model.
commonStudentErrors: Treating strength as only physical or moral toughness, without testing whether the memoir presents that idea as adequate.
Retelling the attack and the hospital stay in order, without connecting either to the question of what strength means.
Claiming Malala is fearless, which the memoir does not support and which leaves the question of vulnerability unanswered.
Describing the Taliban as simply cruel, without showing how their idea of strength depends on intimidation and silence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
To a considerable extent, I Am Malala invites you to reconsider your understanding of strength. Most readers begin with familiar ideas: strength as physical power, as the ability to impose your will on others, or as the capacity to endure without showing fear. The memoir, written with the journalist Christina Lamb, tests each of these assumptions. The Taliban's control of the Swat Valley rests on force and intimidation, and the book asks the reader to see that kind of power as dependent on other people's silence. Malala's own strength is a moral and intellectual courage, the willingness to keep speaking and learning when silence is demanded. The memoir does not present her as fearless, however, and it complicates strength further by showing how much of it is shared, sustained and rebuilt rather than simply possessed.

The early sections establish the Taliban's version of strength. In Mingora the militants closed girls' schools, and from January 2009 girls were no longer allowed to attend school in the town. Their authority is maintained through threats and punishment rather than consent. The most striking demonstration of this is the attack of 9 October 2012, when a gunman boarded the school bus, singled out Malala and shot her. The attack is the ultimate display of force, and its purpose was to silence a fifteen-year-old girl. Yet the memoir exists because she survived, and her account of that day turns the gunman's act into evidence against his own idea of strength.

Malala's resistance began in writing. From January 2009 she wrote for the BBC Urdu blog under the pseudonym Gul Makai, describing life under Taliban rule. The choice of a pseudonym matters. It shows that she understood the danger of speaking openly and chose to speak anyway, which is a more complicated form of strength than open defiance. The memoir invites the reader to see her courage as a combination of fear and action. She was not free of fear, but fear did not decide what she wrote or what she believed about girls' education. The first way the book reconsiders strength is therefore by locating it in persistence and speech rather than in dominance.

This leads to the second part of the question, the exploration of human experience. The memoir gives considerable space to fear: fear of the threats that surrounded the girls who went to school, fear for her family, and fear of what the valley had become. Rather than treating these feelings as a failure of strength, the memoir presents them as an ordinary human response to violence. This matters because it moves strength away from the heroic ideal of invulnerability. Courage is not the absence of fear but a decision made in its presence, and the book shows that decision being made by an ordinary schoolgirl rather than by a superhuman figure.

Strength in the memoir is also collective. Malala's father, Ziauddin, is an educator who runs a school in Mingora, and his commitment to learning shaped her own. The reader sees that her conviction about education was formed in a home where learning was valued and where resistance to intimidation had an example to follow. This complicates the picture of the lone hero. Her strength is drawn from the people around her, and the memoir's attention to her parents' love and worry shows that strength and vulnerability often sit together. A reader who expects strength to look like invulnerability finds instead a frightened family and a girl who draws courage from it.

The later sections, which follow the attack and her treatment in Birmingham, extend the idea of strength into endurance. Recovery is slow. The memoir describes learning to walk again and an operation to repair her face, far from home and in a country whose language and customs were unfamiliar to her. Here strength is a patient, daily discipline rather than a dramatic gesture. The attention to physical and emotional recovery shows that surviving is itself a form of strength, one that is rarely celebrated in the way that defiance is.

The reconsideration is not complete, however. The memoir is ultimately the story of an exceptional individual, and some readers may still find in it the familiar heroic model in which one brave girl stands for everyone. The book's wider attention to Swat's history and to girls' education as a right corrects this to some degree, but its focus on Malala's own survival keeps the older idea of strength as individual endurance in place. A reader is therefore invited to hold two views at once: strength as a visible act of courage, and strength as a shared and uncertain experience that many people undergo without public recognition.

Overall, the memoir reconsiders strength to a considerable extent. It moves the idea away from force and invulnerability towards courage that coexists with fear, persistence in speech and learning, and the support of family and community. The closing sections turn the story outward to education as a cause, which suggests that strength is most useful when it is directed at others. Malala's account implies that strength is most convincing when it admits weakness, and that a power which relies on silence is undone by the decision to keep speaking, even at great risk.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates to a considerable extent, tests the Taliban's idea of power against Malala's courage, and admits the limits of its own reconsideration. The strongest move is linking the pseudonym to the claim that courage means acting while afraid. To lift it further, replace some of the description of the attack and recovery with precise, closely worded references to the memoir.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The memoir I Am Malala changes how a reader might think about strength, though it does so in stages. At first strength seems to mean the power the Taliban hold in Swat. They close girls' schools and use violence to make people obey, and Malala describes this threat. The attack on her school bus in October 2012 shows how far they are prepared to go. This is a kind of strength, but the book shows that it rests on fear.

Malala's own strength is different. She writes a blog for the BBC under the name Gul Makai, so that she can speak out without being identified. This takes courage, and it shows she is not afraid to say what she believes about education. The book also shows that she is afraid, so strength does not mean having no fear. Her father is important as well, because he runs a school and supports her education. This suggests that strength can come from family.

After the attack Malala is taken to hospital in Birmingham. The memoir describes her recovery, including learning to walk again, and this shows another kind of strength, the strength to keep going while she is healing. She is far from home and this is difficult for her. Strength in this section is less dramatic and more about patience.

The memoir also deals with human experience more widely, including the feelings of her family and of the people who lived in the valley. These feelings show that many people were frightened, and that Malala's courage was one response among many. A reader can see that the book is not only about one girl.

Overall, the memoir does change the reader's understanding of strength. It shows that strength is about courage, speaking up and family support, not just physical power. It also shows that strength is connected to vulnerability. Readers might still think of strength as heroism, but the book suggests that ordinary people can also be strong when they face fear.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how the memoir complicates strength, but it moves through events by summary and offers few textual references. The pseudonym is the best point, and the answer would move up by using it to test the Taliban's idea of power more closely, rather than adding retelling of the hospital stay.

sampleAnswers.answer: Malala Yousafzai is a girl from Pakistan who was shot by the Taliban in 2012. In I Am Malala she writes about her life in Swat, where the Taliban stopped girls from going to school. Her father ran a school and she wanted to learn. The Taliban attacked her school bus, and she was taken to hospital in Birmingham, England, where she was treated. The book shows that she was brave and that she did not give up when people tried to stop her. She keeps speaking out about education, even after the attack. The story is about a girl who wanted to go to school and what happened to her afterwards. Reading it, I think strength is also about carrying on with school, even when it is frightening. So the book changes how we think about strength, because it shows a girl who was not frightened into silence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the attack and the hospital stay in order, makes general claims about strength, and refers to the text very little. The lift would come from naming one moment, such as the pseudonym, and explaining what it shows about strength, supported by a detail from the memoir.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Billy Elliot invite you to reconsider your understanding of commitment?
markerNotes: The stem asks 'to what extent', so the strongest answers say how far the film reconsiders commitment and where it stops short. An answer that declares the film overturns the idea is usually making a claim it cannot sustain.

The picket-line scene, where Tony stops Jackie from crossing, is the most useful episode for this question because it puts two kinds of commitment in direct conflict. Answers that build the argument around it, rather than mentioning it in passing, separate themselves.
Mrs Wilkinson shows commitment as attention to one person rather than loyalty to a group. A strong answer uses her to show what the other characters' commitments are actually made of.

Billy's answer about electricity at the audition is the best evidence that some commitments cannot be put into words. Use it to explain the gap between feeling a commitment and being able to describe it.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the audition and the closing flash-forward in order without asking what either shows about commitment.
Calling the strike simply admirable, or simply futile, and missing that the film gives its loyalty dignity while also showing what it costs Billy.
Presenting Jackie as a villain who changes all at once, rather than tracing his shift from enforcing a family code to backing Billy's dream.
Describing the closing performance as a happy ending without explaining how it rewards the commitments made by the family and the community.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The exploration of human experience in Billy Elliot does invite a considerable reconsideration of commitment, though not a complete one. The conventional view treats commitment as fidelity: holding to a cause, a community or a family tradition whatever it costs. Stephen Daldry does not reject that view. The miners' loyalty to the strike is shown with dignity, but the film also shows that commitment to one person or one dream can require a person to break faith with their group. Through the Elliot family, Mrs Wilkinson and Billy, commitment is tested, revised and paid for by people other than the one who commits.

The strike is the film's first and most public picture of commitment. Set in County Durham during the 1984–85 miners' strike, it shows Jackie Elliot and his son Tony both out on strike, and Tony is the union delegate, so his loyalty is institutional as well as personal. Daldry gives this loyalty weight: the community's sense of being discarded is the film's social argument. Yet the strike has a direct cost for Billy. Tony is arrested in a clash between police and striking miners, and Billy misses the Royal Ballet School audition as a result. Commitment to a collective cause can take a boy's future away without anyone intending it.

Jackie's commitment is the film's most sustained test. At first it takes the form of a masculine code: he sends Billy to the gym to learn boxing, and when he discovers the ballet lessons he forbids them. His protectiveness is real, but it is also loyalty to an image of what his family should be. The turn comes when he catches Billy and Michael dancing in the gym and sees how serious his son is. When Mrs Wilkinson tries to persuade him to let her pay for the audition, Jackie refuses, saying Billy is his son and does not need charity. The refusal is pride, but it is also a commitment: he will be the one who pays.

The sharpest collision comes when Jackie tries to cross the picket line to pay for the London trip, and Tony stops him. A brother's loyalty to the strike physically blocks a father's loyalty to his son. Neither man is simply wrong. Tony's commitment is real, and so is Jackie's desperation, and the two men each believe they are doing right by the family. The resolution comes from the community. The miners and the neighbourhood raise some money, so the solidarity of the strike is turned towards one boy's future. Jackie pawns Billy's mother's jewellery to cover the rest, spending a memory of his dead wife on his son's future.

Mrs Wilkinson's commitment is of a different kind. She is a weary teacher who keeps working with a boy who wandered into her class, believes he is talented enough for the Royal Ballet School, and tells Jackie about the missed audition. Her loyalty is to a pupil's talent rather than to a community or a family. The miners' solidarity and Jackie's code come to them through the town and the household, whereas hers is a choice made about one boy.

Billy's own commitment is the most absolute, and the film asks us to see what it costs. He goes on dancing after he has been forbidden to, and at the London audition his frustration boils over: he punches another boy and fears he has ruined his chances. When the panel asks what dancing feels like, he struggles for words and says it is "like electricity". Commitment to an art is rarely fluent, and the film lets the audience feel the gap between feeling and explanation. The commitment also takes him away: the acceptance letter arrives in 1985, when the strike ends, and Billy leaves home for London.

The closing flash-forward complicates the picture again. In 1998, Billy, now twenty-five, dances as the Swan in Matthew Bourne's Swan Lake, with Jackie, Tony and Michael in the audience, and Jackie is overcome with astonishment and pride. The ending rewards the father's change of heart, but it also shows that Billy's achievement was paid for by his family and community. The film does not present his departure as a betrayal of home. It presents it as the thing the home had worked for.

To a considerable extent, then, the film invites reconsideration. It shows commitment as something revised under pressure, paid for by people other than the one who commits, and often in conflict with loyalties that are genuinely admirable. What it does not do is condemn the strike or the community's solidarity. The reconsideration is therefore a widening of commitment rather than a rejection of it. The strongest commitment in the film can change direction without ceasing to be a commitment to people, and a viewer who expects commitment to mean holding one line will leave with a more complicated and more generous understanding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it treats commitment as tested and revised across the strike, the father, the teacher and Billy, and each claim is tied to a specific episode. Its strength is the picket-line scene, read as a direct collision of two commitments. The move that would lift it is to test the reconsideration against Tony's position more fully, so the argument does not rest on the father alone.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Billy Elliot shows commitment through its characters, and I think it does make the audience think about commitment in a different way. At the start, Billy's dad sends him to the gym to learn boxing, which is what a miner's son is expected to do. Billy is pulled into the ballet class by curiosity rather than by any plan. He doesn't like boxing, and he ends up joining a ballet class that is using the gym because the usual studio is being used as a soup kitchen for the striking miners. When his dad finds out, he forbids the classes, but Billy carries on in secret. His teacher, Mrs Wilkinson, thinks he is good enough to get into the Royal Ballet School.

There are several kinds of commitment in the film. The miners are committed to the strike, and Tony is committed enough to be arrested in a clash with the police. Because of that, Billy misses his audition. This shows that commitment to a cause can affect other people. Jackie is committed too, but his commitment is to his family in a traditional way. He is angry at first, but later he changes his mind after he catches Billy and Michael dancing in the gym. He also tries to cross the picket line to get money for the trip to London, but Tony stops him. This shows the two commitments clashing. The film also has Michael, Billy's best friend, who is gay, and Billy is supportive of him, so there is another kind of loyalty between friends.

Billy's commitment is the most obvious one. He works hard at dance, and at the audition he gets frustrated and punches another boy, which makes him think he has ruined his chances. When he is asked what dancing feels like he can't explain it, and he says it is like electricity. This shows that some commitments are hard to put into words. His commitment is also a kind of rebellion, because his dad has forbidden the lessons.

At the end, Billy is a professional dancer and his dad is proud of him. So the film seems to say that commitment to your own dream is right, even if it costs your family something. The letter from the Royal Ballet School comes in 1985, around the time the strike ends, so the film links the two endings. This makes the audience reconsider what commitment means, although the film doesn't really make the miners look wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains what each character does and what it shows, but it asserts its points rather than analysing how the film makes them. Its strength is the clear link between the picket-line scene and the clash of commitments. The move that would lift it is to choose one moment, such as the audition, and show how the film's handling of it shapes what the audience feels about commitment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Billy Elliot is about a boy who wants to be a ballet dancer. Billy is only eleven when the story starts, and his mum has died, so the family is short of money. His dad wants him to do boxing, but Billy goes to the ballet class instead, and his dad is angry about it. Billy's brother Tony is on strike with the other miners and gets arrested. Billy has a teacher called Mrs Wilkinson who helps him, and in the end he gets to go to London for an audition. Later his dad changes his mind after seeing him dance, and the miners and the neighbours raise money so Billy can go. The film shows commitment because Billy is committed to dancing and his dad changes his mind. At the end Billy is a dancer and his family is in the audience watching him, so the film is saying that commitment pays off in the end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the plot and asserts that commitment pays off without analysing any scene. Its strength is an accurate outline of Billy's path from boxing to London. The move that would lift it is to choose one scene and say what it shows about commitment.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Go Back to Where You Came From invite you to reconsider your understanding of fear?
markerNotes: The stem asks about fear, so the strongest answers ask which fear is at stake: the participants' fear of asylum seekers, or the fear the refugees carry through the journey. An answer that treats fear as one emotion rarely reaches the top band.

Reconsider is the operative word. Look for evidence that the viewer's understanding changes, not only that the participants feel afraid. The best answers track a shift from the starting views to what the journey does to them.

Close reference to the prescribed episodes matters more than a summary of the route. The boat crossing, the Malaysian raid, the camp in Kenya and the final episode in Goma and Baghdad are most useful when each is tied to what it shows about fear.

The Response is where focus is most easily lost. Use it to test the reconsideration: ask what happens to fear when the most frightening moments are replayed for a studio audience, rather than recapping the series.
commonStudentErrors: Treating fear as a single emotion, so the answer never separates the participants' fear from the fear of the refugees they meet.
Retelling the journey stop by stop, from a boat to Baghdad, without asking what each stop shows about fear.
Assuming the series simply changes the participants' minds, without assessing how far the format, the voice-over and the studio framing shape what the viewer is asked to feel.
Describing The Response as a summary of the series rather than as a studio program that replays its most confronting moments.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Go Back to Where You Came From, directed by Ivan O’Mahoney for SBS, takes a group of Australians with firm views on asylum policy along the route refugees take to reach Australia, but in reverse. The participants have no money, phones or identification. The prescribed episodes, Series 1 Episodes 1, 2 and 3 and The Response, move them from a boat crossing that ends in a rescue at sea, through Malaysia and Kenya, to Jordan and then to Goma and Baghdad. The series does invite a real reconsideration of fear, because it moves fear out of the public debate about boats and strangers and into the bodies and daily lives of the people who feel it, and it explores human experience at close range. But the reconsideration has limits. The television frame, the voice-over and the studio program that follows all shape what fear the viewer is asked to understand, so the series changes how fear is understood more than it shows what fear is like for the people who live with it.

The starting point matters. Each participant is introduced in the first episode with some background and a stated view on asylum seekers, and the premise is built to test those views. The fear the participants bring is, in the terms of the premise, a fear of the stranger on the boat, the figure the debate has made into a threat. The series asks the viewer to examine that fear as something learnt rather than observed. The participants have never been in the position they imagine, and the first episode makes that gap visible. The political and geographic background supplied by the narrator, Colin Friels, frames each view as a position that can be tested rather than a settled fact about the world.

Fear becomes physical once the boat crossing ends in a rescue at sea. Malaysia extends it. The participants live with refugees and then witness a raid, so the fear shifts from the boat to the constant possibility of being found and taken, with no papers to show anyone who asks. Here the series shows fear as powerlessness: the lack of documents and money removes the ordinary means of control. Kenya and Jordan show a different fear, fear as a long condition rather than a sudden event. The camp in Kenya is one of the world's biggest refugee camps, where daily survival is the struggle, and the slums in Jordan show that fear is not only about persecution but about having nothing that makes the future predictable. The final episode, in Goma and Baghdad, takes the participants into places of open violence, where they are protected by UN peacekeepers and the United States military. That protection is revealing. It shows that safety is itself organised and conditional, and that the people who need it most do not share the same access to it.

The hosts are the strongest counterweight to fear in the series. Former refugees now living in Australia answer the participants' questions about why they live here and how they arrived, and the participants question them directly in interviews. This turns fear from a statement about a group into a conversation with particular people, each with a history. The series also intercuts direct experience with expert opinion, so the emotional encounter is set beside an explanation of why the conditions exist. That combination asks the viewer to feel and to understand at once, which is the clearest evidence that the series wants fear reconsidered rather than simply intensified.

The limits of this reconsideration must be weighed honestly. The participants' fear is always bounded. They are taking part in a fixed challenge, they know they are being filmed, and the series ends. The refugees they meet cannot leave their situation in the same way, and the fears that come with that situation, such as being sent back or losing family, can only be observed by the viewer, not lived by the participants. The series can show the conditions that produce fear, but a televised challenge can only approximate those conditions.

The Response, the studio follow-up held in June 2011 before an audience of families, friends, refugees and advocates, returns to the most extreme moments as a highlights package and asks the participants to comment on the public reaction. The format risks turning fear back into spectacle, since the frightening moments are replayed for an audience that already holds a view. Yet it also acknowledges that the fear the series produced belongs to a wider public, not only to the people on the journey. The participants must account for what the journey has done to their views in front of the people they met, which is the series' most direct test of its own reconsideration.

The series invites a substantial reconsideration of fear, especially the idea that fear is produced by powerlessness, uncertainty and the loss of documents, money and home, rather than being a simple reaction to strangers. The extent is limited, however. The television frame keeps fear inside a structure the viewer can leave, and the most intense fear, that of refugees who cannot leave, is something the series can witness but not reproduce. The viewer finishes with a more precise understanding of fear, though not a complete one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates the extent of the reconsideration rather than only describing the journey, and it separates the participants' fear from the fear that the refugees carry. The references to the boat, the Malaysian raid, the camp in Kenya and the final episode are well chosen. To lift it further, the final paragraph could weigh the studio follow-up more closely against the claim that the series changes what the viewer understands.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Go Back to Where You Came From is a documentary series in which Australians with views on asylum policy follow the route refugees take, but in reverse. The participants have no money, phones or identification. In the prescribed episodes they move from a boat crossing that ends in a rescue at sea, through Malaysia and Kenya, to Jordan, and then to Goma and Baghdad. The question asks to what extent the series invites a reconsideration of fear, and the series does make the viewer think about fear in several ways.

At the start, the participants bring their own views about asylum seekers, and the series introduces them early in the first episode. When the boat is rescued at sea, the fear is physical and sudden. In Malaysia the participants live with refugees and then see a raid, so the fear becomes the fear of being found. This shows that fear is linked to having no papers. In Kenya the camp is one of the largest refugee camps and survival is hard every day. Jordan shows the slums. The final episode is set in Goma and Baghdad, where the participants are protected by UN peacekeepers and the United States military. This shows that fear is a long condition as well as a single event.

The hosts are also important. They are former refugees who now live in Australia, and they answer the participants' questions about why they live here. The participants ask them questions in interviews. The narrator, Colin Friels, gives political and geographic background in a voice-over, which helps the viewer understand where the fear comes from. Direct experience is cut together with expert opinion, which helps explain the conditions.

The Response is the studio program that follows the series. There is an audience of families, friends, refugees and advocates, and the participants respond to highlights of the most extreme moments and comment on the public response. This shows the fear again, to a different audience.

The series changes how fear is understood to some extent. The participants start with fear of asylum seekers, and by the end they have seen the fear that refugees carry. However, the participants know the challenge will end, and the refugees cannot leave their situation in the same way. For this reason the series does not fully show what their fear is like, so the reconsideration of fear is real but limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the journey and the participants' fear competently, but it describes the stops in order rather than analysing what each reveals about fear. References are fewer and thinner, mostly the hosts and the narrator, and the conclusion repeats the thesis without testing it. To lift it, choose one stop, such as the boat or the camp, and explain how that scene changes what fear means for the viewer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Go Back to Where You Came From is a series about refugees. Some Australians go on the journey refugees take, but in reverse. They have no money, phones or ID. In the first episode they get on a boat and are rescued at sea. In Malaysia they meet refugees and see a raid. In Kenya there is a camp, and in Jordan there are slums. The last episode is in Goma and Baghdad. Fear runs through many of these places, and the show makes the viewer think about fear. The Response is a studio program where people talk about the series. The people in the series are afraid because they have no papers and no money. This is a reconsideration of fear because the participants learn something about it, but it is not clear how much they change their minds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the journey stop by stop and names fear without developing an argument about what the series shows. Textual reference is minimal, and the answer does not reach a judgement on the extent the question asks about. The lift would come from choosing one moment, such as the boat rescue, and explaining what it shows about fear that the participants did not expect.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Waste Land invite you to reconsider your understanding of power?
markerNotes: The question asks for an extent, so the strongest answers reach a judgement early and test it against the film's own evidence, rather than describing the catadores and adding a sentence about power at the end.
Power has to be defined before it can be reconsidered. Answers that treat it only as money miss the film's shift towards organisation, representation and who decides what the work is worth.

The Marat portrait is the richest image for this question. A strong answer explains the reversal it sets up, a catador given the authority of a martyred political figure, rather than only noting that the reference exists.
The best answers keep the film's limits in view. The art market, the sale and the government campaign show that the reconsideration is partial, and a convincing answer says so.
commonStudentErrors: Treating power as wealth alone, and so missing the film's movement towards collective organisation and self-representation.
Retelling how the portraits are made without asking who controls the image or what the pickers gain from it.
Presenting the sale of the photographs as simple charity, without considering who sets the price and decides where the money goes.
Answering with a general claim that art empowers the poor, without a judgement on how far the film supports that claim.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Waste Land invites us to reconsider power to a considerable extent, though not the one its premise first suggests. Lucy Walker's documentary follows Vik Muniz as he photographs the catadores at Jardim Gramacho, the enormous landfill outside Rio de Janeiro, and then works with them to rebuild their own images from the refuse they sort every day. Through this collaboration the film explores human experience in a community most viewers never see. Power here is less a matter of wealth or institutions than of who represents whom, who organises, and who decides what the pickers' work is worth. The film shows these forms of power shifting, but it also shows how much stays in other hands, and that tension makes the reconsideration convincing.

Before the film begins, most viewers would locate power in the authorities who run a city's waste, the wealth that sets the price of art, and the artist whose name gives a photograph its value. The catadores sit beneath all three. They make their living from the rubbish of people more fortunate than themselves, with no conventional employment, so a film about them could easily be a film about powerlessness.

The film complicates this at its centre, which is the question of representation. Muniz's first aim was to paint the catadores with garbage, so the authority to frame them was his. That method hands much of the authority to the people in the frame. He photographs each picker at the landfill, projects the images onto the floor of a massive warehouse, and then works with the catadores to rebuild the images from materials they gather at the dump. The pickers choose and arrange what they salvage, so each finished photograph is a joint record of what they can make and how they see themselves. Power to define a person's image, which in a conventional documentary rests with the filmmaker, is partly reclaimed by its subjects.

The clearest sign of a different kind of power is collective. Tião, the young and charismatic leader of the pickers' association, has built a co-operative that pools their labour and resources, and the film presents this organisation as their source of strength. Valter, the group's elder statesman and recycling guru, declares the crucial role the pickers play in dealing with the results of overconsumption, a claim to social value that wider society has long refused them. Power here is built from shared work rather than held by one person at the top, and it gives the pickers a standing they did not have before.

The reversal is also visible through art history. One of Muniz's portraits reworks Jacques-Louis David's 1793 painting of Jean-Paul Marat, the revolutionary murdered in his bath, and the portrait made in that pose is of Tião. Placing a catador in the position of a martyred political figure lends him some of the authority David gave Marat. The image carries extra weight because Tião was inspired by political texts he found in the waste. The film's poster repeats the composition. Walker's film asks the audience to see the landfill worker as a political subject rather than only a casualty of the economy.

The reconsideration is tested most sharply where the money is. Muniz decides that the proceeds from the photographs go back to the catadores, and that money keeps the co-operative's trucks running, pays for schooling and helps build a library. That is a real transfer of resources. Yet the value of the work depends on an art market in which the artist's name and an auction set the price. The pickers supply the labour and material, but the decision to sell, and the terms on which the images circulate, remain with Muniz. They gain resources without gaining control of the market that gives their labour its worth.

Power over the pickers' future also lies with government. The authorities closed the landfill in June 2012, ending the work that gave the community its livelihood, a decision the pickers could not make for themselves. The Brazilian government is also using the film in a national recycling campaign, which absorbs the catadores' achievement into a public message it controls.

Finally, the reconsideration applies to the film itself. Waste Land is directed by a British filmmaker with Brazilian co-directors, and its director has great access to the whole process. The audience sees the pickers through a frame that someone outside the community controls. The film gives the catadores a voice and a self-portrait, but it is also an award-winning film made from their lives. Recognising this does not undo its achievement. It shows that power in this text is relational and unevenly distributed.

To that extent, the film does invite a reconsideration of power: it moves power away from wealth and rank and towards organisation, self-representation and dignity. Its own evidence shows that these gains depend on outside money, a market and government decisions, so the audience ends with a more complicated understanding than the hopeful premise suggests. Power, the film implies, is not simply seized from the powerful. It is contested, shared and sometimes lost again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it judges the extent to which the film reconsiders power and builds that judgement from specific features, the reversal in the portrait process, the co-operative, the Marat portrait and the sale. Its sustained argument that power is relational and unevenly distributed is the main strength. To lift it, the final paragraph could test the film's own frame more closely, such as how the director's position shapes what the audience learns about the catadores.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Waste Land is a documentary about the artist Vik Muniz and the catadores, the workers who pick recyclable material from the dump at Jardim Gramacho near Rio de Janeiro. The film explores their human experience through the portraits they make together, and it does help the audience think about power. This answer explains the forms of power the film shows and how far they change the viewer's understanding.

Muniz's first aim is to paint the catadores with garbage. He photographs them at the landfill, then projects the pictures onto the floor of a warehouse. The catadores collect materials from the dump and recreate the pictures with them. This shows that the pickers have some power, because they take part in making their own images, and Muniz does not decide alone what the picture looks like.

Tião leads the association, which works as a co-operative so that the workers can pool their money and equipment. This is an example of power, because a group working together can do more than individuals. The money is used for trucks, schooling and a library, which improves the pickers' lives. It is important because it shows that the pickers are organised and that they can act together.

Valter is an elder statesman and talks about the role the catadores play in recycling. He says that people consume too much and throw things away carelessly, and that the pickers deal with the results. This is a claim to some importance, and it could make the audience think differently about who is powerful in society.

Muniz sells the photographs and gives the money to the catadores. This is a generous act, and it shows that the art world can help poor people. However, the artist still controls the sale, so the pickers do not have full control over the market for their work. They depend on him for this, which limits their power.

The landfill was closed in 2012, and the government is using the film for a recycling campaign. These events show that the government has power over the pickers' future. Overall, the film changes the audience's understanding of power to some extent, because it shows the pickers as organised and creative, but it also shows that they depend on others. The viewer is left with the impression that power is spread around, although most of the big decisions are made by people outside the dump.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the forms of power the film shows, but it rarely analyses how a particular image or technique produces them, and its references are general. Its clear strength is the sequence from the portraits to the co-operative and the money. To lift it, analyse one image closely, such as the portrait that reworks David's Death of Marat, and judge how far it changes the audience's view of power.

sampleAnswers.answer: Waste Land is a documentary by Lucy Walker about Vik Muniz, an artist who makes pictures out of rubbish in Brazil. He works with some workers at a dump called Jardim Gramacho. They are called catadores and they pick things out of the rubbish to sell. Muniz takes their photographs and then they make pictures of themselves out of rubbish, and the pictures are photographed. The pictures were sold and the money went to the workers. This shows power because the artist has power and uses it to help people who have less. The workers also have some power because they are in a group together. So the film changes what people think about power a little, because the people at the bottom of society are shown to be strong and able to do things. The film shows people working hard in bad conditions and it is an interesting film to watch.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the film and the pickers' work, with almost no textual reference and no judgement of how far power is reconsidered. Its strength is an accurate account of how the portraits are made. To lift it, name one scene or image, such as the portraits built on the warehouse floor, and say what it shows about power.

prompts.question: Analyse how your prescribed text represents the ways individuals respond to the challenges they face. In your response, make reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The stem asks how the text represents the ways individuals respond, so the strongest answers compare several responses and say what each reveals about the Party's control.
Winston's diary and his memories of his mother are the strongest evidence of inner resistance. Answers should quote the diary and the memory precisely rather than summarise them.
Julia's pleasure is a different kind of response. The best answers show why Orwell presents it as individual rebellion while also showing its limits.
The ending is the test of the whole representation. Answers that treat 'He loved Big Brother' only as a plot resolution miss how the novel shows private feeling being absorbed.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the Ministry of Truth and the torture scenes in order without asking what each response shows about individuals.
Treating Winston as the only individual who responds, which misses Julia, Parsons and Syme.
Presenting the proles as a simple source of hope without examining why Orwell leaves them outside the action.
Presenting the betrayal of Julia as something done to Winston alone, when the novel shows the betrayal as mutual.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Analyses skilfully how the prescribed text represents the ways individuals respond to the challenges they face; Presents an insightful response supported by well-chosen textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a coherent and sustained response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context

9-12 marks: Explains how the prescribed text represents the ways individuals respond to the challenges they face; Presents a response supported by some textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a response using variable control of language appropriate to audience and purpose
5-8 marks: Expresses limited understanding of ideas about individuals and/or challenges represented in the prescribed text; Describes aspects of the texts; Writes a response with minimal control of language
1-4 marks: Refers to the prescribed text in an elementary way; Attempts to compose a response

sampleAnswers.answer:
Nineteen Eighty-Four represents individuals responding to the challenges of a state that controls memory, language and feeling, and it shows that every response carries a cost. The responses are varied. Winston Smith resists through writing and memory, Julia resists through private pleasure, the proles remain outside the Party's attention, and others such as Parsons and Syme are either made to submit or destroyed. Orwell's account is bleak, but it is precise about what each individual can and cannot do against a system that treats private feeling as a threat.

Winston's first response is his diary. Writing “DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER” is a thoughtcrime, and the diary becomes a space where he can test whether he still has an independent mind. Its most important entry, “If there is hope”, is followed by the claim that “it lies in the proles”. The hope is real, but it rests on people the Party has largely ignored, so Winston's resistance depends on a future he cannot reach. His second response is memory. He recalls his mother and sister, and the moment when, after the last of the chocolate was gone, his mother clasped the child in her arms. He comes to see that his mother's standards were “private ones”, so her love was an act the Party could not reach. The recurring dream of a sinking ship, in which his mother still looks up at him, shows that memory preserves what the state wants erased.

Julia responds in a different way. She “didn't much care for reading” and is more interested in her own body than in the Party's doctrine. When Winston speaks of “little knots of resistance” that might leave records for later generations, she replies, “I'm not interested in the next generation”, and then that she is “interested in US”. Winston tells her she is “only a rebel from the waist downwards”, which exposes the limits of her defiance. Yet her pleasure is an individual refusal of the Party's demand that all desire be directed towards it, and the Party treats it as dangerous enough to destroy.

Other responses show how the Party makes individuals complicit. Parsons, Winston's colleague, is arrested after talking in his sleep, and he is proud that his seven-year-old daughter denounced him: “It was my little daughter.” He thanks the Party for saving him, which is submission dressed as gratitude. Syme, a philologist working on the Newspeak Dictionary, is a more troubling case. He vanishes without explanation, and his name quietly leaves the Chess Committee list, leaving Winston to conclude that Syme has “ceased to exist”. The Party does not need to punish everyone, because the fear of being reported makes ordinary people take part in their own erasure.

The novel's final responses confirm the Party's power over the inner life. Winston and Julia, who once met in the room above Mr Charrington's shop, betray each other, and each says “I betrayed you”. O'Brien explains the Party's purpose without pretence: it seeks “power entirely for its own sake”, and its image of the future is “a boot stamping on a human face”. Once the torture has done its work, Winston's resistance is broken from within. He has “won the victory over himself”, so the Party has won more than obedience. It has changed what he wants. The reader is left to see that the individual response, however brave, was never separate from the system that tried to govern it.

The last line completes the representation: “He loved Big Brother.” Orwell does not offer one heroic individual against a monolithic state. He offers a range of responses, from Winston's writing and memory to Julia's private pleasure and Parsons' pride, and he shows how each is absorbed by a system that treats feeling as a threat. The proles, who might have carried hope, stay outside the action. The novel's achievement is to show that the question of individual response is not whether people resist, but how much of themselves survives the attempt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it sustains one argument, that Orwell's varied individual responses are each absorbed by the Party, and supports it with precise references to the diary, the sinking-ship dream, Julia's pleasure and the ending. The move that would lift it further is to test the proles more closely, because the answer gives them hope in one sentence and does not examine why Orwell keeps them outside the action.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Nineteen Eighty-Four shows how individuals respond to a totalitarian state. Winston Smith is the main character. He works at the Ministry of Truth, where he changes old records so that they match the Party's current version of events. This job makes him aware of how the past can be altered. He begins to keep a secret diary, which is dangerous, and he writes things against Big Brother in it. He also remembers his mother and his sister, who disappeared when he was a child. These memories show that Winston has a personal life that the Party cannot fully control.

Julia is the other main character, and she responds differently to the Party. She and Winston have a secret relationship, and they meet in a room above a shop owned by Mr Charrington. Julia does not care much about books or politics. She is not interested in the next generation and mainly wants her own pleasure. This shows a rebellion based on private pleasure rather than on ideas, and Winston sees that it is a kind of rebellion, even if a limited one.

Other people respond in other ways. Parsons is arrested after he talks in his sleep, and his daughter has reported him to the authorities. He is proud of her and he thanks the Party for saving him. This shows how the Party can make people complicit in their own punishment. Syme, who works on the Newspeak Dictionary, disappears. Winston notices that his name has been removed from a list, and he realises that Syme has ceased to exist, which means the Party has erased him completely.

At the end of the novel, Winston is tortured by O'Brien and he betrays Julia, and Julia betrays him too. Winston comes to love Big Brother. This shows that the Party has defeated him, and that the individual cannot resist the power of the state. Orwell therefore presents individual responses as limited and often unsuccessful, although the novel is also interested in what people feel and remember.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies Winston, Julia, Parsons and Syme and explains what happens to each, but it mostly retells the plot and makes only brief reference to the text. Its strength is the clear sequence from Julia's pleasure to the ending. The move that would lift it is to choose one passage, such as Winston's memory of his mother holding the child, and analyse how Orwell's language makes that response personal.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nineteen Eighty-Four is about a man called Winston Smith who lives in a country where the government watches everyone. He works at the Ministry of Truth and changes old newspapers. He secretly writes in a diary, and he meets a woman called Julia. They have a relationship that the Party does not allow. They meet in a room above a shop, which shows how small the space for private life has become. In the end they are caught, and Winston is tortured. He is changed by what happens to him, and at the end he loves Big Brother. The book shows that the government is very powerful and that ordinary people find it hard to resist. Some people try to hold on to their own thoughts, but they do not succeed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the plot and characters without analysing how Orwell represents an individual's response. It offers almost no textual reference, and the claim that the Party is very powerful is asserted rather than shown. The move that would lift it is to name one response, such as Julia's, and quote a short phrase that shows how Orwell presents it.

prompts.question: ‘A text can ignite ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world.’ To what extent do you agree with this statement in relation to your prescribed text? In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The statement asks for a judgement about extent, so the strongest answers state a clear position on the statement and qualify it by reference to the text.
The shooting and its aftermath show collective experience through named classmates. Answers should use the book's specific details rather than generalising about Pakistan.
The reception is evidence that the text ignites argument. The strongest answers use the ban and the threats to show that the book's ideas are contested, which enriches the view of the world.
Close reference matters most here: one reported event or family detail, quoted briefly and explained, outweighs a summary of the book's chapters.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising the shooting and recovery without assessing the statement.
Treating Malala's story as representative of all Pakistani girls, without noticing the family's position and the book's single narrator.
Overstating the book's effect on the world, for example claiming it ended the Taliban's campaign against schools.
Writing about Malala's courage as a personal virtue alone, without linking it to the shared experiences of the girls of Swat.
