sampleAnswers.answer:
I am Malala tells two stories at once. One is the personal story of a girl who wanted to go to school. The other is the collective story of the people of the Swat Valley, where the Taliban closed girls' schools and turned education into a public contest. To what extent the statement holds depends on how far the memoir's shared experiences reach beyond its narrator. I argue that Malala Yousafzai's book does ignite ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world, though its vision is shaped by one family's position and by the controversy it provoked.

The shared experience begins in the family's commitment to education. Her father, Ziauddin, opened the Khushal School, and her mother, Toor Pekai, brought children in need into the household, while Ziauddin gave free places in his schools to poor children. Schooling in this memoir is a family and community enterprise rather than a private privilege. The collective threat arrives through the Taliban's “Radio Mullah” broadcasts, which condemned music and dancing and told women to stay at home. The restriction reaches every household in the valley, so the family's private loss becomes a community's loss.

The shooting on 9 October 2012 gives the collective its clearest image. After an exam, two men stopped her school bus, and one asked who Malala was before firing. Her friends Shazia and Kainat were also injured, so the attack falls on a group of students rather than on one girl alone. The memoir names one of its sections “Three Bullets, Three Girls”, which frames the attack as a shared event as well as a personal wound. The book makes the reader see the injured body as the place where a public struggle over education is fought.

The collective extends far beyond Swat. Malala received many cards after the attack, and she spent months in hospital in Birmingham, where she worried about where her father was and about the cost of treatment, which the Pakistani government covered. Her recovery depended on governments, doctors and strangers who sent messages across borders. A personal wound becomes a public story, and the memoir shows that a girl's survival is measured in shared attention as well as in surgery. The question of girls' schooling becomes a matter of international concern.

The book's reception shows that its ideas ignite argument as well as sympathy. The All Pakistan Private School's Federation announced that the book would be banned in its 152,000 member institutions, saying that it disrespected Islam, and the Pakistani Taliban threatened bookshops that sold it. These responses are part of the collective experience the memoir reveals: a world in which a girl's account of schooling can be read as either an attack on faith or a demand for justice. The book enriches our view of the world not by settling the question, but by making the contest visible.

The qualification is that the memoir's collective is shaped by one family's position. Her father owned schools, which gave the family a standing that many families in the valley did not have. The book was co-written with Christina Lamb, and one reviewer objected to the voice of a foreign correspondent running alongside Malala's. The memoir ignites ideas about shared suffering, but it speaks most clearly for a girl with a platform, so readers must look elsewhere for the voices of girls who had none.

Yet the statement largely holds. The memoir's most enduring idea is that education is a right that no single family can secure alone, and that idea depends on the collective. Malala's own ambition, to be known for fighting for education, moves the story from self to shared cause. The book ignites ideas about collective human experiences, and in doing so it asks readers to see Swat not as a remote place but as part of a wider world in which girls are denied a classroom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it takes a clear position on the extent of the statement, qualifies it through the memoir's narrator and its reception, and anchors each claim in specific events such as the bus shooting and the Khushal School. The move that would lift it further is to sharpen the final paragraph by naming one image from the memoir that carries the collective idea, rather than relying on the general claim that education is a right.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I am Malala is a memoir about a girl who wanted an education and was shot by the Taliban. It describes her life in the Swat Valley and her father's schools. Her father, Ziauddin, opened a school called the Khushal School, and he gave free places to poor children. Her mother also brought children who needed help into their home. This shows that education was a shared activity in the family and the community, and it helps explain why the Taliban's actions affected so many people.

The Taliban grew powerful in Swat and banned girls from school. Malala describes the radio broadcasts that criticised music and dancing and told women to stay at home. She also wrote a blog for the BBC in Urdu under a pseudonym, which shows how she was already speaking out before she was shot. Her school was shut down after a Taliban order in 2009, and her family had to move away for a few months. These events show a collective situation, because many families had to make the same kinds of decisions.

On 9 October 2012, two men stopped the school bus that Malala was travelling on and shot her and two of her friends. Malala survived and was flown to hospital in Birmingham. The shooting is the most dramatic event in the book, and it shows how far the Taliban were prepared to go. Malala's friends were also hurt, which makes the attack about more than one girl. Malala received thousands of cards from people around the world, which shows that her story reached beyond Pakistan.

The memoir has also caused debate. Some private schools in Pakistan banned it, saying it disrespected Islam, and the Pakistani Taliban threatened bookshops that sold it. This suggests that the book has ideas that people find controversial. Overall the book tells a story about education and courage, and it helps readers understand the experience of girls in Swat, although it is written from Malala's point of view and so does not show every person's experience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the Swat background and the shooting in order and identifies the collective effects, but it mostly describes the events and rarely analyses how the memoir presents them. Its strength is the accurate account of the school closure and the family's displacement. The move that would lift it is to take one passage, such as the bus attack and the friends who were hurt, and explain how the telling makes the attack a shared experience.

sampleAnswers.answer: I am Malala is about a girl from Pakistan who was shot by the Taliban because she wanted to go to school. She grew up in the Swat Valley, and her father ran schools there. The Taliban closed the girls' schools, and her family had to leave for a time. In 2012 she was shot on her school bus. She was flown to hospital in England and survived. The book also explains that many people supported her, and that the book itself has been banned in some places. The story shows that education is important and that girls should have the right to go to school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes Malala's shooting and move to Birmingham without analysing how the memoir represents collective experience. It offers no textual reference beyond the main events. The move that would lift it is to name one passage or event from the book and explain how it presents the experience of many girls, not only Malala.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts; analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 1, Section II — Texts and Human Experiences (20 marks). Allow about 45 minutes.

dotPoints.description: Compose creative and critical texts that affirm or challenge ideas, values and perspectives represented in a range of texts

prompts.question: Construct a short creative or critical text that affirms or challenges an idea represented across a range of texts you have studied, then give a brief rationale explaining your choices.
markerNotes: A challenge needs a defensible counter-position. Show what the idea gets wrong or leaves out, then offer something in its place.
The rationale should name the texts in the range that the composed piece answers, so the connection is clear to the marker.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a view on the idea without developing it through the composed text.
Writing a rationale that describes the story rather than the choices that affirm or challenge the idea.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6-7 marks: Constructs a text that affirms or challenges the idea with critical or creative control across its structure and language, and the rationale explains the choices precisely and connects them to the range of texts studied
4-5 marks: Responds clearly to the idea in a composed text with some control, and the rationale explains most choices
2-3 marks: States a view on the idea with limited development, and the rationale describes the choices in general terms
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the idea without a composed text

sampleAnswers.answer:
Everyone in my town said the city was where stories began. The books we studied treated leaving as the only true adventure, and I believed them until my grandfather stopped me at the gate. 'Stay,' he said, not as a command but as a question. Instead of the speech I had rehearsed about ambition, I looked at the fence he had mended every spring for forty years, and understood that staying can be a story too. The idea that the city is the centre of meaning has hardened into a rule. I want to challenge it.

Rationale: This piece challenges the idea, shared by the texts we studied, that leaving home is the only route to meaning. I wrote it as a creative first-person reflection so the challenge feels personal rather than argued. The grandfather's question is the critical element, because the ideas in those texts cannot easily answer it. The mended fence affirms a different set of values, and the closing line leaves the question open. The piece therefore counters the city as the centre of stories without offering a rival rule, which is the defensible position a challenge needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes invented texts and a town for illustration. The composed piece challenges one idea by staging it against a personal moment, and the rationale ties the challenge to the texts studied and to the image that affirms an alternative value. The control of both the creative and the critical element is what earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Everyone thought the city was the best place for stories. I want to challenge that idea. My grandfather asked me to stay, and I think staying can also be good.

Rationale: I wrote this to challenge an idea from the texts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Responds clearly to the idea with some control, but the composed text is brief and the rationale describes the choices only in general terms, so it sits in the 4-5 band.

sampleAnswers.answer: I wrote about a city and a farm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a topic without a view on the idea or a developed composed text, so it sits in the 2-3 band.

prompts.scenario: Year 12 student Lina is composing a piece for a school anthology that responds to a range of texts studied in class. The texts she has studied present leaving home as the only route to adventure and meaning. Her teacher asks her to affirm or challenge one idea those texts present, and to explain her choices in a short rationale.

prompts.question: Explain how a creative text you have read affirms or challenges a value represented across a range of texts, using ONE stylistic choice as evidence.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism: say what the choice does to the reader's acceptance or resistance of the value.
Name the value precisely, for example belonging or ambition, rather than values in general.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a stylistic choice without explaining how it affirms or challenges the value.
Describing the value in the text without identifying the choice that carries it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains clearly how one stylistic choice in a creative text affirms or challenges a value across the texts, with a precise link
2 marks: Explains a stylistic choice with a general link to a value
1 mark: Names a stylistic choice without linking it to a value

sampleAnswers.answer: Creative texts affirm or challenge values when a stylistic choice makes readers accept or resist an idea. Here the repeated word home affirms the value of belonging, because the repetition makes the idea feel settled. The same choice is a challenge to texts that treat home as a place one must escape. By insisting on the word in every line, the piece asks whether leaving is the only measure of worth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how one stylistic choice affirms one value and challenges another, with a precise mechanism and a link to the range of texts. That is the full 3-mark answer. The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration.

sampleAnswers.answer: The word home is repeated, which affirms the value of belonging. It also challenges other texts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links a stylistic choice to a value with a general explanation and no mechanism, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The word home is repeated in the poem.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a stylistic choice without linking it to any value, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 class is discussing how a short creative text in an anthology responds to the texts studied in the unit. The anthology text is invented: it repeats the word 'home' in every short line, and the texts studied in the unit treat home as a place one must escape. Their teacher asks each student to explain one stylistic choice that either affirms or challenges a value.

dotPoints.description: Compose texts using structures, language features and stylistic elements for specific audiences, to reinterpret ideas and perspectives

prompts.question: Construct a short text for a specific audience that reinterprets an idea or perspective from a text you have studied, using structure, language features and stylistic elements, then give a rationale.
markerNotes: Reinterpret means offering a new reading of the idea, not restating the original. Look for what the new text sees that the original did not.
Choices should be matched to the audience. A reader of the composed text should feel that it was written for them.
commonStudentErrors: Using a young audience as a label while keeping adult vocabulary and sentence structure.
Retelling the studied text rather than reinterpreting the idea it carries.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Constructs a text that reinterprets the idea for younger students through a deliberate structure, language features and stylistic elements, and the rationale explains how each choice suits the audience and the reinterpretation
5-6 marks: Reinterprets the idea for the audience with clear choices of structure and style, and the rationale explains most choices
3-4 marks: Addresses the audience with a general reinterpretation, and the rationale describes the choices in general terms
1-2 marks: Offers little reinterpretation or does not suit the audience, and the rationale is absent or only restates the piece

sampleAnswers.answer:
Dear Year 7,

When our teacher first mentioned courage, I thought it meant the moment a hero steps forward. The text we studied suggested something quieter. Its protagonist does not charge into the storm; she keeps the lighthouse lamp burning so that someone out at sea can see the rocks. I want to reinterpret that idea for you. Courage can be a lamp kept burning in an ordinary room, and you do not need a sword to carry it.

Try this. Think of one small thing you do each day that someone else depends on. Maybe you open the door for the little ones, or you finish your reading even when it is hard. Those are the lamps. Nobody writes songs about them, but they keep people safe in their own way.

So the next time you feel afraid of speaking up in class, remember the lighthouse. You do not have to be the loudest voice. You only have to keep the light on for the person who is looking for it.

From your older friend, the writer.

Rationale: I used a letter form, short sentences and direct address because the audience is Year 7 students, and the structure moves from the original interpretation to a reinterpretation, then to an invitation so the reader can follow a clear path. The language features are deliberately simple, using imperatives and everyday examples such as opening a door, so that the idea is accessible to a younger reader. The lighthouse image is one of several stylistic elements, and it reinterprets courage as steady care rather than dramatic action. I wanted the text to reinterpret the idea for a young audience without losing the perspective of the original text. I also checked the piece against its purpose: the text should leave the younger reader with a clear action, and the closing paragraph is designed to do exactly that. The care taken with vocabulary matters because a reinterpretation that the audience cannot follow does not reinterpret anything.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration. The composed letter reinterprets courage as steady care, and its structure, direct address and everyday examples are matched to a Year 7 audience. The rationale explains how each choice suits the audience and the reinterpretation, which is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Dear Year 7, courage is not only about heroes. The story we read has a lighthouse keeper who keeps the light on. You can be brave like that too. Remember the lighthouse when you are scared.

Rationale: I wrote a short letter for Year 7 because they are young. I used short sentences. The lighthouse is the main idea.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Reinterprets the idea for an audience with a clear letter structure, but the language choices are few and the rationale only restates them, so it sits in the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Courage is good. Be brave at school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes little reinterpretation and does not show any choice matched to the audience, so it sits in the 1-2 band.

prompts.scenario: Year 12 student Dev is writing a short text for younger students in a school literacy program. The studied text's protagonist keeps a lighthouse lamp burning rather than charging into a storm. The text must reinterpret one idea from a studied text, using a structure and stylistic elements that suit a young audience, and it must be followed by a rationale.

prompts.question: Demonstrate, with a short example, how a stylistic element of a studied text can be adapted for a new audience when an idea is reinterpreted.
markerNotes: Show the before and after. A strong answer sets the original choice beside the adapted choice and explains the difference for the new audience.
Adapting does not mean simplifying everything. Keep the element that carries the idea and change only what the audience needs.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the adapted text without showing what changed from the original.
Changing vocabulary alone while leaving the stylistic element unchanged.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates with a precise example how a stylistic element is adapted for the new audience, with a clear account of the reinterpreted idea
3 marks: Demonstrates an adaptation with a general account of the audience
2 marks: Names an adaptation without showing how it changes for the audience
1 mark: Refers to the audience without an adaptation

sampleAnswers.answer: Harriet adapts the stylistic element of the storm passage's long, dense sentence. In the original, subordinate clauses suit an adult reader who wants to linger. For Year 9, the same idea of danger is reinterpreted through three short imperatives, each ending on a sharp image, so the pacing quickens and the language features are simpler. The stylistic elements of tension and threat are kept, and the reinterpreted idea is that danger is a series of decisions rather than one overwhelming event. The audience can follow the sequence without losing the threat.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Shows the original stylistic element beside the adapted one, explains the change in pacing and language for the audience, and states the reinterpreted idea. The before-and-after reasoning is what earns the top band. The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration.

sampleAnswers.answer: Harriet makes the sentences shorter for the Year 9 students. This helps them read it more easily.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names an adaptation but does not show the original element or how the change works for the audience, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Harriet changes the story for younger students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Refers to the audience without describing a specific adaptation, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: Year 12 student Harriet is adapting a passage from a studied text for a Year 9 audience. The passage describes a storm in one long, dense sentence of subordinate clauses. Her teacher wants her to demonstrate how she changes one stylistic element when the idea is reinterpreted for a new audience.

dotPoints.description: The ways personal, social, cultural and historical contexts shape meaning in texts

prompts.question: Examine how the personal, social, cultural and historical contexts of your prescribed text shape its meaning.
markerNotes: Examine asks for a close look at evidence. Take each context in turn, name a textual feature it touches, and say what it does to the meaning.
The strongest answers show two contexts pulling the meaning in different directions, then weigh which effect dominates.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the four contexts without linking any of them to a feature of the text.
Treating the historical context as the date of publication without explaining its effect on meaning.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Examines in detail how several contexts shape meaning in the text, linking each context to specific textual features and to different readers' responses
4 marks: Examines how two or more contexts shape meaning, with clear textual evidence
3 marks: Explains one or two contexts and their effect on meaning, with general evidence
2 marks: Identifies a context with a general statement about its effect
1 mark: Names a context without linking it to meaning

sampleAnswers.answer:
Contexts shape meaning by determining what readers recognise and what they question. In this invented novel, the personal context of the narrator's grief makes small domestic details, such as a cup or a coat, carry emotional weight. The social context of financial struggle adds a second meaning: readers see those objects as signs of hardship as well as affection. The cultural context of a community that values silence in mourning makes the narrator's restraint read as respect rather than evasion. The historical context of publication during an economic recession makes the loss resonate with readers who have faced similar uncertainty.

These contexts pull in different directions. The personal grief and the cultural expectation of silence reinforce each other, while the historical context makes the social and personal meanings more immediate, because readers in a recession may bring their own experience of loss.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented novel for illustration. It links each context to a reader's response and, for the personal, social and cultural contexts, to a specific feature of the text, and it weighs how they combine. That linking of context to textual feature is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The narrator's personal grief makes the reader notice small objects. The social context of money problems also changes how the objects are read. These contexts shape meaning in a general way.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains two contexts and their effect on meaning, but the evidence is general and the historical and cultural contexts are not addressed, so it sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The text was written in a recession.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a context without linking it to meaning, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is preparing an examination response on a text whose meaning depends on the time and place in which it was written and read. The text is an invented novel narrated by a woman grieving her father, in which a family struggles financially and a community values silence in mourning, and which was published during an economic recession. Her teacher wants her to examine how context shapes the text's meaning for different readers.

prompts.question: Clarify the difference between a personal context and a cultural context, and state how each one can shape meaning in a text.
markerNotes: Clarify means making the difference plain. Put the two side by side on one point, such as scale or source.
A definition is not enough on its own. Add the effect each context has on what a reader notices.
commonStudentErrors: Defining both terms in the same words, so no difference is clarified.
Treating cultural context as the author's nationality rather than the shared beliefs of a community.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies the difference between personal and cultural contexts, with a precise example of how each shapes meaning for readers
2 marks: Clarifies the difference with a general example of how one context shapes meaning
1 mark: Defines one context without showing how it shapes meaning

sampleAnswers.answer: A personal context is the individual experience a reader or writer brings to a text, such as a family loss, which makes some details significant. A cultural context is the shared beliefs of a community, such as expectations about grief, which shape what readers find moving. The difference is scale: a personal context belongs to one life, while a cultural context is shared by many readers. Both shape meaning because they decide which features seem important.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies the difference through a single point of comparison, scale, and gives an example and an effect for each context. That is the full 3-mark answer. The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration.

sampleAnswers.answer: A personal context is the reader's own life. A cultural context is what a community believes, and this changes what readers think about a text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies the difference with a general example and little on how each context shapes meaning, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cultural context is a community's beliefs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines one context without showing how it shapes meaning, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing a short glossary entry for her class on the terms used to describe context in texts. She must clarify the difference between a personal context and a cultural one, and show how each shapes meaning.

dotPoints.description: The ways specific language features and forms of texts influence perceptions of ourselves, other people and a range of cultural perspectives

prompts.question: Contrast how TWO of your prescribed texts use specific language features and forms to influence readers' perceptions of other people and of cultural perspectives.
markerNotes: Contrast needs one point of comparison held steady. Compare the two texts on the same feature, such as voice or distance, so the difference is visible.
Say what the contrast does to the reader's perception, not only what the difference is.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the two texts separately without drawing the comparison.
Contrasting the characters or events rather than the forms and language that present them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Contrasts the two texts precisely, showing how their language features and forms influence perceptions of other people and of cultural perspectives, with sustained evidence
4 marks: Contrasts the two texts with clear evidence of language features and forms and a link to perceptions
3 marks: Contrasts the texts with some evidence and a general link to cultural perspectives
2 marks: Describes the features of each text with limited contrast
1 mark: States that the texts differ without evidence

sampleAnswers.answer:
The two texts influence perceptions of other people and of cultural perspectives through different language features and forms. The first, a first-person short story, uses a warm, colloquial voice and a loose, episodic structure, so the reader sees the community's characters as neighbours whose habits are understandable. The second, a formal third-person essay organised around one argument, uses generalisations and a measured tone, so the reader sees the same community as practices to be evaluated. The contrast lies in the influence each form has on the reader's position: the story invites empathy from inside a single viewpoint, while the essay encourages judgement from a distance.

The closing lines complete these perceptions in opposite directions. The story ends with a warm invitation, so the reader feels belonging, while the essay ends with a policy recommendation, so the reader feels responsibility.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes two invented texts for illustration. It holds one comparison steady, the reader's position, and shows how each text's language features and forms produce a different perception. The sustained contrast is what the top band rewards.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first text uses a first-person voice and a loose structure, so readers feel close to the characters. The second text is formal and uses generalisations, so readers judge the community more. Both texts affect how cultural perspectives are seen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Contrasts the texts with some evidence and a general link to cultural perspectives, but the comparison is not sustained, so it sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The texts are different in their language.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a difference without evidence, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is comparing two texts from a unit on language, identity and culture. The texts are invented: a first-person short story about a community of neighbours that ends with a warm invitation, and a formal third-person essay about the same community that ends with a policy recommendation. She must contrast how each text uses language features and forms to shape the reader's view of other people and of different cultural perspectives.

prompts.question: Interpret how your prescribed text uses its forms to influence your own perceptions of a group of people.
markerNotes: Interpret means explaining what the text means through its forms. Say how the form works on you, then what it asks you to think about the group.
Track the form across the text. A change of form that shifts the reader's view is often the strongest evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Stating what the group is like without showing how the forms create that impression.
Confusing the content, such as the group's actions, with the forms used to present them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Interprets with precision how the text's forms influence the reader's perceptions of a group of people, with specific textual evidence
3 marks: Interprets how the forms influence perceptions, with some evidence
2 marks: Makes a general interpretation of the text's influence on perceptions
1 mark: States a view of the group without reference to the forms

sampleAnswers.answer: The text interprets a group of people through its forms, and this has a strong influence on my perceptions of them. The text is structured as interviews, so the group speaks in its own words, and I form a view of its character from what it chooses to reveal. The direct speech makes each speaker seem trustworthy, which leads me to accept their accounts. However, when the interviewer's commentary breaks in with a summary of the group's habits, the form shifts to a more distant register and my perceptions become more critical. The interplay between interview and commentary moves me from sympathy to suspicion, so the forms, not the content alone, shape what I carry away.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration. It tracks the form across the text, shows the shift from direct speech to commentary, and explains how each shift changes the reader's perception. That tracking of form is what earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The interviews make the people seem believable. The commentary makes me less sure about them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general interpretation of the forms' influence without showing how the change works, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: I think the people in the text are interesting.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a view of the group without reference to the forms, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing a short analytical paragraph for a class discussion on how texts shape a reader's view of a group of people. The text is invented: it is structured as a series of interviews with members of a group, with commentary from the interviewer that summarises the group's habits. Her teacher wants her to interpret one text's forms and what they do to her own perceptions.

prompts.question: Prose fiction relies primarily on setting to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: Strong answers take the word “primarily” seriously and argue how far setting carries the tension, rather than agreeing or disagreeing in general terms.

The Drover’s Wife gives the clearest evidence, but the best responses test the claim against a second story, such as the funeral in The Union Buries Its Dead, where the heat and dust act on the mourners.
Specific episodes do more work than summary. The nineteen-mile ride with the dead child shows what isolation takes from the woman; a retelling of the snake episode alone argues nothing.
Lawson’s narrator is part of the cultural argument. Responses that treat the narrator as a neutral reporter miss the irony that keeps the reader between admiration and judgement.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the snake episode in order without saying what the setting does to the family’s sense of safety.
Treating the bush as a backdrop rather than as the place where the legend of the drover is tested.
Describing the funeral in The Union Buries Its Dead as sad without showing how the heat and the drinking expose the town’s divisions.
Taking the bushwoman’s stoicism at face value and missing the humour in the narrator’s treatment of her.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Evaluates effectively the extent to which the statement accurately reflects the prescribed text; Presents an effective response using relevant, detailed textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas effectively using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Evaluates competently the extent to which the statement accurately reflects the prescribed text; Presents a competent response using relevant textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas competently using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Explains the extent to which the statement accurately reflects the prescribed text; Presents a response using some textual knowledge; Organises and expresses ideas adequately using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes aspects of the text with some reference to the statement; Presents a response using limited textual knowledge; Attempts to organise a response in a limited way
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the text; Attempts to organise a response in an elementary way

sampleAnswers.answer:
Henry Lawson’s prose fiction makes the bush the first thing a reader meets, and in The Drover’s Wife the setting does much of the work of creating cultural tension. The statement overreaches, however, when it says setting works primarily. The tension in these stories comes from a collision between the bush as legend and the bush as it is lived. Setting supplies the pressure, but characterisation and the narrator’s irony decide what that pressure means. I agree to a considerable extent, but not that setting operates alone.

The opening of The Drover’s Wife is a landscape built to produce isolation. The two-roomed house of round timber, slabs and stringy-bark stands on flat country, and the narrator describes “bush with no horizon” in every direction. The nearest sign of civilisation is a shanty nineteen miles away. The drover, an ex-squatter, is away with sheep, and his wife is left with four children and a dog. A single snake in that setting becomes a crisis. Lawson does not need to invent a threat, because the place supplies one.

Most of the story’s events come from the land. A black snake hides in the slabs, a thunderstorm sends the children onto the kitchen table, a bushfire has to be beaten out with a green bough, and a flood breaks the dam she has tried to save with an overflow gutter. A drought has already ruined the family’s property. The most painful episode is a child dying while she is alone. She rides nineteen miles for help, “carrying the dead child”. The distance here is not scenery. It measures what the bush takes from a woman with nobody to call on.

The legend these stories inherit is built on the drover: a mobile man, a mate on the track, a figure whose freedom makes him a national type. Lawson keeps that figure offstage. The husband has not been heard from for six months, and when he returns his wife is glad but does not gush. She is the one who has held the land together, and she is the one the narrator watches. The closing words belong to her son, who says, “I won’t never go drovin’”. The next generation rejects the myth, and the setting makes that rejection believable.

The city appears only as an ideal. The Young Ladies’ Journal gives her all the excitement she needs, and on Sundays she dresses the children and herself as carefully as she would for a walk to “do the block in the city”. The walk leads nowhere, because there is nothing to see and “not a soul to meet”. Lawson makes the monotony of the trees a force that pushes a man to break away, and the woman, who has no such option, stays. The pull of the city and the reality of the bush never meet, so the tension sits in the space between them.

The other stories use the same method. The Union Buries Its Dead is set in a town beside the Darling at midday, where the heat glares off the iron roofs and turns a union funeral into a farce of drink, sectarian suspicion and cheap ceremony. Once the holy water dries, the coffin cloth looks “a dusky grey”. The narrator’s own verdict is blunt: “Liquor, however, is stronger than Unionism”. Creed, class and drinking habits show through the heat, and the setting exposes them rather than merely housing them.

Shooting the Moon finds its tension in a pub yard. Two swagmen plan to lower their swags from an upstairs window, and one of them is caught sneaking out the back by the landlord. The landlord asks why they did not come straight to him, and the narrator admits he felt mean at once. The narrator’s mate, Jack Mitchell, mocks “city swells” who walk in their sleep, but the joke turns back on the bushmen’s own pride. The listener’s verdict on the publican is that “he was white, any road”. The pub, the yard and the moral economy of the bush are the setting, and the story depends on them.

The statement is most convincing when applied to the narrators. The narrator of The Union Buries Its Dead drains the funeral of sentiment, and he shrugs off the clay falling on a stranger’s coffin with “nothing does”. The narrator of The Drover’s Wife shows the woman weeping over her two best cows, then laughing at her ruined handkerchief. Lawson’s irony keeps the reader between admiration and judgement, and the bush is where that double vision is tested.

I agree to a considerable extent. Lawson’s settings create the conditions for cultural tension: isolation, drought, heat and the monotony of the trees make the myths of the bush visible as myths. Setting alone does not produce that tension, however. It needs a woman who measures her life against the legend, a publican whose decency shames the swagmen, a narrator whose irony refuses easy sentiment, and a boy who will not become a drover. The statement is right that setting is essential to these stories, and wrong that it is primary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it tests the word “primarily” rather than simply agreeing, and it moves through The Drover’s Wife, The Union Buries Its Dead and Shooting the Moon with specific episodes. The one move that would lift it is to link the Shooting the Moon paragraph to the bush’s moral codes more directly, since it currently describes the plot more than the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Henry Lawson writes about the bush in The Drover’s Wife as a harsh and isolated place, and this is where the cultural tension in prose fiction begins. The story is set on flat land with no hills, and the nearest shanty is nineteen miles away. The statement says that setting is the main way Lawson creates tension, and I partly agree with that. The setting makes the characters’ lives hard, so the reader feels the difference between the bush and the life people expect.

There are many things in the story that happen because of where the family lives. A snake gets under the house and the dog catches it, and the wife beats it with a stick. A storm comes up at sunset, and the children have to sleep on the kitchen table. She also fights a bushfire and a flood, and when her two best cows die she cries. All of these show that the bush is dangerous and that a woman has to look after everything on her own while her husband is away.

The bush also shapes the family history. A drought ruined the husband, who had to go droving again, and the wife has not heard from him for six months. One of the children died while she was alone, and she rode nineteen miles to get help. These details show how hard the bush is, and Lawson uses them to show the reader something about women’s lives on the land. The story does not state these points directly, so the reader has to work them out.

The other stories also use setting. The Union Buries Its Dead takes place in a hot town near the Darling River, where the funeral turns into a joke. The people drink and fight, a publican holds a straw hat over the priest’s head, and the narrator says that liquor is stronger than unionism. The heat and dust are part of the funeral’s sadness and its farce, so the setting shows the town’s divisions.

Shooting the Moon is set in a pub with a backyard. Two swagmen try to sneak away without paying, and the landlord catches one of them. The landlord is kind to them, which makes them feel bad. The story shows that bushmen think a lot about their mates and about their pride. The moon and the mulga camp frame the yarn, and the setting helps the reader see the men.

Overall, the setting is important in these stories, but the characters and the narrator matter too. The statement is partly right, because Lawson uses the bush to create tension, but I do not think setting is primary. The story shows a woman, a town and a pub, and each of these needs people to make the tension clear.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how the bush affects the family and names the setting of each story, but the references are brief and several sentences retell events rather than analyse them. To reach the 13-16 row, each story needs one close reference to a specific image or line, with an argument about what that image does to the cultural tension.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Drover’s Wife is about a woman who lives alone with her children in the bush while her husband is away droving. The setting is flat, and the nearest shanty is nineteen miles away. There is a snake in the house, and the woman kills it with a stick while the children watch. A storm comes, so the family sleeps on the kitchen table. She also fights a bushfire and a flood, and she has to deal with these alone. Lawson’s story shows how hard life is in the bush. The setting makes the story sad, and it is part of why the tension is there. The other stories are also set in the bush, so setting is important in Lawson.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the events of The Drover’s Wife and says the bush is harsh without showing how the setting creates cultural tension. To move up, it needs an argument about the statement and at least two specific references that show the bush acting on the characters.

prompts.question: Poetry relies primarily on symbolism to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: Strong answers test the word “primarily” and explain which poems rely on symbols and which rely on other means, rather than treating the anthology as one kind of poem.

Translucent Jade and Circular Breathing give the clearest symbols, but the best answers show how each symbol is set against something else: the jade against the speaker’s doubt, the didgeridoo against commercial goods.
Read the symbol as the poem uses it. Naming the jade as a symbol of luck adds little unless the answer shows what the poem does with that idea.

Mother and New Accents are useful counter-examples: one works through literal history, the other through wordplay. Answers that include a counter-example usually sit higher than those that argue only from the strongest poem.
commonStudentErrors: Listing symbols across several poems without saying what each one carries for the cultural tension.
Reading the didgeridoo in Circular Breathing as an Asian symbol, when the poem’s contrast is between an enduring sound and the commercial goods around it.
Describing the jade in Translucent Jade as a decorative object, without explaining its link to the speaker’s name and her sense of belonging.
Claiming that symbolism is the only device in the anthology, which ignores the direct questions and wordplay in several poems.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Contemporary Asian Australian Poets, symbolism does a great deal of the work of creating cultural tension, and it is one of the anthology’s main tools. The statement overreaches when it says symbolism works primarily. The poems also rely on direct self-questioning, rhetorical questions, wordplay and juxtaposition, and the tension comes from these as well as from symbols. I agree to a considerable extent, but not that symbolism is the primary means.

Maureen Ten’s Translucent Jade is the clearest case of a symbol carrying tension. The poem begins with a gift from the speaker’s grandfather, and the jade becomes an inherited object that holds family history and luck. It is linked to the speaker’s Chinese name, so the object carries a family identity the speaker must decide how to hold. The speaker feels like an impostor, partly belonging to two cultures, and she asks questions rather than offering answers. “What vibrations are these?” asks what the jade does to her, but it also asks whether she can feel her inheritance at all. The symbol is not decoration. It is where the speaker’s divided identity sits.

Jaya Savige’s Circular Breathing places a different symbol in a different setting. A didgeridoo player is busking in a Rome piazza at night, and the crowd gathers around a single sustained drone that seems older than the surrounding monuments. Nearby, counterfeit goods and designer labels are on sale. The didgeridoo stands for an enduring Aboriginal music set against commercial objects, and the contrast depends on the sound outlasting the goods. The speaker is unsettled as well as comforted. The line “Surely not this hemisphere” shows the sound seeming to come from another place altogether, and memory breaks the mood, because similar players go unnoticed at home. The symbol both consoles and wounds.

Vuong Pham’s Mother is less symbolic, and that difference tests the statement. Its power comes from the literal history of a mother who escaped the war in Vietnam, and the imagery of missiles and flames is direct rather than coded. The poem then sets that history against the steadier life of the son, who now teaches English, which was the work the mother had wanted. The classroom carries the hope of the ending, but the emotional force comes from the mother’s experience being told plainly. Where the poem uses symbols, they grow out of history rather than standing in for it.

Miriam Wei Wei Lo’s Home is closer to a symbol of belonging. The speaker’s dream of a safe home moves from longing to a place of rest and then back to the home she already has. The strongest symbol is the mulberry tree, which the poem calls “that foreigner”: a plant introduced from elsewhere that has nonetheless settled into the garden. The tree is an image of the speaker herself. The tension sits in the gap between longing for a home and accepting the one she has, and the tree makes that gap visible.

Ouyang Yu’s New Accents shows where the tension is not symbolic at all. The speaker recalls late-1990s conversations in Melbourne, and the central figure, “C from Canton”, has his university studies blocked by professors who judge him on his accent. The wordplay on English and anguish makes the tension audible through sound rather than image. The reader finds no object to carry the meaning. The damage is named directly, and irony does the work that a symbol does elsewhere in the anthology.

Taken together, the anthology treats symbolism as one important technique, but not the primary one. Translucent Jade and Circular Breathing rely on objects and sounds that stand for inheritance and place, and those symbols carry much of the tension. Mother, Home and New Accents show that the poets also depend on literal history, self-doubt and wordplay. The statement is right about the power of symbols and wrong about their primacy, because the tension depends on what each symbol is set against.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it tests “primarily” against several poems, and it reads the jade and the didgeridoo as symbols set against something specific in each poem. To lift it further, the Home paragraph should show how the mulberry tree’s position in the garden changes the symbol, not only what it stands for.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Contemporary Asian Australian Poets uses symbols to show cultural tension. The poems are about identity and about being an immigrant, and symbols help to show these ideas. The statement says poetry relies primarily on symbolism, and I think that is partly true. Some of the poems use objects and images to show what the speaker feels, so symbols are important in the anthology.

Maureen Ten’s Translucent Jade uses a piece of jade as its main symbol. The speaker’s grandfather gives her the jade, and the jade has meaning in Chinese culture. The poem also talks about the speaker’s name, which shows her family history. The speaker feels like she is not fully Chinese or Australian. This shows that the symbol helps to create tension between the two cultures.

Jaya Savige’s Circular Breathing uses the didgeridoo as a symbol. The poem is set in Rome, where a man is playing the didgeridoo in a square. There are shops selling fake goods and designer labels, and the didgeridoo is different from these things. The sound is a symbol of Aboriginal culture, and the speaker is homesick in a foreign city. This shows that the poem sets an old culture against modern consumer goods, and the contrast is what makes the poem work.

The other poems also use symbols. In Home the mulberry tree is an imported plant, so it is a symbol for the speaker, who is an immigrant. In Mother the imagery of war is vivid, and the mother’s story is told clearly. The poems together show that the poets use symbols to talk about culture and identity, which is why the question is about symbolism.

Overall, symbols are important in these poems, but the poets also use other techniques. The statement is partly right because the symbols do create cultural tension, but it is not right to say symbolism is primary. The poems are also about history and about wordplay, so the answer depends on the poem being discussed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it names symbols in three poems and links them to cultural tension, but the readings are stated rather than analysed, and New Accents is not used at all. To reach the 13-16 row, each symbol needs a closer look at how its poem uses it, and the answer should test the word primarily against at least one poem where the tension is not symbolic.

sampleAnswers.answer: Contemporary Asian Australian Poets is a collection of poems by several poets. In Translucent Jade, Maureen Ten writes about a jade gift from her grandfather and her Chinese name. In Circular Breathing, Jaya Savige writes about a didgeridoo player in Rome, and the speaker feels homesick. In Mother, Vuong Pham writes about his mother and the war. In Home, Miriam Wei Wei Lo writes about a home and a mulberry tree. The poems are about identity and culture, and some of them use symbols. This shows that the poetry is about culture.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the poems one after another and mentions symbols without explaining what any symbol does or how it creates tension. To move up, it needs an argument about the statement and at least two readings of how a symbol is used in a poem.

prompts.question: Drama relies primarily on characterisation to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: Strong answers treat characterisation as the way Shaw makes class visible: each major character holds a different view of speech and status, and the argument sits in how they clash.
Eliza is the best evidence, because her change is the play’s argument. Answers that trace her from the flower-girl scene to the final quarrel show how the tension moves.
Doolittle is a useful counterweight. His speech on the undeserving poor makes the class system look ridiculous from below, so the strongest answers use him rather than simply describing him.
Setting and language appear in the stage directions and the dialect, but a strong answer argues that they become tension only through the characters who use them.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Higgins as a villain without explaining the view of speech and class that drives his behaviour.
Treating Eliza’s final refusal to be managed as simple independence, without showing how her sense of self is built through the play.
Retelling the garden party as a comedy of manners without asking what it reveals about the class system.
Treating the sudden turn towards Freddy at the end as proof of Higgins’s change of heart, rather than as Shaw’s own comment on the outcome.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Pygmalion, drama relies primarily on characterisation to create cultural tension, and I largely agree. Bernard Shaw builds the class conflict out of people: Henry Higgins, who hears class in vowels; Eliza Doolittle, whose worth is measured by her speech; Alfred Doolittle, who turns poverty into a philosophy; and Mrs Higgins, who voices unease at what the experiment costs. Setting and dialect matter, but they matter because the characters make them matter. The tension is cultural because the play asks what a person’s speech says about who they are, and only the characters can answer that question.

Higgins’s boast in Covent Garden sets the terms. He says that in three months he could “pass that girl off as a duchess”, and he calls Eliza’s speech “kerbstone English”. Higgins believes that a person’s place can be read from their sounds, and that the right instruction can move that place. He describes his own work as “simply phonetics”, which makes his science sound neutral. Yet when Eliza’s distress is put in front of him, he calls her irritation “purely subjective”. Higgins turns feeling into sound and manners, and that habit is the source of the play’s cruelty.

Eliza is the play’s most exact test of the cultural argument, because she changes most. In Act I she insists that she is “a good girl”, and her dignity depends on the respect she is owed. Through the lessons she learns to speak like a duchess, and by the garden party she has succeeded so well that Higgins’s relief comes out as “Thank God it’s over!” Her answer in Act IV is the play’s turning point: “I sold flowers. I didn’t sell myself.” Higgins has changed her speech, but he has not trained her sense of self as he imagined. The tension grows from the gap between what she has been made to become and what she has found out she is.

Alfred Doolittle sharpens the argument from the other side of the class line. He arrives in Act II to claim his daughter, and his demand for five pounds is delivered as a philosophy of the “undeserving poor”. He insists that middle-class morality is “just an excuse for never giving me anything”, and he turns down the respectable careers Higgins offers him. Higgins half-admires the argument and Pickering objects, but Doolittle is the character who makes the social system visible by exposing its hypocrisy. He is a more reliable guide to class than either gentleman.

The supporting characters complicate the picture without softening it. Mrs Higgins voices the play’s unease about what the experiment does to Eliza, and her manner marks a difference from her son. Freddy Eynsford Hill is a figure of the middle class in decline, whose infatuation shows how a voice can be mistaken for a self. Pickering’s kindness is real, but he is complicit in the experiment and enjoys its success. Each of these characters makes the culture of class visible through what they say and do.

The last acts make characterisation into argument. Eliza refuses the role Higgins has written for her, and their quarrel turns on independence and dependence. She tells him she is nothing to him, “not so much as them slippers”, and he answers that her distress is only a passing mood. Higgins calls independence “middle class blasphemy” and insists that everyone depends on everyone else. Shaw’s epilogue then has Eliza marry Freddy, against Higgins’s prediction that she would marry an ambassador. The resolution comes from a choice a character makes, not from the plot alone.

Setting and language matter too. Covent Garden in the rain, the Wimpole Street laboratory and Mrs Higgins’s at-home each mark a different social world, and phonetics gives Higgins a way of reading people by their ears. These are tools the characters use, however. Drama can rely on setting or language to make a culture visible, but Pygmalion places its tension in the choices of Higgins, Eliza and Doolittle. The statement is largely right: characterisation is the primary means by which Shaw creates cultural tension, and without it the play would be a lecture on phonetics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it argues that characterisation carries the tension and tests that claim against Higgins, Eliza and Doolittle, with close use of Act I and Act V. The one move that would lift it is to sharpen the Mrs Higgins paragraph, which describes her unease but does not yet show how a specific line of hers makes the class argument.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Shaw’s Pygmalion uses characterisation to create cultural tension between the upper and lower classes. Higgins is a professor who believes he can turn a flower girl into a duchess by teaching her to speak. Eliza starts with a strong Cockney accent and sells flowers in Covent Garden. The play shows that speech is connected to class, and the characters argue about this throughout, so the tension is clear to the audience.

Higgins is the character who creates most of the tension. He thinks people can be defined by how they speak, and he treats Eliza as a project. When he says he could pass her off as a duchess, he shows that he thinks class can be learned. Eliza finds this hard, and she tells people she is “a good girl”. This shows that she has her own idea of what is right, which Higgins does not understand.

Eliza changes a lot during the play. At the start she is an uneducated girl who sells flowers, and by the end she has been taught how to speak. At the garden party she passes as a duchess and the people there are fooled. In Act IV she says she sold flowers, not herself. This is an important moment, because it shows that she has a sense of dignity that Higgins has not thought about, and that the lessons have not removed it.

Doolittle is Eliza’s father, a dustman, and he comes to Higgins’s house to ask for money. He says he is one of the undeserving poor. He does not want to be respectable, and he thinks middle-class morality is an excuse for not giving the poor anything. This shows the class system from the lower side. It adds to the play’s cultural tension because it makes the upper-class characters uncomfortable.

Overall, the characters create most of the tension in the play, although setting and language are also important. Higgins and Eliza are the most important characters, and the play shows how their relationship changes over the course of the lessons. The ending, where Eliza marries Freddy, shows how the characters decide the outcome for themselves. The statement is partly right, because Shaw uses characters to show the cultural tension, but the drama also depends on other parts of its design.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the class conflict and Eliza’s change, but the references are few and general, and several sentences retell the plot instead of analysing it. To reach the 13-16 row, it needs to tie one or two lines, such as Higgins’s boast about a duchess, to the argument and show what each line does to the tension.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pygmalion is about a professor called Henry Higgins who teaches a flower girl called Eliza to speak properly. Eliza comes from a poor part of London and speaks with a strong accent. Higgins makes a bet with Colonel Pickering that he can pass her off as a duchess. Eliza has lessons, and she eventually goes to a party where she is well dressed and talks well. Later she is upset with Higgins and says she will not be treated like a servant. At the end she decides to marry Freddy. The play shows the difference between the upper and lower classes, and this is the cultural tension of the play.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the plot of Pygmalion and names its class theme without showing how characterisation creates the tension. To move up, it needs to name one specific moment from a character and explain what it shows about class.

prompts.question: Nonfiction relies primarily on storytelling to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The strongest answers test the word primarily instead of accepting or rejecting the statement outright. Look for a qualified position and evidence that storytelling sits beside structure, everyday detail and framing.
Pung's opening sentence is a deliberate choice about how the migrant story is received. Candidates who notice what the first line refuses are analysing the storytelling, not summarising it.

The cultural tension here lives inside the family and between generations, not only between Cambodian and Australian ways. Answers that place Alice between her mother and her paternal grandmother, and follow that conflict through the text, reach the upper rows.

The memoir is open about drawing on family stories and on Pung's reading for the Cambodian past. Answers that treat every recalled story as settled fact overstate the evidence and are marked down for it.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the family's flight from Cambodia as a plot summary without analysing how Pung tells it.
Reading storytelling as the same thing as the story, with no attention to structure, the opening sentence or the epilogue.
Agreeing or disagreeing outright without testing the word primarily against the memoir's other techniques.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. As nonfiction, Alice Pung's Unpolished Gem does rely heavily on storytelling: the memoir is built from the stories a family tells about itself and the stories a daughter inherits and retells. Its cultural tension, and the way it treats identity and language, depends on that storytelling. But the word primarily asks more than that. The tension is also made through the memoir's structure, through small observed scenes of migrant life, and through Pung's open admission that she reconstructs a past she did not witness. The statement is most persuasive when it is tested against the form of the book.

The first sentence, "This story does not begin on a boat", declines the migrant story most readers expect, the story of flight and suffering at sea. Pung has said she wanted to capture "the joy and the exuberance" of new migrants, and her early chapters show a family discovering a new country through ordinary things. Her father, who saw Australia as a wonderland, named her after the heroine of Alice in Wonderland, and the book keeps returning to the gap between that hope and daily reality. The opening therefore creates tension by withholding the expected drama. The reader has to work out the cultural weight of ordinary moments, and that choice is a storytelling decision as much as a story.

The most intense tension sits inside the family. Pung describes how her mother and her paternal grandmother used her as a weapon against each other. Alice is caught between two women who hold different versions of the family's history and different ideas of what a daughter owes her family. Because each woman speaks from her own position, the reader never receives one settled account of the past, and the cultural conflict becomes a conflict over whose story counts. That is the statement's strongest case: the competing narratives generate much of the book's force, and they do so largely through conversation, memory and argument rather than through plot.

The Cambodian history is where storytelling is most visible and most exposed. The memoir's account of Cambodia under the Pol Pot regime draws on the family's stories and on Pung's reading, and the book is open about that dependence. The grandmother's stories are vivid and emotionally direct, and one reviewer found them more compelling than the sections on Pung's own adolescence. This matters for the statement. If the sense of cultural identity comes mainly from inherited stories, the memoir's authority depends on how it frames them, and Pung frames them as things the family argues over rather than as a fixed record.

Several of the book's most telling moments are not stories in the usual sense. The mother makes and sells gold jewellery from the home, and the work is described as hard, so the cost of survival appears in daily routine rather than in a narrative event. A passage set in the Midway Migrant Hilton, where refugees hoard sugar, jam and honey from the breakfast table, presents scarcity and bewilderment through a single image. Other scenes, including a supermarket trip with her mother and Aunt Que, a school lesson on paganism and a valedictory dinner, place Alice between two cultural codes, and the tension comes from the contrast between them. These moments work through juxtaposition and understatement rather than through story.

Adolescence brings the conflict into the present. Pung's education, her choice of study and her career are shaped by her parents' wishes, and her romantic life as a teenager and young adult is constrained in similar ways. A chapter in Part 4 depicts her experience of depression, which shows the personal cost of holding these expectations together. Here the cultural tension is embodied in relationships and in the body, not carried by stories alone. The gap between a young woman's wish for independence and a family's sense of obligation is the strongest evidence against a purely narrative reading of the memoir.

The frame matters too. The memoir is organised as a prologue, five parts and an epilogue, and the epilogue has the family gathered at a cemetery on the anniversary of the paternal grandmother's death. That ending does not settle the conflicts between mother and grandmother. It turns competing stories into shared ritual, which suggests that cultural identity survives argument rather than being resolved by it. The structure is therefore a second kind of storytelling, one that shapes how the family's stories are received.

Overall, storytelling is the main vehicle through which Unpolished Gem makes cultural tension felt, and I agree with the statement to that extent. I disagree that it works alone. The inherited stories of Cambodia and the rivalry between two women supply much of the tension, while the opening, the everyday scenes and the structure shape how that tension is understood. The memoir's real achievement is that its stories never settle the question of identity for the reader.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates the statement and holds a qualified position on primarily, supported by close references to the opening sentence, the mother and grandmother, and the epilogue. Its strength is the way it tests storytelling against structure and everyday scene. The move that would lift it is to weigh the Cambodian stories and the migrant scenes directly against each other, so the reader sees which carries more of the tension.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. Unpolished Gem is a memoir, so storytelling is obviously important, and Alice Pung tells many stories about her family. Her family are Chinese-Cambodian, and they escaped the Khmer Rouge before coming to Australia. The stories are about the family's history and about how they settled in Melbourne. This creates cultural tension because the family has different ideas about its culture and Alice has to deal with them. However, storytelling is not the only thing that creates tension in the book, so I do not fully agree with the statement.

The book begins with the line "This story does not begin on a boat". This is an interesting way to start because many migrant stories are about dangerous journeys by boat, so Pung is doing something different. It shows that the book is going to be about ordinary life in Australia and not only about the Khmer Rouge. The book also describes Australia as a wonderland, which is why Alice's father named her after the character in the book.

The relationship between Alice's mother and grandmother is important for the cultural tension. The two women do not get along and Alice is caught between them. Pung shows that they used her against each other. This is a source of tension in the family, and it is connected to culture because the grandmother and the mother have different ideas about what the family should do. The book shows this through stories, so storytelling is important again.

The family also has to work hard to survive. The mother makes gold jewellery at home, which helps the family financially. Alice goes to school and has to fit in with other Australian children. There is a lesson about paganism at school and a valedictory dinner, and these scenes show Alice moving between two cultures. Pung also writes about refugees at the Midway Migrant Hilton, where people hoard sugar, jam and honey.

The structure of the book also creates tension. There is a prologue, five parts and an epilogue. The epilogue takes place at the cemetery, where the family pays respects to the grandmother. This shows how important the grandmother is to the family and how the family remembers her.

Overall, storytelling is an important part of the book and it creates cultural tension. The family's stories about Cambodia and the conflict between the women are the main examples. However, other things like the family's work and the structure also contribute to the tension, so the statement is only partly true.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the family's stories and their conflict, but it rarely analyses how a technique creates tension, and its references to the opening line, the jewellery work and the cemetery are brief and largely retold. Its strength is a clear position that the statement is partly true. The move that would lift it is to take one scene, such as the mother's jewellery work or the Midway passage, and analyse how Pung's choice of detail produces the tension.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Unpolished Gem is a memoir by Alice Pung about her family. They are Chinese-Cambodian and they came to Australia after escaping the Khmer Rouge, and they lived in Melbourne. The book has lots of stories, especially the stories the grandmother tells about Cambodia and the past. Alice has a difficult time with her mother and grandmother, who argue a lot and sometimes fight over her. Her mother has a business making gold jewellery at home.

Alice goes to school and wants to be like other Australian kids, and her parents want her to do well at school and get a good job. Pung also tells us about school, which is part of how she grew up. The book ends with the family at the cemetery.

I agree a bit with the statement because there are lots of stories in the book, but there are other things in it as well, like the family's work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the family and retells the memoir's situation with minimal textual reference, and its view of the statement is asserted rather than argued. prompts.question: Film relies primarily on dialogue to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The strongest answers test how far dialogue carries the cultural tension, rather than treating every line as culture. Look for a qualified position on primarily and for the way the film's setting and performance share the work.

The courtroom scene is the best place to test the statement, because the legal language and the family's speech collide there. Candidates who show how the comedy depends on that collision are analysing dialogue, not describing it.

The Mabo reference is contested. Candidates who raise the criticism that the film may naively link the Kerrigans with Indigenous dispossession, and then weigh it, show the evaluative skill this question rewards.

Catchphrases are easy to list and hard to analyse. Strong answers say what a line does for the family's identity, how the audience is positioned to laugh with the family, and why that matters to cultural tension.

Summarising the court case and the house without linking either to dialogue or to cultural tension.
