sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. Dialogue does a great deal of the work in Rob Sitch's The Castle. The Kerrigans' catchphrases, the opening words and the courtroom speeches make cultural identity audible, and the comedy depends on the gap between how this family talks and how lawyers, developers and officials talk. But the word primarily underestimates the film. The cultural tension is also built through setting, performance and the physical world of the house, which shows things that the characters never say. Dialogue is central, but it is not the only source of tension in the film.

The film opens with Dale telling us "this is my story", and that framing matters. From the first scene the audience is invited to see the Kerrigans from the inside, as a family with its own language, pride and sense of what counts. Their speech is full of sayings that turn ordinary things into family rituals. Darryl's "tell him he's dreamin'" returns across the film as a sign of his stubborn optimism, and "going straight to the pool room" turns a cheap find into a joke the family shares. These lines do more than entertain. They show a culture that values small pleasures and loyalty above status.

The courtroom is where the dialogue creates the sharpest friction. Dennis Denuto, the protest group's solicitor, argues from the constitution and from Mabo, and the speech slides into the claim that the case turns on "it's the vibe". The comedy works because the legal vocabulary is serious and the content is absurd, but the scene also makes a cultural point. The Kerrigans' attachment to their home is expressed in language the court cannot hear, while the formal language of law is shown to be just as loose. The audience hears a culture judged by a vocabulary it does not share, and it laughs at the legal world as well as at the family.

Critics have noticed the risks in this use of dialogue. Mabo is the case that rejected terra nullius, and the film's invocation of it can be read as naively linking the Kerrigans' fight with the dispossession of Australia's Indigenous peoples. That reading challenges any claim that the dialogue creates a clear cultural meaning. The irony is sharp: the words that should carry the most weight are the ones the film treats most lightly, so the cultural tension is exposed rather than resolved.

Much of the tension, however, is visual and spatial. The house sits on a former landfill site beside an airport runway, and that location is why the family's home is wanted. The house is ordinary, but the film makes it the centre of the family's identity. The shack at Bonnie Doon, built beneath towering power lines, is another space where setting carries meaning. The family does not see the pylons as ugly. Dale's reading of them as a reminder of human power to make electricity is a line of dialogue, but it reframes a setting the audience can see for itself. Words interpret the image, so the two cannot be separated easily.

The most convincing answer is therefore a qualified one. Dialogue creates the film's humour, its sense of family and much of its satire of lawyers, developers and officials. Yet the cultural tension depends on what the audience sees: the landfill, the runway, the shack under the pylons, the house the family fights to keep. The film says the Kerrigans are ordinary, and it shows an ordinary house as a site of struggle. To say that dialogue works primarily alone is to forget that the film argues through images as well as words.

Overall, dialogue is the film's most memorable means of creating cultural tension, and its catchphrases and courtroom speeches show how language marks a suburban working-class culture against a legal and governmental one. But dialogue shares that work with setting and with the film's ordinary spaces. The Castle is therefore best described as a film whose words and images create tension together, and the statement holds only in part.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates how far dialogue carries the cultural tension in The Castle, using precise references to the opening words, the courtroom speech and the house. Its strength is the link between Denuto's legal language and the family's own speech. The move that would lift it is to test the Mabo reference more closely, since that is where the film's dialogue is most open to criticism.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. The Castle has a lot of dialogue that is funny and memorable, and the family's catchphrases are a big part of why people remember the film. Dialogue is important for the cultural tension because the Kerrigans talk differently from the lawyers and officials. However, the film also uses the house and the airport, so I do not fully agree that it relies primarily on dialogue.

The film begins with Dale saying "this is my story", which tells us the film is about the family. The family says things like "tell him he's dreamin'" and "going straight to the pool room". These lines are funny and they show what the family is like. Darryl says a lot of things that show his personality, and the audience enjoys them. The family's sayings are part of their culture, so they connect to the statement.

The courtroom scene is where the dialogue is most important. Dennis Denuto is the lawyer for the protest group, and he is not very good at his job. He talks about the constitution and about Mabo, and then he says it is about the vibe. The audience laughs at him, which shows that the lawyers are not as serious as they think. The scene shows a conflict between the family and the legal system, and the dialogue makes that conflict funny.

The Kerrigans live in a house near an airport, and the government wants to take it so the airport can extend its runway. The house is built on a landfill site. Darryl also has a shack at Bonnie Doon, which is under power lines. These places are important to the family. The film shows that the family loves these places even though other people would not want to live there, so the setting also creates tension.

The dialogue creates cultural tension because the family's ideas are different from the government's. The lawyers talk in a formal way and the family talks in a casual way, and this difference is what makes the film funny. The film is about Australian culture, which is shown through the Kerrigans' life in the suburbs.

Overall, dialogue is an important part of The Castle, but the house and the setting are also important for the cultural tension. The statement is therefore partly true.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the catchphrases and the courtroom scene, but the references are thin and partly retold, and the analysis of the house and setting is asserted rather than shown. Its strength is a clear qualified position. The move that would lift it is to take the courtroom speech and analyse how its legal vocabulary is used for comic effect.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Castle is a film by Rob Sitch about the Kerrigan family, who live near an airport in Melbourne. The government wants their house, so the family and its neighbours fight the plan with a solicitor called Dennis Denuto. The father, Darryl, says funny things like "tell him he's dreamin'", and his son Dale opens the film by saying "this is my story".

Denuto is not very good and talks about the constitution in court. The family is working class and the film is funny, with lots of jokes. Many Australians remember the film for its sayings.

Dialogue is important because the characters say funny lines, so I agree with the statement a lot. The house is also important to the family, and the family cares about it.

prompts.question: Media relies primarily on images to create cultural tension. To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The strongest answers test primarily rather than accepting that a documentary must be carried by its pictures. Look for a qualified position and for an account of how image and speech work together.
Merewether's dual role as director and cinematographer matters. Candidates who use the fact that the images come from a filmmaker present in the landscape show a sharper sense of the medium.
The title is an argument about where culture lives. Candidates who read it as a claim about people as carriers of culture, not only about land, reach the upper rows.

The historical tension, the boarding schools and the separation of children from herding life, has to be linked to the images to count. Answers that describe the landscape without linking it to the policy stay in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the landscape and reindeer without saying how the camera builds meaning from them.
Treating Saami culture as a general Indigenous culture, or writing about it as if it were Australian Aboriginal culture.
Stating what the film's narration or interviews contain without checking the film.
Ignoring the language mix, so that the film's English and Northern Saami is never analysed.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. Reindeer in my Saami Heart is a documentary, so images carry much of its meaning: the Arctic landscape, the herds, and the places where Inghilda Tapio lives and works. Janet Merewether, who directed the film and also shot it, uses those images to make the tension between Saami culture and state policy visible. But the word primarily underrates the film's words. Tapio's life story, the mix of English and Northern Saami, and the title itself carry as much argument as the pictures, so the cultural tension depends on how image and language work together.

As a media text, the film makes its argument before the first image appears. The title, Reindeer in my Saami Heart, places an animal, a herding tradition and a people inside a single phrase. It suggests that culture is carried in people rather than only in the land. That is a verbal idea, and it sets up the film's central claim: a culture that has been moved, schooled or removed can still live in the person who carries it. The landscape is then read through that idea rather than admired as scenery.

The historical tension is established through Tapio's childhood. She was born in 1946 into a reindeer-herding family in the Swedish Arctic. At seven she was removed from her family for months at a time, after the Swedish government ended mobile schooling and sent nomadic children to residential boarding schools. The tension here is cultural and political: a state policy separated children from the herding life that defined their families. The landscape then becomes evidence. The open land is the world the boarding school tried to take away, and the continuing herding practice shows that the policy did not finish the culture.

Merewether's camera work matters here. She was the film's cinematographer, and she travelled north of the Arctic Circle three times to make it, sometimes in severe cold. Because the images come from a filmmaker present in the landscape, they carry an authority that archival photographs could not. The herds and the snow read as part of a living relationship between a family and its land, not as scenery arranged for a visitor. That is a strong use of the medium, and it explains why images are central to the film's argument.

The threats to the herding life are presented in a similar way. Mining, forestry and hydroelectric development threaten the herding life, and the film makes those pressures visible in the land itself. This is where the statement is most persuasive, because an image can show a route cut or crossed by industry in a way that narration alone could not. Yet the claim is not made by images alone. Tapio's life is the frame through which the audience is asked to understand the threats, and the film is introduced through her eyes rather than through a neutral view of the land.

Language is the other half of the argument. The film blends English and Northern Saami, the minority language Tapio writes in, so the audience hears the culture before it fully understands it. A film made only of images could show a herd, but a film that places Saami speech beside English makes the viewer aware of a language set against Swedish, the language of the state that sent her to boarding school. The tension between the two languages is part of the film's cultural meaning, and pictures alone cannot carry it. Tapio's two languages also reflect a life lived close to a national border, in Karesuando on the Sweden-Finland frontier.

Overall, images are the film's most powerful medium, and the landscape and herding life carry much of the cultural tension. But the title, the bilingual speech and Tapio's life story do equal work, because they tell the audience what the images mean. The statement is only partly accurate. Images create the feeling of a culture under pressure, while language and story explain why that pressure matters. Merewether relies on both, and the tension is strongest where the two meet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates the extent to which images carry the film's cultural tension, drawing on the title, the bilingual speech and Tapio's history as well as the landscape. Its strength is the point that Merewether's own filming gives the images authority. The move that would lift it is to name one or two particular images from the film and analyse their composition, since the answer currently argues about images in general.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I partly agree with this statement. Reindeer in my Saami Heart is a documentary, and it has many striking images of the landscape and the reindeer. These images help to show the cultural tension between the Saami people and the Swedish government. However, the film also uses other things, such as language and its title, so I do not fully agree that it relies primarily on images.

The film is about Inghilda Tapio, who is a writer and poet. She was born in 1946 into a reindeer-herding family. When she was seven she was sent away to a boarding school, and she was separated from her family for long periods. This shows the cultural tension between her family and the government, because the government wanted children to attend school in towns.

The images are important in the film. The landscape is very big and empty, and there are reindeer. Janet Merewether made the film, and she was also the cinematographer. She travelled to the Arctic Circle three times to film. The images show the herding life and the snow, which makes the film look real. The audience can see how the family lives on the land.

The film also uses language. It has English and Northern Saami in it. Tapio writes in Northern Saami, so the language is important for her culture. The title Reindeer in my Saami Heart also suggests that the culture is in people's hearts and not just in the land. This is a nice idea that the film supports.

The film shows threats to the herding life, such as mining and forestry. These threats are shown in the landscape. This makes the audience worried about the future of Saami culture. A viewer who knows about the boarding schools may also read the empty land as a place where families were divided.

Overall, the images are very important in the film and they create cultural tension. However, the language and the title are also important, so the statement is only partly true.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the film's subject and history, but its references are general and its image analysis is thin, relying on description of the landscape rather than analysis of how the camera builds meaning. Its strength is a clear claim that the statement is partly true. The move that would lift it is to analyse one sequence and show how image and speech combine to produce the tension.

Reindeer in my Saami Heart is a documentary by Janet Merewether about Inghilda Tapio, a Saami writer. It shows the reindeer and the landscape where she lives, in Sweden. Tapio went to boarding school when she was a child and was separated from her family, which is sad.

The film uses English and Northern Saami. The images of reindeer are very nice to look at and show what life is like for the Saami people. The director is from Australia, which is interesting.

I agree that images are very important in this film because you can see the reindeer and the snow. The film is about culture and change, and it is good to watch.

Its strength is a correct identification of the subject and the language. The move that would lift it is to choose one image and explain what it shows about Saami life.

prompts.question: Analyse how language creates a sense of identity for individuals within a community in your prescribed text. In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks how language creates identity, so the strongest answers treat speech as an act that makes and limits a community, not as a feature of characterisation.
The lay-off is the key concept. Answers that show how the men's idiom turns a seasonal break into a shared creed do more than describe their holiday.
Pearl and Johnnie Dowd are the outsiders who test the community's language, and the strongest responses use them to show where that language draws its boundaries.
The smashed doll at the end is the play's clearest statement about language and identity. Responses that connect the final image to the earlier speech earn the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the men as laconic Australians without showing how their words create identity for individuals within the community.
Treating Lawler's dialect as comic colour only, and missing that it marks belonging and class.
Summarising the acts in order and leaving the language analysis to a single paragraph at the end.
Claiming that the play simply praises the bush, without noticing that the men's world is shown to be ageing and ending.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Ray Lawler's Summer of the Seventeenth Doll shows language creating a sense of identity for individuals within a community, and it also shows that the community's language is its limit. Roo and Barney speak a loose, colloquial Australian English, and that speech binds them into a bond of mateship the play treats as admirable and fragile. Lawler spells the men's speech phonetically and uses their idiom to mark them as cane cutters from Queensland, then sets it against the city talk of Pearl, Olive and the Melbourne household. In this play identity is spoken into being, and it can be spoken out of being as well.

The central phrase of the men's language is the lay-off, the annual break from cane work they spend in the city. Lawler lets the men define it in their own words. The rest of the year is a grind, which Olive calls "killin' themselves", and the lay-off is "a time for livin'". The phrase carries the whole value system of the men: work is endured, and identity is found in the holiday. Olive shares that creed. She sees Roo as an outback hero and builds her happiness around his return, so the language of the lay-off becomes a bond that includes the women as well as the men.

The women's language works differently, and the contrast is part of the play's argument. The play opens with women talking about Nancy's wedding, so the audience learns at once that the summer community is already changing. Olive's talk of Roo as an outback hero is a language of idealisation. It keeps the lay-off alive for her, but it also asks Roo to be a figure he cannot sustain. Her words build a shared identity that depends on the men staying what they were, and the play shows the cost when they cannot.

Language also sorts people into insiders and outsiders. Pearl, the newcomer, speaks in innuendo and sub-text, and she says Nancy "made herself cheap", which sets her apart from the community the men have made. Johnnie Dowd is another outsider. He is a bush man brought into the city who cannot see what Roo and Barney value in the place. Barney introduces him to Bubba in the second act, as though a newcomer must be vouched for in the men's own terms. In each case the characters' talk reveals what they think of each other, and Lawler shows that identity forms in the gap between how individuals speak and how the group speaks.

Roo's relationship with Olive shows the cost of this language. Each year he gives her a kewpie doll, so the dolls become a private record of their life together, a language of gifts that Olive treats as a sign of loyalty until Roo asks her to marry him and she refuses. At the end Roo smashes the seventeenth doll against the piano. The breaking is a visual sentence, and it is all the more forceful because the play has spent three acts listening to people talk around what they feel. When the ritual that was carried in words and gifts breaks, the community that the language supported breaks too. The final image says what the men cannot, and it is the play's clearest statement about language and identity.

Lawler's achievement is that these characters are recognisably Australian without being caricatures. Their speech is ordinary and their humour is blunt, and the audience is invited to recognise the men's loyalty and the women's pride. The play suggests that a community's identity lives in the stories it tells about itself, and that when those stories stop fitting the people who tell them, the individuals must find a new language. Roo's first gesture of acceptance late in the play is that new language, and it is far quieter, and far harder, than the men's talk of the lay-off.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it treats speech as the thing that makes and limits a community, tracing identity through the lay-off, Pearl, Johnnie Dowd and the broken dolls. The move that would lift it further is to put one more line of the men's dialogue under close analysis, showing how a single phrase sets the men apart from the city women.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Ray Lawler's play shows language creating identity for the men. Roo and Barney talk like cane cutters, and their speech makes them part of a community of mates. The men's language also divides them from the women and from the city people. The play uses the word lay-off to describe the time they spend in Melbourne, and this shows that the men see their holiday as something special.

The lay-off is important because it is the time when the men feel most themselves. Lawler presents the rest of the year as hard work and the lay-off as a time of enjoyment. The men's way of speaking shows this, because they describe their life with simple words about work and fun. This makes the community seem real and gives the audience a sense of who the men are.

Olive is an important character in this. She admires Roo, and she sees him as an outback hero. Her language about him shows that she has an idea of what a man should be. This idea is part of her identity and it links her to the community of cane cutters, though it also limits her.

The women's speech is different, and the play lets the audience hear the difference. Olive's admiration of Roo is a way of holding on to the lay-off, and it asks him to remain the outback man she first knew. Pearl's innuendo is a city style, and her remarks mark the boundary between the women who have stayed in the city and the men who return from the cane fields.

Pearl is different. She is a newcomer to the group, and she speaks with innuendo. She says Nancy "made herself cheap", which shows that she sees herself as separate. Johnnie Dowd is also an outsider and does not understand what Roo and Barney value. These characters show that language separates people as well as connecting them.

The doll is the last important symbol. Roo gives Olive a doll each year. At the end of the play the doll is smashed, and this suggests that the community and its language are ending. The play therefore shows that identity depends on shared language, and that it can be lost when the shared language no longer works.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it shows that the men's language creates a community, but the points are explained rather than analysed, and the references to the play are thin. The move that would lift it is to take the phrase lay-off and show how the men's use of it defines who belongs and who does not.

sampleAnswers.answer: Summer of the Seventeenth Doll is about two men, Roo and Barney, who are cane cutters from Queensland. They come to Melbourne for a break every year and they stay with Olive. The men talk to each other in a casual way and they call their holiday the lay-off. Roo gives Olive a doll each year and the dolls are important. Pearl is a new character who does not fit in. Johnnie Dowd is another man from the bush. At the end of the play a broken doll lies on the floor. This shows that something has changed and that the characters are not as happy as they were. The language of the play helps to show the characters and their community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the situation and lists the characters without analysing how language forms identity or quoting the play. The move that would lift it is to choose one line of the men's speech and explain what it tells the audience about how they see themselves.

dotPoints.description: The ways mode and medium shape meaning

prompts.question: Describe how the mode and medium of your prescribed text shape meaning for its audience.
markerNotes: Describe means setting out the features and their effect. Name the mode or medium, give one example, then say what it does for the listener or reader.
Compare the two modes on one point, such as pace or emphasis, so the description shows what is specific to each medium.
commonStudentErrors: Confusing mode (the form of communication, such as spoken or written) with medium (the channel, such as a podcast or a magazine).
Describing the content of the text rather than the way the medium carries it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes precisely how the mode and medium of the text shape meaning for its audience, with specific examples of each
3 marks: Describes how the mode or medium shapes meaning, with some examples
2 marks: Names the mode or medium with a general statement about meaning
1 mark: Identifies a medium without linking it to meaning

sampleAnswers.answer: The mode and medium of the podcast shape meaning for its audience in ways a printed article could not. In its audio form, the text relies on the mode of spoken voice, so listeners hear hesitation, emphasis and breath. These sounds create intimacy and suggest sincerity, because the audience feels the speaker is thinking aloud. The medium also lets listeners work while they listen, so the text builds meaning through pacing and repetition rather than layout. A printed article would rely on headings and images, and a reader could pause to re-read a paragraph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented podcast and article for illustration. It names the mode and medium, gives specific effects of the spoken voice and the audio channel, and compares them with print. The examples and effects together are what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The podcast uses spoken voice, which makes it feel personal. People can listen while doing other things.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the mode and medium with a general statement about meaning and no detailed example, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: It is a podcast, not a magazine.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a medium without linking it to meaning, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is comparing how a short podcast episode and a printed magazine article present the same story. Her teacher asks her to describe how the mode and medium of a text shape its meaning for an audience.

prompts.question: Distinguish between how the spoken mode and the written mode of your prescribed text shape meaning for readers and listeners in a medium.
markerNotes: Distinguish means identifying what separates the two. Pick one point of difference and show what each mode does with it.
Separate mode from medium in your answer. The mode is spoken or written; the medium is the channel that carries it.
commonStudentErrors: Claiming the transcript has no meaning beyond the words, when the layout and reading pace also shape it.
Listing differences without saying which difference changes the meaning.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Distinguishes clearly between the spoken and written modes, showing with examples how each shapes meaning
2 marks: Distinguishes the modes with a general reference to meaning
1 mark: Identifies a difference without linking it to meaning

sampleAnswers.answer: The spoken and written modes shape meaning in distinct ways. A spoken text carries pauses and tone, so listeners read intention into the voice. The written version loses those cues, so the reader must supply tone alone. The medium also differs: a recording is experienced in time, while a transcript is read at the reader's own pace. The distinction is one of control: the written mode leaves the reader in charge of meaning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes the two modes on a clear point, the cues available to the listener or reader, and shows how each mode changes the meaning. Its link to the medium, time or pace, is what earns the full mark. The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration.

sampleAnswers.answer: The spoken text has tone and pauses. The written text does not, so readers have to imagine them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes the modes with a general reference to meaning and no explanation of the effect, so it sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Spoken texts are recorded and written texts are on paper.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a difference between medium and mode without linking it to meaning, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 class is comparing a recorded interview with a transcript of the same interview. Students must distinguish how the spoken and written versions of the text shape meaning for their audience.

dotPoints.description: The ways context and implicit cultural assumptions influence the perspectives and ideas of authors

prompts.question: Assess the extent to which an author's context and implicit cultural assumptions influence the perspectives and ideas in your prescribed text. In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: Assess asks for a judgement of extent. Weigh the author's influence against what the text does to challenge it, then state how far the context determines the ideas.
Implicit assumptions need evidence of their own. Show how the text treats something as obvious, not only what it says.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the author's background without showing how it appears in the text's ideas.
Assuming the author's context determines every idea without testing that claim against the text.
prompts.markingCriteria:
9-10 marks: Assesses the extent to which context and implicit cultural assumptions influence perspectives and ideas, weighing competing influences against evidence and reaching a sustained, explicit judgement
7-8 marks: Assesses the influence of context and assumptions on perspectives and ideas with clear evidence, reaching a developed judgement
5-6 marks: Assesses the influence with a clear judgement and some evidence, though the weighing of competing influences is brief
3-4 marks: Describes context and assumptions and their effect on perspectives, with a general judgement
1-2 marks: Makes a general statement about the author's influences with little evidence, or states that context affects authors without assessment

sampleAnswers.answer:
To assess the extent to which an author's context and implicit cultural assumptions influence the perspectives and ideas of a text, it is necessary to weigh the author's position against the evidence the text provides. The text I have studied was written in a period of rapid social change, and the author's context shapes its ideas in visible ways. The narrator's view of work, family and duty reflects expectations that were common in the author's community, and these shape the perspectives the text presents as natural. The influence of context is strong, but it is not total, because the text also challenges the ideas it inherits.

The most significant influence is the implicit cultural assumption that a good life is measured by stability. The text never states this assumption; it appears in the way the narrator judges characters who move frequently, describing them as restless or unreliable. A reader from a different background may not share this judgement, which suggests the assumption is embedded rather than argued. This embedding matters because it means the perspectives in the text are presented as common sense. The author's cultural position therefore determines not only what is said but what seems self-evident, and the text's ideas follow from that position.

Against this influence, the text complicates its own assumptions. In the later sections, the narrator begins to doubt the value of stability, and the language of these passages becomes more tentative, with questions replacing confident judgements. This shift shows that the perspectives are not fixed by context alone. The author has allowed the text to test its inherited ideas, and the reader sees the tension between the author's context and the narrator's growing scepticism. The influence of context is evident, but the text also shows an author able to reflect on the assumptions they were raised with.

Weighing these influences, I judge that context and implicit cultural assumptions are the dominant forces shaping the text's perspectives, but they do not determine its ideas completely. The embedded assumption about stability establishes the frame in which the narrator thinks, and most of the ideas are developed within that frame. Yet the later doubt shows that the author has made room for a different perspective, so the text is strongest where it reveals the limits of its own context. In my assessment, the influence is substantial and deliberate, and it is the text's willingness to question that influence that makes its ideas memorable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration. It weighs the author's context and an embedded assumption against the text's own questioning, and reaches an explicit judgement of extent. That weighing of competing influences is what earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The author's context influences the text's ideas, because the narrator shares the expectations of the author's community. The assumption that stability is good is important and affects the perspectives. The text also has some doubts later, so the influence is not complete. Overall, context has a strong effect on the perspectives.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a clear judgement with some evidence about how the context shapes perspectives, but the weighing is brief and the later doubt is noted without analysis, so it sits in the 5-6 mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The author's time and place affect the text, so the ideas are old.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about the author's influences with little evidence, so it sits in the 1-2 band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing an evaluative essay for a critical reading task. The text is an invented novel, written in a period of rapid social change, in which the narrator judges characters who move frequently as restless or unreliable, and later doubts the value of stability. She must assess how far the author's context and unstated cultural assumptions determine the perspectives and ideas presented in the text.

prompts.question: State TWO implicit cultural assumptions that an author's context might introduce into the perspectives and ideas of a text, with ONE example for each.
markerNotes: State is a recall task. Two assumptions, each named plainly and matched to one example, is the full answer.
An assumption is something the author takes for granted, not a fact about the author's life.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a personal opinion as an assumption without linking it to the author's context.
Giving an example that does not show the assumption at work in the text.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: States two implicit cultural assumptions, each with an example of how it shapes a text's perspectives or ideas
1 mark: States one assumption, or gives an example without stating the assumption

sampleAnswers.answer: Context can carry two implicit cultural assumptions an author holds: family duty outranks ambition, and men lead. A character who quits a career unquestioned makes the first seem natural. A woman's choices judged as failures shape perspectives and ideas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States two implicit cultural assumptions, each linked to an example of how it shapes perspectives and ideas. Both are stated plainly and connected to the author's context, which is the full 2-mark answer. The exemplar describes an invented text for illustration.

sampleAnswers.answer: An author might believe that family is important.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States one assumption without an example of how it shapes the text, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is preparing a short quiz on how context shapes writing for her class. She must state two implicit assumptions an author might carry, and give an example of each.

prompts.question: To what extent does your prescribed text disrupt assumptions about culture?
markerNotes: The question asks for the extent of disruption, so the strongest answers judge how far the novel goes and where it stops. A flat claim that the novel overturns everything is weaker than one that tests the limits.
Levy's four narrators are the evidence that matters most. Answers that show how each narrator's assumptions are exposed, rather than treating the novel as one view, reach the top band.

Hortense's picture of England is the strongest case of an assumption disrupted. The best responses explain why the belief seemed reasonable to her when she was taught it, and then show what it costs her.
Bernard and Queenie give the answer its range. Responses that use them to test the novel's claim against the reader's own expectations do more than summarise the London setting.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the plot of Small Island in order without asking which assumption about culture is disrupted, or how.
Treating Queenie's kindness as proof that the novel has no racism, and ignoring Bernard's attitudes.
Describing London as simply welcoming or simply hostile, without noticing that the novel shows both.
Presenting the characters as representatives of whole cultures, rather than as individuals whose assumptions the narration exposes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Evaluates effectively the extent to which assumptions about culture are disrupted in the prescribed text; Presents an effective response using relevant, detailed textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas effectively using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Evaluates competently the extent to which assumptions about culture are disrupted in the prescribed text; Presents a competent response using relevant textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas competently using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Evaluates the extent to which assumptions about culture are disrupted in the prescribed text; Presents a response using some textual knowledge; Organises and expresses ideas adequately using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes aspects of the text with some reference to the question; Presents a response using limited textual knowledge; Attempts to organise a response in a limited way
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the text; Attempts to organise a response in an elementary way

sampleAnswers.answer:
Andrea Levy's Small Island disrupts assumptions about culture to a considerable extent, though it does so by making its characters' beliefs visible rather than by simply correcting them. The most important belief it overturns is one the characters carry with them: that England is the Mother Country, a settled and superior culture into which colonial subjects may be absorbed if they are polite, educated and loyal. Levy builds that belief into Hortense Roberts and then lets London prove it false. The disruption works through form as well as plot, because the novel refuses to let any single culture speak for the nation.

The four first-person narrators do much of this work. Hortense, Gilbert Joseph, Queenie Bligh and Bernard Bligh each tell the story from their own viewpoint, so no one voice has the authority to define England or Jamaica. Because the narrators look back over their lives, each voice also reveals what the others leave out. Hortense is courteous and articulate, and her English is the product of a colonial schooling that taught her to admire England. Gilbert, who served in the RAF, expects his war service to count for something. Queenie, a white English woman, rents rooms to the Jamaican men who arrive, while Bernard holds racist attitudes that the others have to live with. Because the reader enters each mind, the assumptions of each are exposed from within rather than delivered as the author's verdict.

Hortense's story shows an assumption being disrupted most painfully. Her schooling gives her a picture of England as a golden city of learning and opportunity, and it gives her a sense of identity built on that picture. When she reaches London she finds it shabby, and the welcome she expected does not come. The disruption hurts because the belief was not foolish; it was taught to her as fact. She has done what the colonial system asked of her, so the rejection is also a rejection of the terms on which she was educated. Levy shows the cost of having been taught it, so a reader who has been told that England is home feels the same loss she does.

Queenie's house is the novel's other challenge to received ideas. Hortense and Gilbert come to her door as lodgers, which means the assumption about England meets its first test in an ordinary English house rather than in a grand public building. In 1948 a white woman who takes in Jamaican lodgers is breaking a social rule, and her neighbours disapprove. Queenie is calm and fair-minded, yet Levy does not make her a simple heroine: her kindness sits alongside the prejudices of her class and her time. The house becomes a place where two cultures share one roof, and the boundaries the wider society insists on are shown to be unstable in ordinary daily life.

The novel is also careful about the limits of its disruption. Bernard's racism is never softened into misunderstanding, and the hatred directed at the Jamaican characters is presented as the reality they must survive. Levy does not claim that the English are simply wrong about Jamaica, nor that the Jamaican characters are free of prejudice. Gilbert's cold reception after the war exposes the gap between a nation that called on Caribbean men to fight and the way it treated them afterwards. The reader is left to weigh each character's view against the others, which is the most direct way the novel disrupts a single account of culture. The title makes a similar point. Jamaica and Britain are both small islands, and each has been shaped by the other.

To what extent, then? Small Island disrupts assumptions about culture substantially. It takes apart the belief in England as the mother country, and it does so by letting the reader hear each character's assumptions from inside. What it does not do is replace one fixed culture with another. Its final effect is to show that culture is made by people who share a history, and that the history of these two islands is one of connection the nation has preferred not to acknowledge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it tests how far Small Island disrupts assumptions about culture, uses all four narrators and the mother country belief, and reaches a considered judgement on the extent. The move that would lift it further is to anchor each paragraph in one short phrase from the novel, so that the claims about Hortense's belief are shown in her own words.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Levy's Small Island challenges assumptions about culture mainly by showing that England's view of itself does not match how its people behave. The novel has four narrators, Hortense, Gilbert, Queenie and Bernard, so the reader hears how each of them sees the world. This means the assumptions of the characters are shown, and the novel's view of England is built from those narrations.

Hortense believes England is the mother country, and she has been taught to think so at school in Jamaica. When she arrives in London she is disappointed, because the city is not the place she imagined. This shows that her idea of England was wrong. The story of her disappointment helps the reader see that the idea was shaped by colonial education, which is one reason the novel is interesting.

Queenie is kind to the Jamaican men who come to her house, even though her neighbours disapprove. This disrupts the idea that white English people would reject them all. Queenie's kindness shows that not every English person held the prejudices of the time, which makes the novel less one-sided.

Bernard is the opposite. He is racist and withdrawn, and his attitudes are a reminder that prejudice was common in England. The novel uses his views to show the hostility that Gilbert and Hortense face. By comparing Bernard with Queenie, the novel suggests that England's culture is divided, and this is why assumptions about culture are disrupted.

Gilbert's experience after the war also shows the difference between what England promised and what it gave. He served in the RAF but is treated badly when he returns. This supports the view that the novel disrupts assumptions about the mother country.

Levy's title points to both Jamaica and Britain, so the novel asks readers to think of the two places as connected. The disruption of culture is therefore clear, although the novel does not give a complete answer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies Hortense's disappointment and Bernard's racism as evidence, but it explains what they show rather than analysing how the narration produces the effect, and it has few direct references. The move that would lift it is to choose one passage of Hortense's narration and show how its wording reveals the assumption she holds.

sampleAnswers.answer: Small Island is about England and Jamaica. The novel has four characters: Hortense, Gilbert, Queenie and Bernard. Hortense comes from Jamaica and wants a better life in England. When she gets there she finds it is not what she expected, and this is a sad part of the story. Gilbert was in the war and then came to England. Queenie has a house where people stay, and she is kind to them. Bernard is racist and not very nice. The book shows that people from different places do not always get along, and that makes the reader think about culture and about how people see each other. It is a long book with many parts, and the reader has to keep track of who is talking.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the four characters and their situations in order, with minimal reference, and it never tests the question's idea of the extent of disruption. The move that would lift it is to pick one character's assumption and show how the novel challenges it.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of how ideas about language, identity and culture are expressed through texts; demonstrate understanding of how language is used to shape meaning about individuals and/or cultural groups; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section I — Module A: Language, Identity and Culture (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

dotPoints.description: The ways content shapes the social, moral and ethical positions represented in texts

prompts.question: Evaluate how effectively the content of your prescribed text shapes the social, moral and ethical positions it represents.
markerNotes: Evaluate asks for a judgement against criteria. Name the criteria first, test each position against them, then weigh the result.
The best answers find the point where the content is inconsistent and say what that does to the position.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising the story's content without judging how well it shapes the positions.
Stating a judgement without naming the criteria it is measured against.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates how effectively the content shapes social, moral and ethical positions against clear criteria, reaching an explicit and well-supported judgement
5 marks: Evaluates the effect of content on positions with clear criteria and a judgement partly supported
4 marks: Evaluates some positions with examples and a general judgement
3 marks: Describes the content and positions with a limited judgement
2 marks: Makes a general judgement about the positions without evidence
1 mark: States a view of the story's content

sampleAnswers.answer:
The story's content shapes its social, moral and ethical positions with varying effectiveness, and I judge it against three criteria: whether the positions are clearly established, whether they are consistent, and whether their consequences are explored. On the first criterion the story is effective. Details such as the empty canteen and the unpaid final wages establish the social position that workers are disposable, without requiring an explicit statement.

The moral position is less consistent. The narrator condemns the manager's cruelty, yet at the end she accepts a favour from the same manager. This contradiction weakens the moral position, because the story asks the reader to judge a character whose own choices are not judged. The ethical position is stronger, since the unresolved compromise forces the reader to weigh it rather than accept it.

On the third criterion the story is less complete. The closure's consequences for the wider community are mentioned but not explored, so the social position remains focused on individuals. My overall judgement is that the content shapes the social and ethical positions effectively, but the moral position is undermined by an inconsistency the story does not resolve.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented story for illustration. It names three criteria, tests the content of each position against them, and reaches an explicit overall judgement. The identification of the inconsistency in the moral position is what earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The story is about a factory closing. The social position is that workers are not valued, which is shown in details like the empty canteen. The moral position is weaker because the narrator changes her mind at the end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates some positions with examples and a general judgement, but the criteria are not named and the ethical position is not assessed, so it sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The story is sad and the content is good.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a view of the content without reference to the positions or any criteria, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing a critical evaluation of a short story for a class debate. The story is invented: it centres on a factory closure, with an empty canteen and unpaid final wages, and its narrator condemns the manager's cruelty before accepting a favour from the same manager at the end. She must judge how well the story's content establishes the social, moral and ethical positions it represents, and state the criteria she uses.

prompts.question: Discuss how the content of your prescribed text presents a social or moral position that a reader may question.
markerNotes: Discuss means presenting more than one side. Show how the content makes the position persuasive, then how a reader can push back on it.
A balanced discussion ends on what the content invites the reader to do, not on a verdict alone.
commonStudentErrors: Stating the position without showing how the content presents it.
Presenting only the position and never the reader's possible challenge to it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses several aspects of the content that present the position, and how a reader might question it, with clear evidence and a balanced judgement
4 marks: Discusses how the content presents the position, with some evidence of how a reader might question it
3 marks: Describes the content and the position with a general reference to the reader
2 marks: Names the position with little discussion
1 mark: States a view of the story without reference to its content

sampleAnswers.answer:
The story presents a moral position, that loyalty to family can justify silence at work. The narrator hides a colleague's mistake, and the content frames this as protective rather than deceitful. The social position reinforces it: the workplace is a hierarchy in which silence is rewarded.

A reader may question this position, however. The content shows the cost of the silence, because the colleague is dismissed without a hearing. A reader who prioritises fairness will see the narrator's loyalty as a failure of responsibility, while another may accept it as a moral good. The content is arranged so that both responses are possible. The discussion is strongest when it recognises that the story offers a position and invites the reader to challenge it at the same time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The exemplar describes an invented story for illustration. It shows how the content presents the moral position, then sets out the specific cost that lets a reader challenge it, and ends on the tension the content invites. The balance between presentation and challenge is what earns the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The story says loyalty is more important than honesty. The narrator hides a mistake, which shows the moral position. Some readers may think this is wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the content and the position with a general reference to the reader, but does not develop the challenge, so it sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The narrator is loyal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a statement about the story without discussing how its content presents a position, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is preparing for a discussion task on a short story whose content presents a moral position that some readers would contest. The story is invented: its narrator hides a colleague's mistake to protect her family, and the colleague is dismissed without a hearing. Her teacher asks her to discuss how the content presents that position, and how readers might question it.

dotPoints.description: Develop an understanding of the ways language features, text structures and stylistic choices shape points of view and influence audiences

prompts.question: Describe TWO language features and ONE text structure that the columnist uses to position readers in the opinion column.
markerNotes: A strong answer names each feature precisely, such as a rhetorical question or a short anecdote, and then says what it does to a reader rather than only what it is.
The verb asks for description, so one clear sentence of effect per feature is enough. A full analytical paragraph does not earn extra marks here.
Examples must come from the column itself. A feature without an example cannot move above the 2-mark band.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features such as 'emotive language' or 'imagery' without pointing to any example from the column.
Describing what the column is about, the library closure, instead of the language and structure the writer uses.
Treating 'text structure' as a single topic sentence rather than describing how the whole column is ordered.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two language features and one text structure accurately, each with a specific example from the column, and links each one to the way readers are positioned
3 marks: Describes two features, or one feature and one structure, with accurate examples, but the link to readers is general or partly missing
2 marks: Names relevant features with a general example and little description of how each one works
1 mark: Names a feature or structure without an example or description

sampleAnswers.answer: The opinion column opens with an anecdote about a retired bus driver who learned to read at the library. This warmth positions the reader, especially ratepayers, to see the library as a place where ordinary people were helped, so closing it seems to take something from them. The rhetorical question, 'Who will teach the next child to read when the shelves are gone?', is another of the language features: it needs no answer, so the reader supplies one and is drawn toward the writer's position. The text structure then moves from anecdote to costs and a single call to action, leading from sympathy to a decision.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two language features and one text structure are described, each with a specific example from the opinion column, and each is linked to how the reader is positioned. This meets the top band of the 4-mark ladder because the description goes beyond naming.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column opens with an anecdote about a retired bus driver, which makes the reader feel sympathy for the library. It also uses rhetorical questions, such as 'Who will teach the next child to read?', which make the reader think about what would be lost.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two features are named with an example each, and their effect on the reader is stated, but the description is general and the text structure is not addressed. This sits in the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column has an anecdote and some questions in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two features are named with no description of how they work and no link to the reader, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading an invented 600-word opinion column, written for this question, that argues the regional council should keep its Riverside branch library open. It was printed in a local newspaper read mainly by ratepayers, and it opens with a short anecdote about a retired bus driver who learned to read at the library. Its middle paragraphs ask rhetorical questions, such as 'Who will teach the next child to read when the shelves are gone?', and it then moves to a list of costs and a single call to action.

prompts.question: Analyse how the column's movement from a personal anecdote to a list of costs and then to a call to action shapes the reader's point of view on the council's decision.
markerNotes: The best answers treat the column as a chain: each section changes what the reader believes before the next section begins, and the analysis should follow that chain.
Analysis means consequences. Saying that the anecdote creates emotion is description; saying that the emotion makes the cost figures look like losses is analysis.
Keep the focus on the decision the column is trying to influence, so the analysis ends with a view of the council's proposal.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising each section in turn without showing how one section prepares the reader for the next.
Asserting that the column is persuasive without tracing how the reader's point of view moves.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the sequence of the column and explains how each movement shapes the reader's point of view, showing the relationships between sections and the cumulative effect on the decision
5 marks: Analyses the structure with clear links between two movements and the reader's point of view, supported by specific evidence
4 marks: Explains the structure with evidence, but the link between sections and the reader's view is only partly developed
3 marks: Describes the sequence with some evidence and makes a general statement about its effect
2 marks: Identifies the sections of the column with little explanation of effect
1 mark: Names the column's structure without explaining its effect

sampleAnswers.answer:
This opinion column is built as a chain, and each movement changes the reader's point of view before the next begins. The opening anecdote about a retired bus driver creates a personal connection, so the reader first sees the library as a place of personal growth rather than a line in a budget. That shift matters because the list of costs depends on it. Once the reader has decided the library is worth saving, the figures no longer look like neutral information: each cost reads as the price of losing something valued. The call to action then turns this altered point of view into a decision. Asking readers to attend the council meeting, a fortnight before the vote, relies on the earlier sections to have made them feel responsible for the outcome.

The structure therefore does more than present an argument. It reframes the council's proposal from a sensible saving into a choice the council must justify to ratepayers who have not yet decided. The anecdote slows the reading, the costs quicken it, and the call to action ends the column before the reader can return to the figures with a critical eye.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each movement is analysed for its effect on the reader's point of view, and the relationships between the sections are traced through to the final decision. The sustained chain of cause and effect is what separates this from explanation or description.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column moves from a personal anecdote to a list of costs and then to a call to action. The anecdote makes the reader feel the library matters personally, so the reader is more likely to respond to the costs. The call to action then asks readers to attend the meeting, so the structure moves the reader towards doing something about the council's decision.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The sequence is explained and the link from anecdote to reader is clear, but the effect of the costs on the reader's point of view is undeveloped and no specific evidence from the list is used. This places it in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column has an anecdote, a list of costs and a call to action, which come in a particular order.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The sections are named in order without any explanation of their effect on the reader, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: The class is studying the invented 600-word opinion column, written for this question, that argues the council should keep the Riverside branch library open. It was published in a local newspaper a fortnight before a council vote, so its readers are ratepayers who have not yet decided what to think. Its final call to action asks readers to attend the council meeting.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of the columnist's language features and stylistic choices in influencing an audience of local ratepayers, using the criteria of credibility, emotional appeal and logical reasoning.
markerNotes: Judgement is the test. The strongest answers say, in plain terms, how effective the column is and for whom, and then defend that view against each criterion.
Use all three criteria. A response that treats only emotional appeal, however well, is confined to the middle band.
Show interaction: an effective piece can be strong on one criterion and weak on another, and the best answers explain how the criteria combine.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the column's argument or features without ever making a judgement about how effective they are.
Giving a final verdict such as 'it is effective' without testing it against each criterion.
Naming the criteria in the introduction and then dropping them after the first paragraph.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained judgement on the effectiveness of the language features and stylistic choices against all three criteria, supported by precise evidence and an account of how the criteria interact
6 marks: Reaches a clear judgement against all three criteria, supported by precise evidence and a logical argument
5 marks: Reaches a judgement against the criteria with evidence, but one criterion is treated only in passing
3-4 marks: Describes the language features and stylistic choices with some evidence, and makes a judgement that is general or only partly linked to the criteria
2 marks: Makes a statement about effectiveness with little evidence and no clear use of the criteria
1 mark: Describes a feature without making any judgement

sampleAnswers.answer: On balance, the column is highly effective with ratepayers who already value the Riverside library, but its effectiveness is uneven when judged against all three criteria. In terms of credibility, the writer is strongest. The opening anecdote about a retired bus driver is specific and checkable against the library's own history, so the reader trusts the writer's knowledge of the community. The column also avoids overstating its case by admitting that the council faces real budget pressure, and this concession makes the rest of the writing appear fair-minded. In terms of emotional appeal, the language features do much of the work. The rhetorical questions and the repeated phrase 'a library is a promise' turn the library into something the reader has to keep, so the appeal is personal rather than abstract and well matched to older ratepayers who remember the building. The emotional appeal weakens in the costs section, where a list of numbers interrupts the warmth and the reader is asked to switch from feeling to calculating. Logical reasoning is the least convincing criterion. The column asserts that closing the branch will cost more in the long run, but it does not show the calculation, and a ratepayer who wants evidence will notice the gap. Taken together, the stylistic choices persuade readers who already share the writer's values and are less effective for a sceptical ratepayer. The writer's strongest tool is credibility, and it carries the emotional appeal, but the weak reasoning means the column is more likely to confirm existing opinions than to change them. A sceptical ratepayer who reads the column once, the way most people read a letter in a local paper, is likely to remember the anecdote and the call to action but not the numbers. For that reader the column's strongest criterion, credibility, is the one that matters most in a short encounter. For a reader who checks the figures, the same features become a liability, because the column asks for trust at the point where it should be giving reasons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A sustained judgement on effectiveness is reached against all three criteria, with evidence from the column for each and an account of how the criteria interact. The verdict is that the column works for a sympathetic reader and fails for a sceptical one, which is the explicit judgement the verb requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column is effective with ratepayers because it uses language features that make them feel the library matters. The anecdote about the bus driver gives the writer credibility, and the rhetorical questions make the emotional appeal strong, so many readers are likely to agree. However, the logical reasoning is weaker because the column claims the closure will cost more without showing how. The stylistic choices work well for readers who already care about the library, but the column is less persuasive for ratepayers who want numbers, so overall it is effective but not complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A judgement is reached and two criteria are used with evidence, but logical reasoning is dealt with only in passing and the answer does not explain how the criteria interact. This is the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The column is effective because it has a sad story and some questions that make people feel sorry for the library and want to keep it open.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A statement about effectiveness is made with little evidence and none of the named criteria are used, which matches the 2-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are writing a critical response for their folio on the invented 600-word opinion column, written for this question, which was published in a local newspaper before a council vote on the Riverside branch. The column admits the council faces real budget pressure, repeats the phrase 'a library is a promise', and says closing the branch will cost more in the long run without showing the calculation. The response must reach a judgement rather than simply retell the column's argument.

prompts.question: Explain how the language used in your prescribed text changed your perceptions about identity. In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks how the language of the memoir changed the reader's perceptions, so a retelling of the family's history without analysis of the prose misses the focus.
The grandmother's stories are the strongest evidence. Answers that show how the storytelling carries identity, and what it costs, reach the top band.
Alice's place as the eldest daughter, caught between her grandmother and her mother, gives the answer a clear point of tension. Use it to show how the memoir's language frames identity as contested.

The adult narrator's distance from the family's stories is what makes a perceptive answer. Responses that notice the difference between what the family says and how the narration judges it are the ones that stand out.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the family's escape from Cambodia as a sequence of events without showing how the narration changes the reader's view of identity.
Treating the book as a simple celebration of Chinese culture or of Australian multiculturalism, without the tension the memoir sets up.
Quoting long passages from memory and presenting them as exact wording.
Confusing the memoir with Pung's novel Laurinda, or treating the family as one fixed Chinese identity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Explains effectively how the language used in the prescribed text changed their perceptions about identity; Presents an effective response using relevant, detailed textual evidence; Organises, develops and expresses ideas effectively using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Explains competently how the language used in the prescribed text changed their perceptions about identity; Presents a competent response using relevant textual evidence; Organises, develops and expresses ideas competently using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Explains how the language used in the prescribed text changed their perceptions about identity; Presents a response using adequate textual evidence; Organises, develops and expresses ideas adequately using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes aspects of the text with some reference to the question; Presents a response using limited textual knowledge; Attempts to organise a response in a limited way
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the text; Attempts to organise a response in an elementary way

sampleAnswers.answer:
Alice Pung's Unpolished Gem changes perceptions of identity largely through its language, because the memoir asks the reader to hear a Chinese-Cambodian family in the voice of a daughter who grew up in Australia. The family fled the Khmer Rouge, spent time in a refugee camp and settled in Victoria in 1980, and the memoir is written in the English of the country that gave them a second start. The gap between the family's inherited language and the language of the narration is the first thing that unsettles the reader's assumptions. Identity here is not a fixed inheritance. It is something produced in the act of telling.

The most important voice in the book is the grandmother, Huyen Thai, whose stories about the old country reach Alice as spoken history. Pung presents this storytelling as the source of the child's sense of her Chinese identity. What changes the reader's perception is the way the grandmother's stories come through the adult narrator's precise and ironic prose. The stories are not nostalgic. They carry hardship and political danger, so the reader must weigh them against the narrator's own adult doubts. Through the grandmother, the memoir complicates the assumption that a culture is handed down whole.

The grandmother's own history gives her stories their weight. She was forced to leave China after speaking out against its government, and she later lived through the upheavals that drove the family out of Cambodia. When she tells Alice about these events, the reader hears an identity shaped by exile and by the need to survive. Pung does not sentimentalise that history. The stories are a way of holding a family together across three countries, and the memoir shows the child trying to understand what she has inherited from a woman who is both a source of strength and a source of conflict.

The birth stories are a second instance. Pung records the custom that husbands wait outside the delivery room to learn whether the newborn is a boy. Told as family lore, the stories look like customs. Told by a granddaughter who has grown up in Melbourne and who is herself a girl, they become a comment on gender and inheritance. The reader learns to see the custom from the position of the child who would have been less welcome in it. The ironic distance produces a shift in perspective: the family custom becomes something Alice can see as a problem rather than as her inheritance.

Alice's position as the eldest daughter, caught between her grandmother and her mother, sharpens this. The language of the family conflict is a language of alliance and grievance. Each woman offers Alice a version of the family's story, and Alice must decide which version to believe. The reader is placed in the same position. The effect is that identity appears as contested. The grandmother's stories of origin and the mother's struggles in the new country are shown as competing claims on the child, and the memoir makes the reader aware that identity is chosen as well as inherited.

Before reading the memoir, a reader might assume that a Chinese-Australian identity is a matter of tradition preserved against assimilation. The book's language shows instead a family negotiating assimilation constantly, in the daily details of school, work and speech. The parents' hope for a life in Australia, and their wish to keep their Chinese identity, appear in the same stories as the costs of that hope. The reader comes to see that the family's Chineseness has been remade in Melbourne, and that Alice's own identity is partly made by the act of writing it down.

The memoir does not resolve the question neatly, and its honesty is part of the change in perception. Pung does not present her family as heroic or her identity as settled. She shows how language carries memory and power, and how a daughter who writes in English can still be claimed by stories told in another tongue. Having read the book, the reader perceives identity as a conversation between generations rather than a possession. That is the most important change the language produces.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it follows the question into the prose itself, showing how the grandmother's storytelling and the adult narrator's distance change the reader's view of identity, and it treats the family's conflict as contested rather than settled. The move that would lift it further is to quote one short sentence from the memoir for each claim about the narration, since the answer currently argues from general description.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Alice Pung's Unpolished Gem changes the reader's view of identity because it is about a family that has moved between countries. The grandmother, Huyen Thai, tells stories about the old country, and these stories help Alice understand her Chinese identity. The stories are important because they pass on history in a spoken form, which makes the reader see identity as something that is handed down.

The memoir also shows the parents trying to build a life in Australia while keeping their Chinese identity. Their hope for a new life is an idea the reader can understand, and this changes how the reader sees migrants. The book is written in English, which shows that Alice has grown up in Australia and has a different way of speaking from her family.

Alice is the eldest daughter and is caught between her grandmother and her mother. This creates tension in the family, and the memoir shows how the family argues about the past. The reader sees that the family's stories are not all the same, and this makes identity seem complicated.

The birth stories are another example. Pung describes husbands waiting outside the delivery room to find out whether the baby is a boy. This shows a gender difference in the family, and it makes the reader think about the way Alice is treated as a girl. The language makes the reader notice this.

The book shows that identity is not fixed. Alice's memoir uses the language of the family and the language of Australia, and this helps the reader see identity as something that changes over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies the grandmother's stories and the family conflict, but it explains their significance in general terms and does not show how the language of the narration changes perception. The move that would lift it is to take one episode and show how the phrasing makes the reader see the family differently.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unpolished Gem is a memoir by Alice Pung about her family. Her parents came from Cambodia and her grandmother told stories about China. The family came to Australia and lived in Victoria. Alice is the oldest daughter and there is an argument between her grandmother and her mother. Alice wrote the book in English and it is about how her family lived. There is a part about the birth of children where the father waits outside. The memoir shows that the family had a hard time and that the language and stories are important to the book. Readers learn about Chinese and Australian identity from the story, and they can see how the family changed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the family's history and mentions the stories without analysing the language or the question's focus on changed perceptions. The move that would lift it is to choose one passage and explain how the wording shifts the reader's view of identity.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of how ideas about language, identity and culture are expressed through texts; demonstrate understanding of how language is used to shape meaning about individuals and/or cultural groups; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section I — Module A: Language, Identity and Culture (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.
