sampleAnswers.answer:
Family is the place in Contemporary Asian Australian Poets where culture is first handed down, and the anthology shows how that inheritance is carried, strained and remade across the migrant generation. In the poems set for study, family is an archive of stories, a field of sacrifice and a source of names that the speaker must learn to read. Culture does not arrive in these poems as a fixed body of tradition. It reaches the speakers through the people closest to them, in languages that do not always agree with one another.

Merlinda Bobis's This is where it begins makes this the clearest. The speaker asks where her urge to tell stories came from, and the poem tests several answers in turn: her grandmother's tales, her grandfather's teasing, her mother's scraps of Spanish, her father's gestures. The question is itself a family inventory. The poem opens in Bikol, moves into Pilipino and then English, so that its form enacts the layering of tongues within one household. The speaker concludes that storytelling is never a solitary act, because the storytellers who came before her live on inside her. Culture here is a voice passed down the family line, and the speaker's own writing is the latest link in that chain.

Family in Vuong Pham's poem Mother is shaped by war rather than by storytelling. The poem places the family's history in Saigon and the Fall of Saigon, and it shows a mother who wanted to teach in a high school. Instead she sewed garments for little pay so that her child could stay at school. Her sacrifice is the family's cultural cost, because the ambition she carried is set aside to secure a future in a new country. The poem then turns on the son's position. He now teaches English, so the work his mother wanted has passed to him in the language of his new country. The poem is also honest about the gap between his carefree childhood and the violence she had lived through, and that gap shows how migrant families carry memory unevenly. A reader who looks only at the son's career may miss how much of the mother's sacrifice is still carried in his work.

Maureen Ten's Translucent Jade extends this into identity and naming. The grandfather gives the speaker a gift at her birth, and her mother gives her a name. The poem thus holds two strands of family, one rooted in Chinese culture and one lived in Australia. Her uncertainty about a culture she was not taught in full suggests the difficulty of inheriting it, a feeling close to being an imposter. The jade is a symbol of luck and belonging that she can hold but cannot yet read. Ten's poem is brief in its statements, yet dense with the gifts the speaker is still learning to interpret. Ten suggests that family transmits culture as an object or a name whose meaning must be recovered, not as a complete body of knowledge.

Taken together, the three poems show that family is both the vehicle and the pressure point of culture. Bobis presents inheritance as a chain of storytellers, Pham shows its cost in migration, and Ten shows the uncertainty that comes when gifts are given before they are understood. Contemporary Asian Australian Poets gathers the writing of migrants, their children and refugees, and in these poems the family is where Asian heritage becomes Australian experience. The anthology argues that culture survives through family not by being preserved intact, but by being reshaped in each generation. The grandmother's tales become the poem, the mother's sacrifice becomes the son's teaching, and the grandfather's gift becomes a name the speaker must learn to say. That is an argument about family which is also an argument about culture.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 criteria row. It explains how the poems inform an understanding of family and culture, uses several detailed references across three poems, and organises the argument with control. To lift it further, the closing paragraph could test the anthology's claim against one poem that resists it, such as a poem with no family figure at all.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Contemporary Asian Australian Poets shows family as the place where culture is passed on, and also as the place where it is put under strain. Merlinda Bobis's poem This is where it begins shows the first of these. The speaker asks where her desire to tell stories came from. She lists her grandmother's tales, her grandfather's teasing, her mother's Spanish words and her father's gestures. The poem starts in Bikol, then moves into Pilipino and English, which reflects the mix of languages in her family. At the end the speaker says that storytelling is not something done alone, because the people who came before her are still with her. This shows that culture is handed down through family, and that the speaker is continuing a tradition she inherited.

Vuong Pham's poem Mother shows a different side of family. It is set in Saigon and refers to the Fall of Saigon, after which the family had to leave Vietnam. The mother wanted to be a high school teacher, but she had to sew clothes for little money so that her son could go to school. The son now teaches English, so he is doing the kind of work his mother had hoped to do. This means that family sacrifice has an effect on culture, because the son gets the chances his mother did not have. The poem also sets the son's happy childhood against the violence his mother lived through, which shows that the family experienced migration in different ways.

Both poems show that family is central to culture. Bobis shows storytelling passing down the family line, and Pham shows the cost of migration for a parent. Family helps people keep their identity, but it also changes when people move to a new country. Both poems also show family as a source of pride as well as hardship. The anthology is useful for this idea because it brings together many poets with migrant and refugee backgrounds, so the reader can compare how different families deal with culture and change. A reader who studies only one poem may see family as a source of comfort, but across the anthology it is also a source of loss and effort.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 9-12 criteria row. It explains how the poems connect family and culture, but the paragraphs lean towards description, with each poem's details given in turn before the argument is stated. To reach the 13-16 row, each paragraph should open with a claim about family and culture and use one poem's specific wording to test it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Vuong Pham's poem Mother, from Contemporary Asian Australian Poets, is about a mother and her son. The mother came from Vietnam after the war. She wanted to be a teacher, but she sewed clothes so she could pay for her son's school. Her son is now a teacher of English. This shows that family matters to culture, because the mother worked hard for her child and the child became a teacher. The poem also talks about the family's life in Saigon and the violence of the war. Family is important in this poem and in other poems in the anthology, which are written by migrants and their children. The poem is about the family's history and how it came to Australia. It shows the mother's hopes and the son's achievement, which ties family to a culture of effort and hard work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 5-8 criteria row. It describes Mother and touches on family and culture, but the references are limited and the response is organised as a retelling. To move up, it needs an argument about how family shapes culture and at least two specific references to the poem.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Alice Pung's Unpolished Gem, family is the main channel through which culture is handed down, and it is also the place where that culture is argued over. The memoir follows a Chinese-Cambodian family that survived the Khmer Rouge and settled in Footscray, in Melbourne's west, where Alice, the first of her family born in Australia, grows up. Because Pung writes nonfiction, the family she shows us is one she has chosen to arrange, and the arrangement tells us what she thinks family is: a set of people who carry a culture to one another, imperfectly, across generations. Understanding family, for Pung, means understanding inheritance, and inheritance means living between two worlds.

The grandmother, Huyen Thai, holds much of the family's past. She was forced to leave China after speaking out against the government, and she brings to Footscray both the memory of that loss and a strong sense of Chinese culture. Her bond with Alice is close, and through her stories and her teaching she passes on a heritage that Alice has never seen for herself. This is culture in its most intimate form, carried by voice from one generation to the next, and it gives Alice a sense of where she comes from that no school or suburb could supply.

The mother, Kien, carries a different part of the family's inheritance. She is practical and driven, shaped by the same history of survival, and the memoir presents her as a forceful presence whose expectations press hard on her daughter. Where the grandmother offers stories, the mother offers demands, and the two women's clashing ideas of how a household and a daughter should be run place Alice in the middle. Pung's decision to show these conflicts rather than smooth them over makes family a site of argument as well as affection. The father, Kuan, moves through the same household with his own losses, so that Alice grows up among adults who are each processing the past in a different way.

Footscray gives the family's story its setting and its pressure. The suburb is where the family's customs meet school, English and Australian ideas of normality, and where Alice learns that what is ordinary at home may be strange outside it. Identity in the memoir is therefore formed less by the journey to Australia than by the daily negotiations of language, habit and belonging. Pung's reader sees the suburb as Alice does, as a place whose rules have to be learnt while the rules of home are still being obeyed.

As the memoir moves into adolescence, the weight of this inheritance grows heavier. The grandmother falls ill and dies, and Alice's depression deepens in the same period. The loss removes the person who gave her the strongest link to a world beyond Footscray, and it leaves her to face her mother's expectations without that ally. Pung shows that family obligation has real consequences for a young woman's mental health, and she does not present love for the family as a simple comfort.

Her relationship with an Australian boyfriend brings the cultural argument into her private life. Her mother sees the differences between them as insurmountable, and Alice ends the relationship, heartbroken. The episode shows how family loyalty can cost a young woman something she values, and how a culture is protected by the people who fear what its loss would mean. Pung does not present the outcome as simple defeat. The memoir's closing movement suggests that Alice comes to a respect for her family's history while claiming a future of her own.

Unpolished Gem therefore presents family as a living, argumentative record of culture. The grandmother's stories, the mother's demands and the daughter's position between them show three generations holding the same inheritance in different ways. Alice's final respect for her family does not erase the conflict, but it shows that she has learnt to hold inheritance and independence together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the top descriptor because it explains family as a relationship between generations and links the grandmother's teaching, the mother's expectations and the grandmother's death to the idea of culture. It uses specific detail and handles the memoir's form with care. To lift it, the answer could examine more closely how Pung's choice of what to include shapes the reader's view of family.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Alice Pung's Unpolished Gem presents family as the main way that culture is passed on. The memoir follows a Chinese-Cambodian family that survived the Khmer Rouge and settled in Footscray in Melbourne, where Alice is the first of her family born in Australia. Her understanding of family is shaped by inheritance and by the pressure of living between two worlds.

The grandmother, Huyen Thai, was forced to leave China after speaking out against the government. She forms a close bond with Alice and teaches her about Chinese culture, so she is the person who connects Alice to a heritage she has never seen. This shows that culture can be passed on through stories and teaching inside a family, and that it gives a child a sense of identity.

Alice's mother, Kien, is shown as a forceful presence who argues with the grandmother about how the household and Alice should be run. Alice is caught between them, which shows that family can be a source of tension as well as comfort. Her father, Kuan, also lives with the losses of the past. Pung writes about these people honestly, and she does not make the family sound perfect.

In the later part of the memoir, the grandmother becomes ill and dies, and Alice's depression deepens. The loss shows how much Alice relied on her grandmother. Her relationship with an Australian boyfriend also shows the limits of her family's culture, because her mother sees the differences as insurmountable. Alice ends the relationship, and the memoir suggests that she eventually reaches a respect for her family while building an independent life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the competent descriptor. It covers the grandmother, the mother and Alice's position with adequate reference, but it moves through the memoir in sequence and explains less than it describes. The middle paragraphs would be stronger if each event were tied to an argument about culture and identity.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Unpolished Gem, Alice Pung writes about her family, who are Chinese-Cambodian and moved to Melbourne after living through the Khmer Rouge. The family settles in Footscray, where Alice grows up. Her grandmother, Huyen Thai, teaches her about Chinese culture and they are very close. Her mother, Kien, argues with the grandmother, and Alice is caught between them. Her father is called Kuan. The grandmother dies later in the book, and Alice feels sad and depressed. In the end Alice ends a relationship with an Australian man, and the family stays important to her. This shows that family is important to culture in the memoir.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer lists family members and events from the memoir and mentions culture only in its final sentence, so it sits at the describing level rather than explaining how family shapes understanding of culture. It would move up by choosing one incident, such as the grandmother's stories, and explaining what it shows about inherited culture.

markerNotes: The question asks how your study of the text informs an understanding, so strong responses move from what the text shows to what the student now understands about change and its connection to culture.
The best answers treat change as something that happens to a culture and to the people within it: they show what is gained, lost or contested, and whose values are at stake.

Module A asks how language represents identity and culture. Top responses analyse the composer’s language and form choices, not only the events of the text, and show how those choices give change its cultural meaning.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Ray Lawler’s Summer of the Seventeenth Doll presents change as the collapse of a settled cycle rather than as slow development. The play is set in Carlton, a Melbourne suburb, in the summer of 1953, and its characters have organised their lives around an annual arrangement. Roo and Barney cut cane in Queensland for most of the year, then return south for the layoff, about five months of partying and romance with Olive and her friend Nancy. Each season Roo brings Olive a doll, and this year’s is the seventeenth, which gives the play its title. The arrangement has held for years, and the play asks what happens when the people inside it begin to age.

The first changes are in the group itself. Nancy has married and left the arrangement, so Olive has to bring in Pearl, a poised and snobbish woman, to take Nancy’s place with Barney. Pearl makes him feel he is not good enough, and her presence changes the whole mood of the summer. Bubba, a young neighbour who has long envied the freedom of Olive and Nancy, stands at the edge of the group and shows how the life the older characters have built is admired and also threatened. The women in the Melbourne house have a life of their own, and the men must fit into it or be pushed out.

Roo’s body carries the clearest sign of time. He has had a poor season in Queensland and hurt his back in the cane fields, so the physical labour that defines his place among the men is no longer something he can rely on. In this context Roo asks Olive to marry him and settle down. Olive refuses, because she wants her old life and her freedom back, and marriage is, to her, the opposite of the life she has. The proposal exposes the central contradiction of the summers. The arrangement offered permanence in the form of a yearly return, but it could never offer a future.

The culture of the play is organised around two worlds, the masculine world of the cane fields and the feminine world of the Melbourne house. Mateship between Roo and Barney gives the men their identity, but it depends on the seasonal break from ordinary life, and a quarrel that began in the cane fields now strains it. The friendship does not survive the quarrel, and the seventeenth doll is broken, which turns the emblem of the layoff into the emblem of its ending. The men’s culture cannot be sustained as an unchanging ritual once the people who perform it have changed.

The seasonal pattern also gives the characters their sense of time. Each summer is a fixed point, a few months in which the men are at home and the women can pretend that nothing has altered. The layoff is a holiday from the labour that otherwise defines the men, and it is also a holiday from the expectations of the city. Lawler makes the audience feel the pressure of that brief freedom. The arrangement depends on both sides agreeing not to look beyond the season, and the play is about what happens when someone finally does.

The play closes with the old pattern broken: the partnership between the men has failed, the doll is broken, and the summer cannot go back to what it was. The change in Lawler’s play is therefore not a single event but a series of losses: a marriage that does not happen, a friendship that cannot be repaired, and a summer that cannot be recovered. Lawler shows that the culture of the cane cutters and the Melbourne women was built on repetition, and that repetition is what time erodes. The change does not come from a choice any one character makes. It comes from injury, ageing, a new woman and a refused proposal, and the play is precise about the cost to the people who lived inside that Australian way of life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 17–20 row. It treats change as the breakdown of the layoff cycle, links each change to the culture of the cane fields and the Melbourne house, and reads the doll and the proposal closely. To lift it further, the discussion of who breaks the doll and how could be handled more carefully, since the sources disagree, and the link between Olive’s refusal and the women’s culture could be developed.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Summer of the Seventeenth Doll, Ray Lawler shows change through the yearly visit of two cane cutters to Melbourne. The play is set in Carlton in the summer of 1953, and it shows how the layoff has become a regular part of the lives of Roo and Barney. Every year they come back from Queensland and spend months with Olive and Nancy. The doll that Roo brings Olive each season is the seventeenth, and this suggests that the arrangement has lasted a long time. The title points to a tradition that is about to come to an end.

Nancy is no longer part of the group because she has married. Olive brings Pearl into the house to take her place with Barney. Pearl is more formal than the others and she is not as much fun, which changes the mood of the group. Bubba is a young neighbour who has always wanted to be like Olive and Nancy.

Roo has had a bad season in Queensland and has hurt his back. He is not able to work in the cane fields as well as he once did, and this affects his position among the men. He asks Olive to marry him and settle down. Olive says no because she wants to keep her freedom, and the proposal shows that Roo wants a different life from the one the summers have given him. Change affects the men and the women in different ways.

The men’s friendship is also important. Roo and Barney have worked together for many years, and their mateship is the main reason the layoff exists. But the friendship is damaged by a quarrel that began in the cane fields, and it does not survive. The seventeenth doll is broken, and the group that gathered every year is no longer able to meet in the same way.

The play shows that the cycle of seasonal work and summer holidays cannot last forever. Lawler presents the culture of the cane cutters as a way of life that depends on men returning to the same women every year. When the characters change, the culture changes too, and the play is about the loss that comes from this.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9–12 row. It identifies the main changes and the characters involved with reasonable accuracy, but the response mostly describes what happens and makes only a few links to culture. To lift it, each change needed to be argued as a threat to the layoff ritual, with more specific close reference to the play.

sampleAnswers.answer: Summer of the Seventeenth Doll is set in Melbourne in 1953. Roo and Barney are cane cutters who come back from Queensland each summer to stay with Olive and her friends. Roo brings Olive a doll each season, and this year it is the seventeenth. Things are different this year. Nancy has married, and Olive brings in another woman, Pearl, to take her place. Roo has had a bad season and hurt his back in the cane fields. He asks Olive to marry him, but she says no. In the end the men’s friendship breaks, the doll is broken and the layoff is over. The play shows how things change over time and how the people in it have to deal with that change.

In Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion, change is never simply a matter of personal growth. It is shaped by the culture that decides who may speak, how they may speak and what authority their speech carries. Through Eliza Doolittle's transformation from a Covent Garden flower seller into a woman who can pass as a lady, the play shows that change in identity is possible yet tightly bound by the social order that judges it.

The play opens in the rain under the portico of St Paul's Church, where Henry Higgins, a phonetics professor, reads the accents of strangers and places each one by origin. His boast in the first act that he could make Eliza a duchess becomes a wager with Colonel Pickering, so that her speech turns into the stake in a bet between men. Language is the marker of culture here: Higgins locates people through their vowels, and the society he moves in treats that knowledge as a kind of authority. Eliza's change therefore begins as an experiment in which she is the subject rather than the agent.

Eliza's own motive is practical. She wants to speak correctly so that she can run a flower shop, and her lessons in vowels and phrasing are a means of entering a respectable trade. The change is also a performance that Higgins directs and tests. When he says he has taught her to speak properly, his language reveals that he regards her as the product of his training rather than as a person who has changed herself. Her pronunciation shifts, but the culture that rewards the shift still treats her origins as a fault.

Alfred Doolittle, Eliza's father, gives the play its second view of change, and his concern is money rather than refinement. When an unexpected fortune lifts him into middle-class circumstances, he calls 'middle class morality' an excuse for never giving him anything. Doolittle shows that respectability is a set of social rules that can be adopted, resisted or exploited. Shaw places father and daughter side by side so that class appears to be a structure that rewards money more readily than it admits the poor.

The central tension in the play's treatment of change arrives in the fourth act, when Eliza tells Higgins, 'I sold flowers. I didn't sell myself.' The line is precise. Trade in the old world was poor, but it left her independent, whereas her new position depends on the approval of the men who taught her. Her transformation has removed her from the flower trade without admitting her to the upper class, so marriage becomes the only secure future left to her. The culture that rewards her refinement has also narrowed her choices. Doolittle's comic defiance is a reminder that the rules of respectability are written by people with money.

In the final act, set in Mrs Higgins's home, the change is complete in outward terms, yet the emotional ending is unsettled. Higgins admits that he will miss Eliza, saying 'I shall miss you, Eliza', and he credits her with having taught him something. The humility is brief, and the play leaves the reader to decide how genuine it is. Eliza's reply reframes the lesson of the play: the difference between a lady and a flower girl lies in 'not how she behaves, but how she's treated'. Class, she suggests, is a matter of recognition granted by others, which makes it a matter of culture rather than manner. Eliza then declares that she will marry Freddy and pursue a career in phonetics teaching.

Pygmalion therefore presents change as real but bounded. Eliza's speech and manners are complete enough to convince Higgins's world, yet they neither secure her independence nor dissolve the class culture that measures her. Shaw uses the flower seller's transformation to show that language is where individual change and cultural judgement meet. A close study of the play shows that the decisive question is not whether Eliza can change, but who holds the power to decide what that change is worth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the top descriptor because it explains how Eliza's change is shaped by class and by Higgins's ownership of her speech, and it anchors that argument in the first, fourth and final acts. Close reference is sustained throughout, and the short quotations do real analytical work. To lift it further, the final paragraph could test Shaw's ending more directly against the claim about culture rather than restating the conclusion.

Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion is a play about change, and in particular about how a person's speech can be altered by teaching while their social position stays fixed. Eliza Doolittle begins as a flower seller at Covent Garden. Henry Higgins, a phonetics professor, makes a wager with Colonel Pickering that he can pass her off as a lady, so the play starts with a question of language that leads directly to the class culture of the society around them.

Eliza's change is visible in her speech. She wants to speak properly so that she can run a flower shop, and Higgins drills her in vowels and manners until she can attend an embassy ball and be taken seriously. Higgins is proud of this and says he has taught her to speak properly. The change succeeds on the terms of the wager, but Shaw also shows that it is a performance, and Higgins treats Eliza as an experiment rather than as a person who has chosen to change herself.

Alfred Doolittle represents another kind of change. He is interested in money rather than refinement, and when he comes into a fortune he becomes a man of middle-class means. He complains about 'middle class morality', which in his view is only an excuse for never giving him anything. Doolittle shows that respectability is a set of rules that can be taken up or exploited, so the class structure appears less natural than it seems.

The most important moment for Eliza comes in the fourth act, when she tells Higgins that she sold flowers but did not sell herself. This shows that she values her independence from the old world, even though that world was poor. Her new position as a lady has removed her from the flower trade without giving her a secure place in the upper classes, and she is left dependent on marriage for her future.

In the final act Higgins says he will miss her, and Eliza responds with a point about how people are treated. Her change of speech has not made her a lady in the eyes of the society she is trying to enter, and the play suggests that class is something other people recognise and grant. Eliza then declares her intention to marry Freddy and to pursue a career in phonetics teaching. Shaw's conclusion is that change in Pygmalion is real but limited by the culture that judges it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the competent descriptor. It explains the play's treatment of change and class with adequate references, but several paragraphs describe Higgins's lessons and Doolittle's remarks rather than arguing from them. Quotations are fewer and less developed, especially in the final-act paragraph. Tying Eliza's final words more closely to the culture that frames them would move it towards the effective descriptor.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Pygmalion, Henry Higgins makes a bet with Colonel Pickering that he can teach Eliza Doolittle to speak like a lady. Eliza is a flower seller who wants to improve her speech so she can run a flower shop, and she takes lessons from Higgins at his home. Higgins teaches her to pronounce her words properly, and she is taken to an embassy ball, where she is presented in society. Her father, Alfred Doolittle, speaks about money and respectability. At the end, Eliza tells Higgins that she plans to marry Freddy. The play shows change in Eliza and class in English society, and it suggests that language is a way of being judged by others and by oneself. Higgins's pride in the result is clear throughout. This is a change of speech rather than a change of class.

To move it up, the student needs one precise reference to a scene, such as the fourth act, and an explanation of what that scene reveals about class.

In Alana Valentine's Shafana and Aunt Sarrinah, change is the pressure that drives every exchange between a niece and her aunt. Both women are Afghan and devout Muslims, yet they have reached different understandings of faith because they have lived through different changes. The play argues that a chosen identity is always tested against the culture that formed it, and that migration can make the same faith look very different to two people of one family.

Shafana's change is inward and deliberate. After 9/11 she studies Islam more closely and resolves to wear a hijab, and she presents the decision as a deepening of a faith she already holds. She was born in Kabul, her family spent time in New Delhi, and she reached Australia as a teenager to join her aunt, while her parents were still in India. The hijab is therefore a public claim to a new identity in a country far from them. Her change is cultural as well as religious, because it makes her faith visible to others.

Sarrinah's change is harder, because migration has imposed it. She had worked as an engineer in Kabul, but in Australia she could not prove her qualifications. She found work in a factory, concealed the fact that her skills were outdated, and taught herself new software in secret. Her story shows that migration can strip away status and force a person to relearn a profession, and her view of faith is shaped by that loss.

The veil itself carries cultural meaning. Sarrinah notes that the word hijab is Arabic, and that Persians are not Arabs, so the garment belongs to a tradition she does not share. She describes her own faith as 'private and cultural', a view that keeps belief out of public display. For Sarrinah the hijab stands for a world she has left, and she fears that visible piety will expose her niece to prejudice in a country where Muslims are often judged as a group. Shafana's answer is that her faith shapes her whole life.

The play's central conflict is therefore a clash between two kinds of change. Shafana insists that her change is personal and authentic, while Sarrinah accepts that Muslims may differ but argues that fear should not decide the matter. When persuasion fails, Sarrinah threatens to demand repayment of a loan given to Shafana's parents, which would force Shafana to leave her studies. The argument shows that obligation, debt and belonging are bound together in a migrant household, and that a change in belief can threaten a young woman's education.

Shafana's scientific work offers a counterpoint. In rehearsing a presentation on deep-sea ecosystems, she argues that scientists must accept what she calls the 'veil of knowing'. Her science suggests that understanding can unfold beyond certainty, and her faith asks her to act before she can be certain of its consequences. The younger woman sees change as an act of trust, while her aunt sees it as a risk to be managed.

Sarrinah's memories of the escape through Pakistan extend the argument into history. On a bus, she pulled off her chador because she could not breathe, and a guard ordered her off. Her family was jailed and sent back to Afghanistan before smugglers they had paid secured their release. Migration for these women was shaped by violence before it was shaped by choice. News coverage of September 2001, which blurred ordinary Muslims with extremists, shows that public events shape private faith.

Shafana and Aunt Sarrinah therefore presents change as a product of both conviction and displacement. Shafana's chosen change tests the culture that formed her, and Sarrinah's imposed change reveals what migration takes away. The argument between them is still open as the play moves towards its closing exchange, which suggests that belonging in a new country is a continuing negotiation rather than a settled condition.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the top descriptor because it argues that the niece's and aunt's changes expose different relationships between faith, migration and culture, and it supports that argument with specific references to the aunt's lost career, the loan threat and the hijab debate. The language is controlled and the structure moves from the younger woman to the elder. A lift would come from examining the dramatic choices more closely, such as the decision to stage the escape as a flashback rather than as present action.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Alana Valentine's Shafana and Aunt Sarrinah presents change as something that happens to people as well as something they choose. Shafana decides to wear a hijab and her aunt opposes the decision, so the two women's arguments show how a change in faith relates to the culture that formed them. The play is about a niece and an aunt, but it also addresses how migration changes the way faith is understood in a new country.

Shafana's change is a deliberate choice. Her study of Islam after 9/11 leads her to want a visible sign of her faith, and she tells her aunt that she wants to make real the change she has already felt inside. She was born in Kabul and reached Australia as a teenager, so her new identity is formed in a country that has not always welcomed Muslims. Her decision is a change in culture as well as belief, because it is public.

Sarrinah's change is different. In Kabul she worked as an engineer, but in Australia she had to work in a factory and conceal that her skills were out of date. She also taught herself new software in secret. These experiences show how migration can take away status, and her opposition to the hijab is partly a reaction to a life she has left behind. She regards her faith as private and cultural, which sets her against her niece's public display.

The conflict between the two women is cultural as well as personal. Sarrinah points out that the word hijab is Arabic, and she argues that Muslims do not all share one way of dressing. When her arguments fail, she threatens to demand repayment of a loan that would force Shafana to leave her studies. Valentine uses this pressure to show how family obligation, money and belief are tied together in a migrant household.

Sarrinah's memories of the escape through Pakistan remind the audience that change for these women was shaped by violence before it was shaped by choice. The play suggests that a person's faith may remain steady while their circumstances change, and the argument between the two women stays open as the play moves forward.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the competent descriptor. It explains both women's changes and the family pressures with adequate reference, but the middle paragraphs lean towards summary of events. The argument about culture would be stronger if the answer explained why the hijab is a public sign rather than only stating that it is.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Shafana and Aunt Sarrinah by Alana Valentine, Shafana decides that she wants to wear a hijab, and her aunt Sarrinah does not agree. Shafana was born in Kabul, and her family moved through New Delhi before she came to Australia as a teenager to join her aunt. She is a university student. Sarrinah was an engineer in Afghanistan, but in Australia she had to work in a factory because her qualifications were not recognised. The two women argue about the hijab, about religion and about money. At one point Sarrinah threatens to ask for repayment of a loan she gave to Shafana's parents, which would stop Shafana studying. The play shows how change affects the family and how the characters hold different ideas about culture and faith.

It sits in the descriptor for describing aspects of the text. A lift would come from one specific reference to the aunt's factory work or the loan threat, linked to culture.

In Rachel Perkins’ One Night the Moon, a 57-minute musical made for television and set in the 1930s outback, change is less about the passing of years than about a settler family’s refusal to change its relationship with the land. The film asks how a newcomer’s claim to ownership collides with a culture that has always known how to read country, and it answers through the disappearance of a child, an Aboriginal tracker named Albert, and a soundtrack that keeps the two men’s voices apart. Change and culture are therefore inseparable in the text: the settler’s world is unsettled only when he is forced to face what Albert knows.

The film builds the settler’s position from its opening. Perkins begins with the mother, Rose, drawing her daughter away from a friendship with the tracker’s daughter, a moment that critic Fiona Probyn reads as the enforcement of segregation. When Emily follows the full moon into the hills, Jim refuses to let Albert direct the search, and the camera registers that resistance. In the search sequence it swiftly circles Jim as he walks in a straight line toward the hills, so that the man who claims the land moves across ground he cannot read. The circling movement is set against the stillness of the land, so the search becomes a contest between a man who surveys ground and a culture that reads it. Rose is the figure who changes. She seeks Albert’s help without her husband’s knowledge, and the film’s shift of focus from the tracker to the mother, a change director Rachel Perkins made during development, makes her grief the emotional centre. Her alliance with Albert is the only act of recognition the family manages, and it comes after her husband’s refusal has already failed.

Culture is carried most clearly by music. The duet “This Land is Mine” is sung by the settler and Albert, and Probyn’s phrase “reconciling harmonies” describes how harmony holds the two voices apart rather than merging them. Jim sings in a high register that Probyn reads as desperation, and the two men’s views of belonging are brought into parallel without being fused. Probyn’s reading treats the duet as an argument rather than a resolution, so the listener is left holding both claims at once. At the end of the song a didgeridoo echoes, sounding the Indigenous knowledge the settler has tried to suppress. The score, by Paul Kelly, Kev Carmody and Mairead Hannan, makes the musical structure itself an argument about belonging, and the sound outlasts any single character’s claim.

Visual technique reinforces the same argument. Bleach-bypass processing drains pink tones from the images, giving the Flinders Ranges a brooding quality, while time-lapse clouds roll over rocky outcrops. The settler is shown looking up at a ridge he cannot climb, a moment Probyn describes as hopeless. The camera often returns in close-up to Rose, wrapped in a shawl on the veranda and gazing across the land, so that the film keeps its attention on a face that knows what has been lost. Australian Screen Online describes the cinematography as sweeping and detail-focused, giving the audience empathy for both Albert and the landscape rather than for the family alone.

The ending turns the argument into consequence. Albert finds Emily’s body in the hills and returns it to her father, and Jim dies by suicide. The settler is last seen walking out of the front door with a rifle. Albert’s wife, Ruby Hunter, sings the funeral song, and Probyn notes that Albert’s own daughter is absent from the funeral, an absence she links to the Stolen Generations. The film does not offer reconciliation as a clean resolution. Change arrives too late for this family, and the cultural knowledge Jim ignored is the only thing that brings Emily back to the people who love her.

In the end, One Night the Moon shows that the land is not an object a settler can survey and own; it is a place read by people who have always known it. The change the film asks for is one of recognition, and its tragedy is that recognition comes only after the child is lost.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the top row: it explains how the film informs an understanding of change and its connection to culture, and it supports each point with detailed reference to scenes, a shot, the duet and the ending. It is controlled throughout. To lift it further, the closing paragraph could weigh the film’s final image more closely against the argument rather than restating it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
One Night the Moon is a film about how a settler family changes, or fails to change, its relationship with the land. Set in the 1930s outback, it shows Jim, the father, refusing to let the Aboriginal tracker Albert help search for his daughter Emily, and this refusal leads to tragedy. The director, Rachel Perkins, follows the settler family closely, but the film also gives Albert a presence through the land and through his knowledge.

The camera in the search sequence circles Jim as he walks toward the hills, which suggests that he is lost in a landscape he believes he owns. Emily follows the full moon into the hills, which gives the story its dark pull toward the bush. Rose, the mother, is the character who changes most. She goes to Albert for help without telling her husband, and later her grief is shown as she sits on the veranda with the camera on her face. These images show the audience how the family is affected by the disappearance.

The music is also important to the film’s culture. The song “This Land is Mine” is sung by Jim and Albert together, and the two voices are not the same. Jim sings higher and it sounds desperate. At the end there is a didgeridoo, which connects the song to Aboriginal culture. The film also uses bleach-bypass processing, which drains the colour from the pictures and makes the landscape look harsh, and time-lapse clouds over rocky outcrops add to the sense of a hostile place. This suggests that the land belongs to Aboriginal people as well, even though Jim wants to own it.

The ending is tragic. Albert finds Emily’s body and gives it to her father. Jim dies by suicide, and the settler is last seen walking out of the house with a rifle. Albert’s wife sings a funeral song. The film suggests that change comes too late for the family, and that the settler’s refusal to listen has consequences that cannot be undone. The ending is hard to watch because the film has shown the audience what Jim could have learned.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the row for explaining competently how the film informs an understanding of change, with adequate references to scenes and the song. It is sound and organised, but it describes more than it argues, and the cultural point about the didgeridoo is asserted rather than developed. To lift it, the answer should weigh the duet’s harmony against the settler’s refusal and explain what that tension reveals about change.

sampleAnswers.answer: One Night the Moon is a musical film about a girl named Emily who goes missing in the outback. Her father, Jim, does not want the Aboriginal tracker Albert to help look for her, and the mother, Rose, goes to Albert in secret. They find Emily dead and bring her back. The film has songs, and Jim and Albert sing This Land is Mine together. The camera follows the father across the hills and uses close-ups of the mother to show how sad she is. Albert knows the land, which shows that Aboriginal people have knowledge the family does not have. The ending is sad because Jim dies. The film shows that change is hard for people who do not listen to Aboriginal people.

It retells the plot in order and gestures at change without developing it, and the cultural point is stated but not explained. To lift it, the answer needs one or two specific references to scenes or sound and a clear claim about what the film shows about culture.

Janet Merewether's documentary Reindeer in my Saami Heart presents change as something a culture lives through rather than something that simply happens to it. Released in 2016 and made in English and Northern Saami, the film follows Inghilda Tapio, a writer, poet, performer and teacher whose life spans the decades in which Saami life in Sweden's Arctic Circle came under pressure from state policy. Through her, the film argues that change and culture are bound together. The forces that disrupted Tapio's childhood also gave her the means to speak for her people.

Tapio was born into a nomadic reindeer-herding family, and the change that defines her early life was institutional rather than personal. After the Second World War, nomadic children were sent to residential boarding schools in towns. At around the age of seven, Tapio was taken from her family's home, herds and parents for months at a time. The documentary places this removal within what it describes as Sweden's stolen generation, and the child who was isolated by the Swedish language and by unfamiliar school buildings and customs is the figure at the centre of its account. The removal is painful, yet Tapio's later life shows that it did not end her connection to her people. Her early schooling was a change imposed from outside, not a choice she made.

Her adult life shows what culture can make of change. She went on to university, and she became a poet, performer and teacher who writes in both Northern Saami and Swedish. Her family still practises traditional reindeer herding, so the older way of life continues alongside the new one rather than being replaced by it. The film's title makes the same claim in miniature. Placing the reindeer inside a Saami heart suggests that culture is not kept in the landscape alone but carried in people, who can take it with them when they are moved, schooled or removed.

The film's own form repeats this argument. Screen Australia describes it as a visually innovative documentary that blends English and Northern Saami, so the minority language is heard in the film alongside English, the language of the wider world the film addresses. Merewether travelled north of the Arctic Circle three times to make the film, which gives its images a physical grounding in the places it describes. An Australian director brings a Saami writer's life to Australian viewers, and the film premiered at the Volvo Scandinavian Film Festival in Sydney in July 2016. Culture becomes visible across distance when change forces it into public view, and the documentary is one way of making that visible.

Change in the film is also presented as ongoing rather than completed. An article about the film's release describes a Saami community that has survived centuries of assimilation attempts and now faces threats from mining, forestry and hydroelectric development. That context changes how a viewer reads Tapio's childhood. The removal to boarding school becomes an early instance of a longer contest over land and identity, and Tapio appears as a witness to a culture still negotiating its place in a changing region. The film's connection to culture is therefore not nostalgic. It is about survival under pressure. A viewer who knows that Saami communities face new pressures will see the childhood removal as part of a continuing story.

The film is strongest when it refuses to treat Saami culture as finished. The change Tapio lived through is not presented as the end of her people's culture but as the start of a new phase in its survival. The boarding school showed what change can take away: a daily life of moving with herds, and a family separated for months at a time. Her writing and teaching show what culture can make of change: a living language, a family still herding, and a voice that reaches people who might otherwise never hear it. The film suggests that the forces which tried to erase Saami culture did not succeed in silencing it, and that is the understanding of change and culture it offers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 13-16 criteria row. It explains how the film informs an understanding of change and culture through Tapio's life, with detailed references to the boarding school, the languages and the continuing herding. It stops short of the top row because it cannot draw on the film's sequences, sound or camera work for close reference. To lift it further, the answer could develop a sharper analytical claim about how the film's blend of languages shapes what the audience understands about change.

Janet Merewether's documentary Reindeer in my Saami Heart is about Inghilda Tapio, a Saami writer and poet. The film was made in 2016 and uses English and Northern Saami. Tapio was born into a reindeer-herding family in Sweden. When she was about seven she was sent to a boarding school and was separated from her family for months at a time. The film describes this as part of Sweden's stolen generation. Tapio later went to university and became a poet and teacher. She writes in Northern Saami and Swedish. This shows that change affects culture, because the school took her away from her family, but she kept her connection to her culture.

The change in the film is shown through Tapio's life. Her early childhood was spent in a nomadic family, but after the war children were sent to schools in towns, so the way of life changed. Tapio was isolated by the Swedish language and by the school's customs. Her later life shows that culture can survive. Her family still practises reindeer herding. The title shows a connection to culture because the reindeer is inside a Saami heart, which means that the culture is inside the person. Coverage of the film also notes threats from mining and forestry to the Saami today, which shows that change is still going on.

The director, Janet Merewether, is Australian. She travelled north of the Arctic Circle to make the film, and the film premiered at a festival in Sydney in 2016. This means the film is about culture in another country, but it is also made for an Australian audience. Viewers can learn about the Saami from the film without having to know much about Sweden already. The film is also a portrait, which means it presents one life as evidence for a wider culture, and that is how it connects change to culture for the viewer.

Overall the film shows change and culture. Tapio's childhood was affected by change, but her writing and teaching show that culture continues. The film therefore helps the viewer to understand how culture changes over time, and why people hold on to it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 9-12 criteria row. It explains how the film informs an understanding of change and culture, but the paragraphs describe the film's facts in turn and the argument is less developed. To reach the 13-16 row, each paragraph should make a claim about change and culture and link it to one specific feature of the film.

When Tapio was a child she was taken from her family and sent to a boarding school. This shows change, because her life changed a lot. Later she became a poet and teacher and wrote in Northern Saami. The Saami live in Sweden's Arctic Circle, and the film was made by an Australian director for audiences in Australia.
