prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of how ideas about language, identity and culture are expressed through texts; demonstrate understanding of how language is used to shape meaning about individuals and/or cultural groups; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section I — Module A: Language, Identity and Culture (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

prompts.question: How does your prescribed text reveal the benefits and challenges of belonging to specific cultures? In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: Strong answers hold the benefits and challenges together rather than listing them in two halves. Eliza's gain in mobility is the same thing that costs her a settled place in her old world.
Use the text's own voices as evidence. Eliza's lines in Act IV and Act V carry more argument than a retelling of the garden party.
Doolittle is the play's counter-voice on culture. Using him to test what Eliza gains shows control of 'specific cultures' without drifting into a general essay on class.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the story from the rain at Covent Garden to the epilogue without tying any event to a benefit or a challenge.
Treating the benefit as money alone, when the text is mostly concerned with recognition and manners.
Attributing Higgins's view of 'kerbstone English' to Shaw himself and then arguing that Shaw endorses it.
Overstating the epilogue as a clean reconciliation of Eliza with her origins, when Shaw leaves her choice and its meaning open.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Explains in a highly effective manner how the prescribed text reveals the benefits and challenges of belonging to specific cultures; Presents a highly effective response using relevant, detailed references to the prescribed text; Organises, develops and expresses ideas effectively using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Explains effectively how the prescribed text reveals the benefits and challenges of belonging to specific cultures; Presents an effective response using relevant references to the prescribed text; Organises, develops and expresses ideas competently using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Explains competently how the prescribed text reveals the benefits and/or challenges of belonging to specific cultures; Presents a competent response using adequate references to the prescribed text; Organises, develops and expresses ideas adequately using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes aspects of the prescribed text with some reference to the question; Presents a response using limited reference to the prescribed text; Attempts to organise a response in a limited way
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the text; Attempts to organise a response in an elementary way

sampleAnswers.answer:
In Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion, belonging to a culture is not a birthright that stays fixed. It is performed, judged and granted by other people, and the benefits and challenges of belonging to specific cultures are measured above all through speech. Shaw opens the play in heavy rain at Covent Garden, where Eliza Doolittle sells flowers and speaks the English of her street. Henry Higgins, a phonetician, dismisses her voice as kerbstone English and wagers Colonel Pickering that he can pass her off as a duchess within six months. That wager states the play’s central claim: language is a passport between cultures. Shaw is interested in what the passport gains Eliza and what it takes from her.

The gains are concrete, and Shaw does not mock them. In the first act Higgins boasts that he could find her a place as a lady’s maid or a shop assistant, which shows how far a change of speech would move her within the economy of the city. By the fourth act the transformation has carried her into society. Pickering describes the garden party as frightfully exciting, and Eliza’s ease in company shows the confidence her new speech has given her. For a girl once judged by her vowels, the drawing rooms of Mrs Higgins offer dignity, opportunity and the chance to be taken seriously. Belonging to a new culture, in this sense, is first of all a matter of access, and the play takes access seriously.

The challenges are just as concrete, and Eliza is the one who names them. In Act IV she confronts Higgins with the line ‘I sold flowers. I didn’t sell myself.’ She adds that he has made her a lady and that she is no longer fit to sell anything else. Her new culture has removed her from the world of the flower sellers without giving her a secure place in the one she has entered. The streets that raised her can no longer be home, and the society she has learned to enter tests her manners before it accepts her person. Shaw presents belonging as a condition that depends on the recognition of others.

Eliza’s own answer, given in the final act, is the most precise statement of the problem. The difference between a lady and a flower girl, she tells Higgins, lies in ‘how she’s treated’ rather than in manners anyone can learn. Higgins still treats her as a flower girl and always will, while Pickering treats her as a lady, and so she can be one to him. This is both a benefit and a challenge. Belonging to the upper culture is available to her only through the regard of particular individuals, and Higgins’s regard looks more like ownership than welcome. The play’s sympathies are clear on this point.

Shaw gives the working-class culture its own voice through Alfred Doolittle, Eliza’s father. He calls himself ‘one of the undeserving poor’ and says that ‘middle class morality’ is ‘just an excuse for never giving me anything’. He wants ‘cheerfulness and a song and a band’ and claims a freedom that respectability does not allow. This is a genuine cultural value: a community that refuses to pretend, keeps its humour and does not apologise for its appetites. Shaw does not romanticise it, however. Doolittle is charged the same prices as the deserving poor, and his freedom to be undeserving also means he has no security.

Act V complicates Doolittle’s position. An American millionaire’s bequest, tied to lecturing for the Wannafeller Moral Reform World League, makes him rich, and he says that three thousand a year ‘shoves me into the middle class’. The money buys him membership of the culture he once mocked, and that membership costs him the freedom to be undeserving. The challenge of belonging is shown from the other side here: the price of entry is the surrender of the values that made the culture distinctive.

The epilogue shows the results of these collisions without rounding them off. Eliza marries Freddy Eynsford Hill, and the couple plan to buy flowers early each morning at Covent Garden, the scene of their first meeting. Freddy’s sentiment is affectionate, but it shows Eliza returning to her origins by choice rather than compulsion. The ending suggests that identity can be chosen and combined, and that a culture is not only something a person loses by changing class. It is also a place one can return to on one’s own terms.

Ultimately, Pygmalion shows that the benefits of belonging to a culture, namely opportunity, confidence, dignity and freedom, are real, and that each carries a matching challenge: dependence on others, loss of origin, and the surrender of the values that made a culture worth belonging to. Eliza refuses to be merely a lady or merely a flower girl, and Doolittle’s uncomfortable rise into respectability shows that class is a set of bargains. Shaw does not resolve these bargains neatly, and that refusal is why his treatment of culture remains persuasive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it explains the benefits and challenges of belonging to the two cultures in a highly effective way, and the close references to Eliza's speeches, Doolittle's and the bequest carry the argument. The conclusion weighs the gains against the losses, which is what keeps it in the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Shaw’s Pygmalion shows that belonging to a culture can be gained and lost through speech. Eliza Doolittle is a flower seller in Covent Garden whose accent marks her as working class. Henry Higgins, a phonetician, bets Colonel Pickering that he can pass her off as a duchess within six months, and the play follows the lessons that make this possible. The benefits of the change are shown when Eliza moves into a new social world. Higgins says he could get her work as a lady’s maid or a shop assistant, and later she attends a garden party and a dinner party.

These scenes show that her new speech brings opportunities she did not have before. Pickering describes the garden party as frightfully exciting, and she is able to take part in conversations with people of a higher class. The play suggests that acceptance in the new culture is valuable, because Eliza gains confidence and respect from people who would previously have ignored her.

The play also shows challenges. Eliza tells Higgins that he has made her a lady and she is no longer fit to sell anything else. She has lost her place in the culture she came from and is not fully accepted into the new one. Her comments about being treated differently show that people respond to her according to their own attitudes. Higgins treats her as a flower girl, while Pickering treats her with more respect. This suggests that belonging depends on other people and not only on what a person can do.

Alfred Doolittle, her father, provides another view of working-class culture. He describes himself as one of the ‘undeserving poor’ and complains about ‘middle class morality’. He enjoys cheerfulness and music, and he does not want to pretend to be respectable. When he inherits money later in the play, he becomes part of the middle class, which Shaw presents as a loss of the freedom he valued.

Shaw’s preface also comments on English attitudes to language. It notes that the English have no respect for their language, which suggests that speech is closely tied to how people are judged. In the epilogue Eliza marries Freddy, and they plan to buy flowers at Covent Garden where they first met. This ending suggests that she keeps some connection to her origins, although the play is more concerned with class than with a personal sense of culture.

In conclusion, Pygmalion shows that belonging to a culture brings benefits such as opportunity and recognition, but also challenges such as losing an old identity and depending on others to accept you. Shaw’s characters illustrate these ideas clearly, and the language they use helps show how class works in the play.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains competently how the play treats benefits and challenges, but much of the middle is description and the references are fewer and thinner. The lift would come from tying each reference to a claim, for example using Eliza's 'how she's treated' speech to argue that acceptance depends on individuals rather than on speech.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Pygmalion, Eliza is a flower girl who speaks with a Cockney accent. Professor Higgins teaches her to speak like a lady so that she can pass as a duchess at a party. She does well and goes to a garden party. Her father, Doolittle, is a poor man who does not like middle class morality, and later he gets money and becomes middle class himself. Eliza does not want to sell flowers any more and says she cannot go back to her old life. At the end she marries Freddy. The benefits of belonging to a culture are that Eliza gets a better life. The challenges are that she does not fit in with flower sellers any more. Shaw shows these things through the characters and their speech. The play presents this as a story about speech rather than about the people themselves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the plot and names benefits and challenges without developing them, and the references are minimal. To reach the next row it would need to explain one challenge in detail, such as Eliza's loss of place among the flower sellers, and support it with a named scene or quotation.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of how ideas about language, identity and culture are expressed through texts; demonstrate understanding of how language is used to shape meaning about individuals and/or cultural groups; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section I — Module A: Language, Identity and Culture (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

dotPoints.description: The ways texts influence and position readers

prompts.question: Identify TWO techniques the narrator uses to position the reader to sympathise with Mira in the short story.
markerNotes: Name the technique, not the effect. Short sentences and first-person narration are techniques; the story is sad is not.
Two techniques must be located in the story. A precise example, such as the removal van, is what moves an answer into the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Naming the story's theme, such as moving house or grief, as though it were a technique.
Using the word imagery for every choice without naming a specific device.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two specific techniques used to position the reader, each named precisely and located in the story
1 mark: Identifies one technique, or two techniques named only in general terms

sampleAnswers.answer: The narrator uses first person, placing readers inside Mira's head. Short sentences, such as her description of the empty removal van, create a clipped rhythm that invites readers to sympathise. Together they position readers to share her view.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two techniques are named precisely, each is located in the story and linked to how readers are positioned, and the answer is specific enough to earn the full 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The narrator uses style to make the reader feel sorry for Mira.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One general technique is gestured at as style without being named, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading an invented 1200-word short story, written for this question, in which sixteen-year-old Mira narrates the week after her family moves to a new city. The story is told in first person and uses frequent short sentences, and the adults in it never explain their decisions. It includes Mira's description of an empty removal van.

prompts.question: Explain how the narrator's first-person perspective influences the reader's view of the adults in the story.
markerNotes: Explain means show the mechanism. Say what the narrator can and cannot see, then say what that does to the reader's judgement of the adults.
The top band notices the gap between narrator and reader. Where the reader sees more than Mira does, the reader's view of the adults becomes richer.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Mira's personality without connecting it to the reader's view of the adults.
Assuming the first-person perspective makes the reader trust the narrator completely.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how the first-person perspective shapes the reader's view of each adult, with precise evidence from the story and a clear account of how the narrator's limited knowledge affects judgement
4 marks: Explains the influence of the first-person perspective on the reader's view of the adults, with specific evidence and some account of its effect
3 marks: Describes the first-person perspective and one adult, with evidence and a general statement about influence
2 marks: Makes a general statement about the narrator's perspective and the adults, with little evidence
1 mark: Names the first-person perspective without linking it to the adults

sampleAnswers.answer: The first-person perspective means the reader sees only what Mira notices, so the adults are filtered through a teenager who is anxious and quick to misread them. When her father is quiet at dinner, Mira takes his silence as disappointment in her, and the reader is invited to share that reading. This shapes the reader's view of the adults in two ways. First, they seem distant and inexplicable, because their reasons are withheld from the narrator and so from the reader. Second, the reader sympathises with Mira's view, which makes the adults seem more at fault than the text might justify. Yet the gap between narrator and reader is also visible: by the final scene the reader notices clues Mira misses, such as her mother's late phone calls, which makes the adults more complex than Mira allows. The perspective therefore has a strong influence on judgement, while exposing its own limits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The first-person perspective is shown to shape the reader's view of the adults through specific evidence, and the answer explains the gap between narrator and reader that makes the adults more complex than Mira allows. This is the full-mark explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first-person perspective means the reader sees the adults through Mira. Her father's silence at dinner seems like disappointment to her, and the reader is likely to think the same way. The narrator makes the adults seem distant because she does not understand them, so the reader sympathises with her view of them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The first-person perspective and one adult are described with evidence and a general statement about influence. The answer does not explain the gap between narrator and reader, so it sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The narrator is a teenager and the adults are her parents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The narrator and the adults are named but the answer does not link the perspective to the reader's view, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading the same invented 1200-word short story (written for this question), in which sixteen-year-old Mira narrates the week after her family moves to a new city. The adults in the story never explain their decisions, and the reader sees them only through Mira's observations. Her father falls silent at dinner, and her mother's late phone calls go unexplained.

prompts.question: Literature reinforces or challenges our understanding of ordinary situations. Discuss this statement, making detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The stem asks for a view on a statement, so the strongest answers take a position on both halves: where the novel confirms ordinary life and where it makes the ordinary strange. An answer that only retells the investigation cannot reach the top descriptors.

Christopher's literal voice is the distinctive quality to test the statement against. Haddon has said in a 2003 interview that he researched the London Underground and Swindon station more closely than he researched Asperger's, so the London sections are the best evidence for how the novel makes the familiar strange.
The Holmes line in the title is a useful way into what goes unsaid in ordinary life, but naming it is not enough. The top answers use it to read a specific silence in the novel.

Form earns credit only when it changes the reader's relation to the ordinary. The prime-numbered chapters and the maps, diagrams and pictures should be explained as devices, not described as features.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the investigation of the dog's death in order without saying whether the novel reinforces or challenges ordinary life.
Treating Christopher's condition as a diagnosis the novel names, when the novel itself never states it.
Describing the policeman's grip as a plot event without explaining why the same contact is frightening to Christopher.
Presenting the ending as a full reconciliation, when Christopher remains wary of his father.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Discusses effectively how the statement reflects the prescribed text; Presents an effective response using relevant, detailed textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas effectively using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Discusses competently how the statement reflects the prescribed text; Presents a competent response using relevant textual knowledge; Organises, develops and expresses ideas competently using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Discusses how the statement reflects the prescribed text; Presents a response using some textual knowledge; Organises and expresses ideas adequately, using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes aspects of the prescribed text; Attempts a response using limited textual knowledge; Attempts to organise some ideas
1-4 marks: Demonstrates elementary textual knowledge; Attempts to organise a response

sampleAnswers.answer:
Mark Haddon's The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time both reinforces and challenges our understanding of ordinary situations, and its distinctive qualities lie in how it makes the everyday visible as a set of hidden rules. The novel is told in first-person narration by Christopher, a fifteen-year-old who investigates the death of a neighbour's poodle. Through his literal and precise voice, Haddon shows that ordinary life runs on codes that most people never have to examine. The result confirms much of what we already believe about families and communities, while challenging the assumption that the ordinary is simple, shared or natural.

The novel first reinforces our sense of ordinary life as a web of loyalties and small deceptions. Its central mystery begins at night, when Christopher finds his neighbour Mrs Shears's dog, Wellington, dead and speared with a garden fork. His investigation takes the shape of a detective story, the kind of Sherlock Holmes tale he admires, and the title comes from a line in Holmes, “That was the curious incident”. That line matters because it points to what is absent from ordinary life: the silence, the omission, the thing nobody says. Readers expect neighbours and families to hide something, and when the adults around Christopher turn out to be lying to him, that expectation is confirmed.

The clearest example is the father's lie. Ed tells Christopher that his mother died of a heart attack, and the reader takes the statement at face value until letters from Judy, dated after her supposed death, turn up in Ed's room. Ed's later confession that he killed the dog in a fit of anger confirms a familiar truth about families: people lie to protect those they love, and the lies can damage the very people they were meant to shelter. Haddon does not make Ed a monster. He is a flawed father whose lies can be read as a mixture of fear and love, and this reinforces what most readers already understand about the damage secrets do at home.

The novel then challenges that understanding by making ordinary contact and ordinary places strange. Christopher struggles to read other people's feelings and does not understand metaphor, so the everyday world reaches him as a set of literal facts. When a policeman grabs his arm, a gesture most people would barely register, Christopher panics and hits him, and he is arrested for assault. Haddon uses the moment to show that procedure is a set of conventions, and that someone who does not share them is punished for failing to read the rules. The reader sees the grip as an invasion, and the officer's reasonable response looks, from inside Christopher's head, like a threat.

The journey to London challenges the ordinary in a different way. Christopher's search for his mother should be a matter of trains and stations, the most mundane things a city offers. Instead the station and the Underground become overwhelming, and the crowds become the real obstacle in the plot. Haddon makes the familiar threatening, so the reader realises that what counts as ordinary depends on who is experiencing it. The novel's distinctive qualities are most visible here: the plain sentences give the noise and the strangers no emotional cushion, and the reader feels the journey as Christopher does.

Form does similar work. The chapters are numbered by prime numbers rather than in sequence, and the book includes maps, diagrams and pictures that are crucial to the plot rather than decoration. These devices belong to a mind that organises the world by logic, so they show how Christopher thinks while suggesting that the ordinary world can be read in more than one way. Haddon's maps and diagrams let the reader work through the journey piece by piece, as Christopher does, instead of accepting a familiar summary.

The ending tests whether ordinary life can be rebuilt. Siobhan, his teacher and mentor, teaches him how society works, and he learns its guidelines as rules rather than instincts. By the end he completes his mathematics A-level and plans for university, and his father gives him a puppy, Sandy, as part of an effort to rebuild trust. These small restorations reinforce a hopeful view of ordinary life. Yet Christopher remains wary of his father, and the reader is left to wonder how much ordinary happiness depends on agreements that Christopher has had to learn rather than feel.

Haddon's novel, then, reinforces our understanding that ordinary situations are held together by loyalties, lies and routines, and it challenges us to see how strange those routines look to someone who cannot take them for granted. The ordinary is not simply a shared world. It is a set of agreements, and Christopher's difficulty with them shows the reader what those agreements cost and what they protect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it argues that the novel both confirms family life through the father's lie and challenges it through Christopher's reaction to the policeman and the London crowds, and it sustains that argument to a balanced close. Its strongest move is tying the Holmes line about the silent dog to what goes unsaid in ordinary life. To go further, it could set one of Christopher's rules against a rule that adults never examine.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Mark Haddon's The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time reinforces and challenges our understanding of ordinary situations. Christopher is a fifteen-year-old boy who finds his neighbour's dog dead and decides to investigate. Many of the things that happen in the book are ordinary, like going to school and talking to his family, and these show how ordinary life works for most people. The novel is told by Christopher himself, so we see everything through his eyes.

The novel reinforces what we already know about families. Christopher's father, Ed, tells him that his mother died, but Christopher finds letters that show she is alive. This happens in many families, where parents keep secrets from their children, and it makes the reader feel sorry for Christopher. Ed's lie is wrong, but the reader can see why a father might tell it. Families are shown as places where people try to look after each other, even when they get things wrong.

The novel also challenges our understanding of ordinary situations. When the policeman grabs Christopher's arm, he panics and hits him, and then he is arrested. For most people a policeman's grip would be routine, but for Christopher it is frightening. This shows that ordinary situations are not the same for everyone. Christopher does not understand metaphors and finds it hard to read people's feelings, so the world looks different to him, and the reader sees how things most people take for granted can be difficult for him.

The journey to London is another example. Christopher gets on a train to find his mother. The trains and crowds overwhelm him, and the station, which should be a simple place to travel from, becomes difficult. The reader sees how hard it is for Christopher to do things most people take for granted, and the journey makes the reader think about how much ordinary life depends on coping with crowds and noise.

The chapters are numbered with prime numbers, which is unusual. The book also has maps and diagrams. These features show the way Christopher thinks, and they help the reader see the world through his eyes. Because the book is organised in this way, the reader has to work out the ordinary world for themselves, rather than accepting it as normal.

Siobhan, his teacher, helps him understand how society works and teaches him the rules that other people follow without thinking. At the end Christopher completes his maths A-level and plans to go to university, and his father gives him a puppy. These events suggest that ordinary life can be rebuilt after a crisis, although the novel does not say that everything is fixed.

Haddon's novel both reinforces and challenges our understanding of ordinary situations, because it shows familiar families and events from an unusual point of view.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it names the father's lie, the policeman and the prime-numbered chapters, but explains each in turn with few quotations and some retelling of the plot. Its strongest point is the policeman's grip, which it shows as an ordinary contact that is frightening to Christopher. To lift it, it should analyse one scene closely and show how a specific technique makes the familiar strange.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the novel The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time by Mark Haddon, Christopher finds his neighbour's dog dead and decides to find out who killed it. He writes a book about the investigation, even though his dad does not want him to. He finds some things hard, like being touched and talking to people. He finds it hard to understand other people's feelings. His dad tells him lies about his mum, and Christopher finds letters from her in his dad's room. He then goes to London on a train to look for her. There are lots of people and it is very noisy, and he finds it frightening. At the end he does his maths exam and his dad gives him a puppy. The novel shows that ordinary life can be hard for some people and that families can be complicated. Haddon writes about a boy who sees things differently from other people. So literature reinforces what we know about families and also challenges our ideas about ordinary things, because it shows that everyday life looks strange to someone else.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the investigation, the lie and the London trip in order, with almost no reference to the novel's techniques. Its one useful idea is that the novel shows ordinary life as complicated. It could develop that by choosing one scene and explaining how Haddon makes it strange.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of a text’s distinctive qualities and how these shape meaning; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section II — Module B: Close Study of Literature (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

dotPoints.description: The ways textual forms, language and stylistic choices shape meaning

prompts.question: Analyse how the diary form and the short, clipped sentences work together to shape the meaning of the boarder's experience of the drought.
markerNotes: Analyse means follow the consequences. Strong answers show how the form changes what the sentences can do, and how the sentences change what the form can carry.
Quote short phrases from the entries. A precise phrase, such as the dam line, earns more than a general claim that the diary feels bleak.
The top band ends with a view of the whole sequence, not with the final entry alone.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the diary form and the short sentences as two separate features with no link between them.
Saying the diary feels sad or bleak without showing which textual choice creates that feeling.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the diary form and the clipped sentences work together, showing the relationships between them and the cumulative effect on the meaning of the drought
5 marks: Analyses the diary form and the sentences with clear links between them and the meaning of the drought, supported by specific evidence
4 marks: Explains the form and the sentences with evidence, but the link between them and the meaning is only partly developed
3 marks: Describes the diary form and the sentences with some evidence and a general statement about meaning
2 marks: Identifies features of the diary form or the sentences with little explanation of effect
1 mark: Names the diary form or the sentences without explaining their effect

sampleAnswers.answer:
The diary form and the clipped sentences work together to make the drought a daily fact rather than a distant event. Because each entry is dated, the form builds a record the boarder cannot escape, so the reader experiences the drought as a sequence of small measurements. The clipped sentences intensify this effect: 'Dam down again. Tank low.' carries no spare words, so the narrator's exhaustion sits in the rhythm of the prose. The brevity also limits what the boarder can say about her feelings, and the meaning sits in the gaps between entries, where fear is inferred from what is left unsaid.

The two features reinforce each other. The diary is private, so the clipped style feels honest rather than performed. By the final entry, which shifts into the present tense, the form and the sentences have prepared the reader to see the drought as a condition of life rather than an event that will end. Taken together, these textual forms and stylistic choices keep the drought at the level of routine. The meaning of the sequence is carried less by what happens than by how little the narrator allows herself to say.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The diary form and the clipped sentences are analysed together, with the relationship between them shown and the cumulative effect traced across the sequence to the final entry. The answer uses textual forms and stylistic choices to build a view of the whole, which is the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: The diary form makes the drought feel like a daily record, because each entry is dated. The clipped sentences, such as 'Dam down again', make the reader feel the narrator is tired. Together these features show that the drought affects the narrator every day, so the reader understands the meaning of how hard life is in the school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The form and the sentences are explained with evidence, but the link between them and the wider meaning of the drought is only partly developed, which places the answer in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The diary has short sentences and a date at the top of each entry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The diary form and the sentences are named without any explanation of their effect, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading an invented sequence of seven diary entries, written for this question, by a sixteen-year-old boarder at a country school during a drought. Each entry is dated, the sentences are short, the entries repeatedly mention a dam level chalked on the classroom wall, one entry reads 'Dam down again. Tank low.', and the final entry is written in the present tense after a day without rain.

prompts.question: Define the term 'motif' and give ONE example of a motif in the diary entries.
markerNotes: A definition needs both parts: the element recurs, and the recurrence builds meaning. Answers that give only one part lose a mark.
The example must come from the diary. A motif named from outside the text is worth nothing here.
commonStudentErrors: Defining motif as a theme or the main idea of the text.
Giving an example of a symbol or a single image without showing that it recurs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Defines a motif accurately as a recurring element, such as an image, word or idea, that builds meaning across a text, and gives a specific example from the diary entries
1 mark: Gives a partial definition, or an example without a definition

sampleAnswers.answer: A motif is a recurring image, word or idea that builds meaning across a text. In the diary entries, the dam level chalked on the classroom wall is a motif that recurs, with each reading showing the drought deepening.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The definition captures both recurrence and the building of meaning, and the example is specific to the diary, so both parts of the answer are earned for the full 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A motif is something that appears again. The dam is one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The definition is partial, with no link to meaning, and the example is given without explanation, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading the same invented sequence of seven diary entries (written for this question) by a sixteen-year-old boarder at a country school during a drought. The entries repeatedly mention a dam level chalked on the classroom wall, and the final entry is written in the present tense.

prompts.question: Clarify how the shift to the present tense in the final diary entry changes the reader's sense of time.
markerNotes: Clarify means make the effect plain. Say exactly what changes for the reader and why the change happens at this point in the sequence.
Place the final entry within the sequence. The shift matters because the earlier entries have already set up a sense of looking back.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the tense changes without saying what the reader now experiences.
Describing the final entry's content rather than its tense.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies precisely how the shift to the present tense changes the reader's sense of time, with reference to the final entry and its place in the sequence
2 marks: Identifies the shift and makes a general statement about its effect on time
1 mark: Identifies the shift without explaining its effect

sampleAnswers.answer: The shift to the present tense makes time feel immediate rather than recorded. Every earlier diary entry looks back on a finished day, so the reader sits at a safe distance. The final entry records its day as it happens, collapsing that distance: the reader is in the room, waiting for rain. Placed last, the change alters the meaning of the whole sequence, from a closed record to an ongoing present.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer clarifies exactly what the tense shift does to the reader's sense of time, places the final diary entry within the sequence, and explains why the change alters the meaning of the whole. This is the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: The final entry changes to present tense, so the reader feels the drought is happening now. This changes how time feels in the story.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The shift is identified and there is a general statement about its effect on time, but the answer does not place the entry within the sequence or explain the change, which matches the 2-mark line.

sampleAnswers.answer: The final entry is in the present tense.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The shift is identified without any explanation of its effect, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: Students are reading the same invented sequence of seven diary entries (written for this question) by a sixteen-year-old boarder at a country school during a drought. Each earlier entry describes a day that has already ended, and the final entry is written in the present tense after a day without rain.

prompts.question: Analyse how different values and attitudes are exposed through the key features of your prescribed text. In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The stem asks how values and attitudes are exposed through key features, so each feature needs an attitude attached to it, not just a description of what happens in it.
Theseus's speech on imagination is the strongest quotation for an attitude to art. Use it to test the lovers' romance, not only to praise the poet.
The mechanicals are the best evidence of class attitudes and of respect for performance. The lovers alone will not carry the answer.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising the four lovers' confusion in the wood without saying what it shows about love.
Calling the play's attitude to love simply romantic, without acknowledging Puck's mockery in 'Lord, what fools these mortals be!'.
Attributing the closing lines to the mechanicals rather than to Puck.
Treating Theseus as only the voice of the law, which misses how his response to the lovers' stories complicates the play's attitude to reason.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A Midsummer Night’s Dream exposes its values and attitudes through a set of key features: the Athenian court and its law, the enchanted wood, the flower that Puck uses on the lovers, and the play within the play performed by the mechanicals. Taken together, these features show that Shakespeare regards love as powerful and arbitrary, distrusts the rational authority that tries to govern it, and values imagination while gently mocking those who claim to control it. The play’s attitudes are never fixed. They shift as the audience moves between Athens and the wood.

The play opens in the palace of Theseus, where the values of law and patriarchal authority are established before any magic appears. Egeus claims his daughter as property and insists that he may ‘dispose of her’ because she is his. He asks Theseus to enforce a law that leaves Hermia with a choice between marrying Demetrius, ‘to die the death’, or abjuring men for ever. Theseus is reasonable rather than cruel, and he gives Hermia time to reconsider, but the rule itself is shown as harsh. Lysander proposes that they escape to a widowed aunt’s house beyond the reach of the sharp Athenian law, and that escape takes the lovers into the wood.

Once the lovers enter the wood, the rules of the court begin to dissolve. The fairy world is introduced through Oberon and Titania, whose opening quarrel, ‘Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania’, exposes a realm as possessive and jealous as Athens. Their dispute over a changeling boy, ‘stol’n from an Indian king’, shows that the fairies also claim people, even children, as things to be owned. Puck applies the flower called love-in-idleness, and the consequence is that love is governed by chance rather than reason. Lovers who wake to find their affections transferred reveal the play’s attitude that love is both comic and unreliable.

The mechanicals’ play within the play is the most revealing of the key features. Quince, Bottom, Flute and their companions rehearse Pyramus and Thisbe with enthusiasm and little talent. Their earnest attempt to stage a tragic story of lovers mirrors the four lovers’ suffering while exposing its absurdity. Bottom is cast as Pyramus, and the rehearsal scenes carry the class difference between craftsmen and the court. The courtly audience treats the performance as a joke, which exposes an attitude of superiority. Yet the mechanicals’ sincerity is also a form of respect for their craft, and Shakespeare lets their earnestness outlast the lovers’ own pretensions. Theseus concedes as much when he says that the worst performance is no worse, if imagination amend it.

Theseus’s speech on imagination is the clearest statement of the play’s attitudes to art and reason. He opens by dismissing the lovers’ stories, saying ‘Lovers and madmen have such seething brains’, and then reaches a more generous judgement: ‘The lunatic, the lover, and the poet’ as figures ‘of imagination all compact’. The play values the poet’s power to shape what cannot be seen, even while the court distrusts it. Puck’s closing lines then ask the audience to excuse the night’s illusions: ‘If we shadows have offended’. The request exposes the play’s view that theatre is a shared act of imagining.

Puck’s judgement, ‘Lord, what fools these mortals be!’, gives the play’s most direct statement of its attitude to human love. The comedy complicates this judgement, because Puck is himself the agent of the confusion. Bottom’s transformation into an ass, marked by the words ‘Thou art translated’, is a key feature that exposes the court’s assumptions about the lower orders. Titania wakes to ask ‘What angel wakes me’, and her devotion to the craftsman mocks courtly love and its romantic extravagance. The scene also gives Bottom a tender comic dignity, since the fairy queen chooses the weaver as her beloved, which reverses the court’s assumptions about rank.

The play exposes the court’s values and then tests them through the mechanicals, the wood and the fairies. Each key feature asks the audience to weigh what it sees against what Athens takes for granted, and the comedy rarely lets either side win outright.

Through the court, the wood, the enchanted flower and the play within a play, the Dream exposes values that prize imagination and the freedom of love, alongside attitudes that are suspicious of authority, dismissive of artistic pretension, and yet tender towards the mechanicals’ earnest craft. The play does not settle these tensions. It leaves the audience weighing reason against illusion and deciding, in the end, which of the two deserves trust.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how values and attitudes are exposed through the key features, including Egeus's claim on Hermia, the wood, the mechanicals and Theseus's speech, and each feature is tied to an attitude. The references are detailed and the expression is controlled. The closing paragraph's claims about the whole play could be argued more closely to push it further.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Shakespeare explores values and attitudes through several key features, including the Athenian court, the wood, the magic flower and the play within the play. The play opens in Athens, where Egeus wants his daughter Hermia to marry Demetrius and Theseus says the law must be followed. This shows that the court values order and the authority of fathers. Hermia and Lysander decide to escape to the wood, which is a different world where the rules of Athens do not apply in the same way.

The wood is where the fairies are introduced. Oberon and Titania argue, and Puck uses a flower called love-in-idleness to confuse the lovers. Love is shown as unpredictable and something that can happen by chance. The lovers behave comically, and this suggests that Shakespeare does not think love should be taken too seriously. The audience sees the lovers’ reasoning fail, which exposes a view that rational choice cannot control desire.

The mechanicals are another key feature. They rehearse a play called Pyramus and Thisbe, and Bottom is cast as Pyramus. The mechanicals are not very skilled, and the play makes them look silly. However, their play is also an example of the value of performance and enthusiasm, and it reflects the lovers’ own stories of love and danger. The contrast between the craftsmen and the court shows an attitude to class that is partly mocking and partly affectionate. Bottom is a weaver rather than a noble, and the play uses his ambition as a source of humour.

Theseus gives a speech about imagination. He says that lovers and madmen have seething brains and that the poet has imagination, which suggests an attitude that reason distrusts imagination but that imagination is nevertheless important. The character who first dismisses the lovers’ stories later values the poet’s role. Puck’s closing lines ask the audience to forgive the play if they have been offended, and this shows the value of theatre as a shared experience between performers and audience.

Bottom’s transformation into an ass is another key feature. The fairy queen falls in love with him, which is comic and shows the play mocking romance. Titania’s love is shown as foolish, but the scene also makes Bottom a character with a kind of dignity. Puck says that humans are fools when they fall in love, which is an attitude that the play partly shares, since the lovers are the ones who are confused.

Overall, the play exposes values about love, authority and art through its characters and settings. Shakespeare shows contrasting attitudes towards the court and the wood, and the audience is invited to consider which is more valuable. The events of the night seem like a dream, and this is part of the play’s meaning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains competently how the key features expose attitudes, but much of the middle is description and the references are fewer and thinner. It would move up by testing each attitude against another feature, for example setting the court's law against the mechanicals' earnest performance, rather than adding more plot.

sampleAnswers.answer: A Midsummer Night’s Dream is a comedy about four lovers in Athens who go into a wood. Their parents want them to marry the right people, and there is a law in Athens that makes it difficult for them. In the wood, fairies use a magic flower to make people fall in love, and the fairy queen falls in love with a man who has an ass’s head. The mechanicals put on a play for the wedding of the Duke. At the end Puck says sorry if the audience was offended. The play shows that love is silly and that different groups have different values, such as the court valuing law and the mechanicals valuing their play. Shakespeare includes these key features to make the audience laugh and think. The play is comic in tone and never really asks the audience to take its lovers seriously.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the play in order, with a list of features and minimal reference to the text. The lift would come from naming one feature and the attitude it exposes, such as the court's rigid law, and supporting it with a quotation.

prompts.question: Analyse how the central ideas of Feed are explored through the distinctive qualities of the text. In your response, make detailed reference to the extract below and your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks for analysis through the distinctive qualities, so the strongest answers treat the automated message and the short final sentence as deliberate choices in the writing, not only as plot.
Use the extract closely. The dash before ‘My body’, the etc. and the Lunar GPS line each carry a central idea, and the best answers show more than one of them.
Connect the extract to the prescribed text without retelling it. Titus’s dependence on credit is strongest when it is linked to the consumer life he lives in the novel.
Identity, the body and communication are all central ideas. A top answer shows how the three are linked, not three separate paragraphs of description.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the extract line by line without asking what the feed does to the narrator’s voice.
Treating ‘So I opened my eyes’ as a happy ending, rather than as a return to the body in a mind still shaped by the feed.
Quoting the novel’s ending from memory rather than the extract, which is the text that can be checked in the question.
Describing Violet’s resistance at the mall without noticing that it depends on the consumer system it opposes.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The extract shows Titus waking after his feed has been cut off, and in a few short paragraphs it explores the central ideas of Feed: identity shaped by consumption, the loss of independent thought and corporate control over communication. Anderson’s distinctive qualities, the teenage voice, the automated message that keeps returning and the abrupt ending, make the reader experience a dependence that Titus only half understands. The prescribed text confirms that these are the novel’s central ideas rather than features of a single scene. Read together, the extract and the novel show a world in which the self has been handed over to a system and must be found again.

The first central idea is identity. Titus’s first feeling is “no credit”, the loss of the currency that organises his world, and he tries to touch his credit as though it were something he could hold. In a consumer society, credit tells a person where they stand, and Anderson makes Titus’s sense of self depend on it. The prescribed text develops this idea. Titus is largely content with a life of buying, and the advertising that runs through his feed shapes what he wants. Without the feed, the extract shows, he has nothing to hold, and the loss of credit exposes how little of his identity feels like his own.

The second idea concerns the body and the difficulty of locating the self. The extract introduces the body with a dash, “My body —”, and then describes an arm that is asleep and a bed he cannot place, because he “couldn’t find the Lunar GPS” to tell him where he is. The feed has been the means by which Titus knows where he is, so its absence leaves a body that is present but not understood. Anderson uses this gap to show how far the feed has taken over the place where a person would normally locate themselves. The body reads as an afterthought in a mind organised around the feed.

The third idea is that communication has been captured by corporate systems. Titus tries to chat Link, then Marty, then his parents on Earth, and each attempt meets the same automated message: there is “no transmission signal”, and he is “currently disconnected from feednet”. The relationships that define his life are imagined as channels the feed controls, and when the channel closes he is left alone. His fear is stated in his own words, “I was starting to get scared”, rather than in the wording of the message. The prescribed text makes the same point through Titus’s friends, who follow trends together, and through Violet, whose call to FeedTech customer service brings no help.

The distinctive qualities of the writing make these ideas felt. The automated message returns inside the narrator’s own sentences, so his fear arrives in the template of a system notice: “I was currently etc.” The “etc.” stands in for words the narrator does not repeat, as if the message were running on without him, and the sentence trails off as if the feed had cut into his thought. The repeated “but” in the passage mirrors the way Titus’s mind moves from one failed attempt to the next, while the short final sentence, “So I opened my eyes.”, returns to a plain physical act. Anderson uses syntax to show a mind shaped by the feed making one small attempt to find its own experience.

The prescribed text carries these ideas forward. Violet’s plan to resist the feed by confusing her consumer profile has the same limits as the extract, because the feed still controls her access to help and to her own body. Titus’s final gestures, ordering the same jeans until he is out of credit and telling Violet their story as a movie trailer, are attempts to speak in a form of his own, but they use the language the feed has given him. The novel ends with the slogan “Everything Must Go” repeated in smaller type, and the extract prepares the reader for that ending. Identity, control and the search for an authentic voice are explored through a narrator whose mind has been shaped by the system he describes, and that is why the distinctive qualities of the text matter so much.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses three central ideas, identity, the body and communication, and links each to a feature of the extract and to the prescribed text. The analysis of the repeated automated message and the final sentence shows the distinctive qualities working on the reader. To lift it, the conclusion could judge whether the ending of the novel is hopeful or bleak, so that the analysis reaches a view rather than a summary.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The extract shows Titus waking after his feed has been cut off. He has no credit, he cannot work out where he is, and he cannot reach his friends or his parents. Feed is about a future where corporations control people through their feeds, so this moment is important to the novel’s ideas.

Titus starts by describing how he feels. He says he has no credit and that he tried to touch it but there was nothing there. This shows how much he depends on credit and on the feed. He also says he is in a bed and his arm is asleep, but he cannot find the Lunar GPS to tell him where he is. The narrator is lost without the feed, and that is the main point of this part of the extract.

Next he tries to chat. He tries Link and Marty, but there is no transmission signal and he is disconnected from feednet. Then he tries to chat his parents on Earth and gets the same message. The repetition makes the message feel as if it is closing in on him. This shows that the feed controls how people speak to each other, and that Titus only knows how to communicate through it. He starts to get scared, and the extract ends with him opening his eyes.

The language of the extract is also important. Titus repeats the message and writes etc., which makes the writing sound like a computer. This shows that Titus’s language has been shaped by the feed. Anderson uses a teenage voice, so the reader hears how Titus thinks and can see the problem for themselves. The writing is therefore part of the meaning, not just a way of telling the story.

In the rest of the novel, Violet tries to resist the feed by asking about things at the mall that she does not want. Titus goes along with it for a while, but he gives in to his friends and to the advertisements. This is an example of the novel’s ideas about conformity and corporate power. The extract and the rest of the book both show a character who is not in control of his own life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the extract and identifies the feed as the source of Titus’s dependence, but much of it retells the passage in order and the references to the prescribed text are thin. It would move up by analysing the repeated automated message and the closing sentence as deliberate choices in the writing, rather than describing what happens.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the extract, Titus wakes up and his feed has gone. He says he has no credit and he cannot chat to his friends or his parents. He is scared by the end, and then he opens his eyes. Feed is a book by M T Anderson about a future where corporations control almost everything. The feed is in people’s heads and it gives them adverts all the time. Titus and his friends like shopping and they do what the adverts tell them. Violet is different and does not like the feed, so she tries to resist it by going to the mall. The book has lots of slang, and that is one of its distinctive qualities. The extract shows that Titus cannot do anything without the feed, and that is one of the central ideas of the book. The book is also sad, and the extract makes the reader worry about him.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the extract and the world of the novel with minimal textual reference and little analysis of the distinctive qualities. Its strength is the basic point that Titus cannot act without the feed. The lift would come from quoting one line from the extract and explaining what it shows about identity or communication.

prompts.scenario: Extract: The first thing I felt was no credit. I tried to touch my credit, but there was nothing there. It felt like I was in a little room. My body — I was in a bed, on top of my arm, which was asleep, but I didn’t know where, I couldn’t find the Lunar GPS to tell me. Someone had left a message in my head, which I found, and then kept finding everywhere I went, which said that there was no transmission signal, that I was currently disconnected from feednet. I tried to chat Link and then Marty, but nothing, there was no transmission signal, I was currently disconnected from feednet, of course, and I was starting to get scared, so I tried to chat my parents, I tried to chat them on Earth, but there was no transmission etc., I was currently etc. So I opened my eyes. prompts.question: Analyse how the central ideas of Gray’s poetry are explored through the distinctive qualities of the poems. In your response, make detailed reference to the extract below and at least ONE other prescribed poem.
markerNotes: The question has two demands: the central ideas, and the distinctive qualities that explore them. Strong answers keep both in view in every paragraph, so the ideas are never described without the technique that carries them.
Use the extract as the centre of the argument. Its colour, syntax and stanza break can be checked against the text, and they give the strongest answers their evidence.
The second prescribed poem must be developed, not added. Show what it adds to the idea the extract establishes, such as the change from shared attention to solitary attention.
Avoid naming themes such as time or belonging as if they were the answer. The best responses show how an image makes the reader feel the idea.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the poems are about time or nature without showing how a particular image makes that idea felt.
Retelling the extract line by line, so the answer describes the harbour and yachts but never reaches the central ideas.
Using the second prescribed poem as a general example of appreciation, without tying it to the extract’s distinctive qualities.
Treating ‘a stone parapet’s fading life’ as only a reference to age, when the phrase links the stone, the day and the speaker’s attention.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Gray’s central ideas in Coast Road are that time passes and fades things, that human attention is both a gift to places and a limited one, and that ordinary scenes hold real beauty. These ideas are explored through the distinctive qualities of his poems: precise colour and texture, sentences that break and stall, and a steady refusal to say what the scene means. The extract from ‘Harbour Dusk’ shows all three in close detail, and ‘Byron Bay: Winter’ shows how the same ideas survive in a different setting.

The extract is built on the idea of time. Its last line places the scene “after the summer day”, and the day that has gone is given an ending that is physical and large in the phrase “a huge, moist hush”. Earlier, the stone has a “fading life”, which sets the stone’s history beside the walk of the speaker and companion. The stone is worn, and the speaker and companion lay their hands on something already passing. The poem does not state an idea about time. It lets the reader feel that the day, the stone and the light are all leaving, and that the speaker’s attention is a brief presence within that movement.

The second idea is the relation between human attention and the places attended to. The speaker and companion are the only people in the extract, and they look, touch and try to see. The verb “make out” implies effort, because the light is failing and seeing is partial. The phrase “oily, aubergine dark” reflects the poem’s distinctive quality of precise colour and texture. The water is named by its oily surface and by a colour named after a vegetable, so the eye and the sense of touch are both engaged. Attention is shown as sensory but never complete, since the yachts are seen with difficulty rather than clearly.

The third idea, that the everyday holds beauty, is carried by the city. The city appears as “fruit shop bright”, a comparison that takes a commercial scene, a lit shop window, and makes it the source of light in the poem. The city is not remote or sublime; it is the sort of brightness a reader passes every day. The contrast with the “crumbling bush” on the far shore sharpens the point. Both are real, and the poem gives them equal exactness, so the beauty of the ordinary is not a sentimental claim but something the reader must notice for themselves.

‘Byron Bay: Winter’, the second prescribed poem, develops the same central idea of ordinary beauty in a different setting. Its speaker is alone on a winter beach, and the poem’s attention moves over the shoreline and the sea without making the scene grander than it is. Solitude makes appreciation the poem’s own act, since nobody else shares the view and the noticing belongs wholly to the speaker. Where the extract shows a shared gesture, with two people laying their hands on stone, ‘Byron Bay: Winter’ shows one person alone, so the idea of human attention is developed in a second form. This change of setting is also a change in the poem’s distinctive qualities, from a shared scene to a private one.

The extract’s form explores these ideas too. The stanza break after “yachts —” separates the watcher from the things watched, so the eye must cross a gap to find where the yachts sit. The second stanza then stacks phrases such as “beneath an overcast sky” and “against a far shore”, which have no main verb, so the scene arrives as a set of observations rather than an argument. This mirrors the central ideas: a view accumulates patiently without being ordered, just as attention and time gather and then fade.

Taken together, the extract and ‘Byron Bay: Winter’ show that Gray’s central ideas are explored through steady, precise attention to what is fading and ordinary. The poems do not announce these ideas. They rely on the distinctive qualities of colour, fragment and stillness to make the reader feel how brief and how valuable such attention is, and how easily it is lost. That is why the ideas linger after the reading ends.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses the extract’s time, attention and ordinary beauty as central ideas, ties each to a distinctive quality such as colour or the stanza break, and develops them through a second prescribed poem. The one move that would lift it is to test the second poem’s solitude against the extract’s shared gesture more directly, so the comparison drives the analysis rather than running beside it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Gray’s central ideas are explored in several ways in his poems, including time, the way people look at places, and the value of everyday things. In the extract from ‘Harbour Dusk’ these ideas are shown through description. The poem also uses distinctive qualities such as colour and an unusual structure. ‘Byron Bay: Winter’ is the second prescribed poem, and it also shows an appreciation of ordinary things, which connects it to the extract.

In the extract, the speaker and companion touch a stone parapet with a fading life, and the harbour is seen in failing light. This shows that time is passing. The phrase “a huge, moist hush” shows that the day is quiet and ending. These images explain the idea of time, but the reader is mostly told about the scene rather than shown how the images work together.

The extract also shows human attention. The speaker and companion look at the harbour and try to see the yachts. The phrase “make out” suggests the yachts are hard to see. The water is described as “oily, aubergine dark”, which is a colourful image. The city is described as bright, which contrasts with the park. These details show that the poem is interested in places and in what people notice in them.

The stanza break and the dash after “yachts —” also make the reader pause, so the search for the yachts becomes part of the experience of looking. This links the form to the idea of attention in a simple way.

‘Byron Bay: Winter’ is about a person walking alone on the beach. The speaker notices the shore and the sea, which shows appreciation of ordinary things. Being alone shows the value of private moments. The poem is quiet and reflective, and this shows the idea of appreciation clearly.

Gray’s distinctive qualities include vivid colours, unusual comparisons and broken sentences. These help the reader see the places. Overall the poems show that places and time matter, and that the reader should think about how people look at the world. The poems have ideas that are important and clear to the reader.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it names time and the value of ordinary places as central ideas, and it refers to the extract with some accuracy. The one move that would lift it is to analyse how an image such as ‘a huge, moist hush’ develops the idea of time, rather than stating that it does.

sampleAnswers.answer: Robert Gray writes about nature and the city in his poetry. The extract is from ‘Harbour Dusk’. It describes a park, a harbour, yachts, a city and some bush. The speaker and a companion are in the park, and it is getting dark. There are some nice colours, like dark water and a mauve sky. The second poem is ‘Byron Bay: Winter’, which is about a beach in winter. In both poems the speaker is looking at things and noticing them. Gray’s ideas are about people noticing things and about the beauty of ordinary places, and that is what the poems are about. The poem is about nature and the city, and it shows people looking at things. The reader can see a park, some water and some sky. The second poem is also about a scene that the speaker looks at closely, so the ideas in both poems are similar.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the extract and the second poem with minimal analysis, and its central ideas are named rather than developed. The one move that would lift it is to choose one image, such as ‘oily, aubergine dark’, and explain how its wording develops an idea about attention.

prompts.question: Analyse how the central ideas of Noonuccal’s poetry are explored through the distinctive qualities of the poems. In your response, make detailed reference to the extract below and at least ONE other prescribed poem.
markerNotes: The extract is the anchor. Strong answers read its line breaks and its final abstract nouns closely, rather than summarising the story of the discovery.

The question asks for the central ideas to be explored through distinctive qualities, so each quality named, such as personification, plain diction or line breaks, should be tied to an idea it makes possible.

The second poem should test the first, not repeat it. The Past's claim that the past is not dead shows the difference between buried memory and inherited memory, and the strongest answers use that difference.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The central ideas of Oodgeroo Noonuccal's poetry in this extract are that the past is buried but never destroyed, and that power is exposed when it is recovered. These ideas are explored through the distinctive qualities of the poem Entombed Warriors: a personified earth, plain diction and line breaks that hold the reader in suspense. The Past, another prescribed poem, extends the same idea into the speaker's own inheritance. Together, the two poems show that memory is held by land and blood as well as by monuments.

The extract opens by personifying the land. Across “For 2,000 years”, the Earth Mother “Nursed her son”, which makes the land a keeper rather than a passive setting. The phrase is plain and the poem does not dramatise the passing of time, so the number stands alone and the reader feels how long the secret has been held. The clauses are broken across short lines, so the poem moves slowly, as if the earth itself were reluctant to give up its secret. The first central idea is therefore that the land protects what it holds, and the personification turns burial into care.

The second central idea is that recovery depends on ordinary labour rather than power. The word “Until” stands alone on its line, followed by “By chance”, so the discovery is delayed and then credited to accident. A pick and shovel, an ordinary tool, does what no ruler could do, and the mismatch between a humble tool and a buried monument makes the reader notice the gap between what power intends to keep and what can actually be kept. “Revealed his secret” then introduces hidden interiority, implying that the buried figure has a private self that the poem will expose. The poem does not name the discoverers or their purpose, so the reader's attention stays on the tool and on what it uncovers.

The final lines develop the idea of exposed vulnerability. “The earth opened up” and “exposed to the world” use the verb exposed, which suggests both revelation and shame. What is exposed is not the grandeur an army guarding a tomb was built to suggest but “His fear” and “His insecurity”. These abstract nouns are blunt, and the poem gives no explanation of them. The central idea is that power and fear sit close together, and that a recovered past can show the human fear beneath a monument. The extract does not return to the Earth Mother after this revelation, so the protective image is left behind and the reader is left with the exposed ruler alone. The reader must decide whether this is pity or judgement, and the openness of the ending is itself one of the poem's distinctive qualities.

The Past extends the idea of recovery into the speaker's own body. Its distinctive quality is its direct imperative. “Let no one say the past is dead” forbids a claim and so places the reader among those who might make it. The speaker then argues that the past is “all about us and within”, which reverses the logic of the extract. In Entombed Warriors the past is buried until chance uncovers it. In The Past it was never buried but is inherited, and the camp fires of the forest “Are in my blood”. The comparison shows that Oodgeroo explores memory in two ways, as something that waits to be found and as something that is carried.

Taken together, the extract and The Past show that the central ideas of Oodgeroo's poetry depend on distinctive qualities: personification, plain diction, pauses made by line breaks and statements that refuse easy closure. Whatever the earth keeps is never fully owned by the people who uncover it, and the poems leave the reader to consider what that means for a nation's sense of its own past. Oodgeroo's plain statements carry large ideas, and her images of care and exposure ask the reader to hold both in mind at once.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how the central ideas are explored through the poem's personification, plain diction and line breaks, and it uses the extract and The Past together to test the idea of recovered memory. The references are detailed and the argument is controlled. To lift it further, the conclusion could weigh more precisely how the poem's openness about fear shapes its meaning.

Oodgeroo Noonuccal's central ideas in the extract are about the past, power and the land. The extract comes from the poem Entombed Warriors, and it has the Earth Mother who nursed her son. This shows that the land looks after things, which is an important idea in the poem. The poem also has a pick and shovel that reveals the son's secret. The reader can see that discovery is by chance and not planned, and this is one of the distinctive qualities of the poem.

The extract ends with his fear and his insecurity exposed to the world. This is the most important part of the extract because it shows that the powerful person was afraid. The poem does not explain the fear, so the reader has to think about it. The distinctive quality here is that the lines are short and plain, which makes the ending stronger. The central idea is that power and fear are connected, and that the past shows us this.

The second prescribed poem is The Past. In this poem the speaker says that nobody should say the past is dead. This is a different idea from the extract, because in The Past the past is always with us and is in the speaker's blood. In the extract the past was hidden and then found, but in The Past it is never lost. The second poem also makes a direct claim, which links it to the plain statements of the extract's ending. Both poems show that the past is important to Oodgeroo, and that the past can help people understand the present.

The distinctive qualities of Oodgeroo's poetry include short lines, plain words and direct statements. These qualities help to explore the central ideas about memory and power, and they make the poems easy to read. Oodgeroo shows that the land keeps the past and that people can find it again, which is the main point of the poems.
