sampleAnswers.answer:
Rankin’s Namatjira explores its central ideas, a divided identity, the renaming of a man and the value placed on his art, through the distinctive qualities of performance: a narrating voice, a mixture of languages and a stage on which a landscape is drawn in front of the audience. The extract shows these qualities at work in one moment, when the mission’s order is disturbed by the arrival of a car and a stranger. Read closely, the extract introduces the central ideas before the play has finished developing them.

The extract opens with a narrating voice: “So there was Albert, between two worlds.” The speaker places Albert in a position that is not fixed. The next words, “Name changed.”, signal that his identity on the mission is something done to him rather than something he chose. Here is the first central idea: the play treats naming as a form of power. He is “Not a man, not a boy”, and the speaker then lists what he is: “Speaking Aranda, German, bit of English”, and “an evangelist, choir, bushman”. The list refuses to settle on one identity. It shows that each role comes from a different system of expectation, whether faith, language or work.

The extract also places Albert within a family that has very little: “Growing family, poor, no house, nothing”. Those words make the central idea of value concrete. His art is measured against that lack before any painting is shown, and the audience is asked to see the poverty and the reputation together.

The arrival of the car disturbs the mission’s order. “A Model T Ford arrives” is a short stage direction, but its effect is large. The car is an “angry mechanical ant”, and the man who climbs from its belly is a “strange little man” who “walks funny, like a bird”. The metaphor makes the car alien, while the bird image tells the audience to watch how the outsider moves through the mission. The men’s reaction, gathered and whispering, responds to an unfamiliar body as much as to a new visitor.

The repeated greeting shows the play’s concern with naming and language most directly. The men call out first, then German, repeat the Aranda line, and finish in English: “Old Heron Man has come.” The sequence is a distinctive quality of the text. The audience hears the greeting in the languages the mission imposed and in the language it kept, so the words carry the tension between two worlds. Naming the newcomer after a heron is an act of community definition, the reverse of the renaming the speaker has just described for Albert. The greeting therefore works as a small model of the whole play: a community speaks, a newcomer is named, and the meaning of that naming is left for the audience to weigh.

The extract closes with Rex stepping from the car, “moving like a heron”, and this image links the two halves of the text. Rex may be the painter who taught Albert, so the arrival is the first step towards the market that the rest of the play examines. The audience reads the stranger’s body before it hears his voice, and the heron image sets the outsider as a figure who watches before he acts. That patience is the quality that makes his method so powerful and so easy to commodify.

Taken together, the extract shows the central ideas in miniature. Identity is divided and named by others, a machine and a stranger arrive together, and the community absorbs the newcomer into its own language. The distinctive qualities of the text, its narrating voice, its layered languages and its physical stagecraft, make these ideas felt before they are argued. In the prescribed text the first act follows Albert on the Lutheran mission at Hermannsburg, and the second follows his fame and his jailing for supplying liquor. The audience hears the rupture first, and the wider play’s movement towards the market and towards remembrance grows out of these opening moments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it names the central ideas and shows how a few lines of the extract introduce them, with close reference to the opening speech, the car and the repeated greeting. It links these moments to the play’s wider movement from mission to market. To lift it, trace the greeting’s languages into one named moment of the prescribed text so the two sets of references are argued together.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Namatjira explores its central ideas of identity, naming and the value placed on art through the play’s distinctive qualities. The extract shows this clearly. The narrator says Albert is “between two worlds”, and the speaker goes on to say “Name changed.”, which suggests that his identity was something other people controlled. The list of his languages and roles follows, showing that he has several identities at the same time.

The extract also introduces the arrival of the car. A Model T Ford arrives at the mission, and the stranger who steps out of it moves like a heron. The men at the mission gather and whisper, and they repeat the greeting in different languages. This shows how the mission community responds to outsiders, and it links the car to the idea of naming. The line “Old Heron Man has come” is important because it shows the mission men giving a name to the stranger.

The extract gives the audience a sense of Albert’s family as well. “Growing family, poor, no house, nothing” places him in a household with very little, so the question of what his painting is worth is raised early, before the painting is shown. The play then turns to the wider text, where the first act follows his life at the mission and the second follows his fame and his jailing.

The extract therefore helps the audience understand the rest of the play. The central ideas of identity and art are introduced here, and the rest of the play develops them through Albert’s painting and his later life. The distinctive use of language and the way the stage is set up show that the play is interested in how different cultures meet. The extract introduces the central ideas of the play in a few short lines.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The extract from the rehearsal in the wood shows how A Midsummer Night’s Dream explores its central ideas through its distinctive qualities. The central ideas are imagination, the unreliability of perception and the power of performance, and the extract explores each through a deliberate act of metatheatre. A play within the play, comic blunders in verse and an onlooker who speaks from outside the scene combine to make the audience question what it sees, and in doing so they reveal the concerns of the prescribed text as a whole.

Puck’s opening lines set the terms of the extract. He mocks the mechanicals as ‘hempen homespuns’ who have wandered near ‘the cradle of the Fairy Queen’. The phrase is comic, but it places the rehearsal in fairy space and establishes that the wood belongs to forces the craftsmen do not understand. Puck is condescending, yet his contempt also acknowledges that the mechanicals have entered a world where they are out of place. That sense of misplacement is one the whole play dramatises, from the lovers to the court.

Puck then announces his double role: ‘I’ll be an auditor’, he says, and then, ‘an actor too perhaps’, if he sees cause. He places himself as audience and performer at once, which is the position the theatre audience occupies. He is an onlooker who may step on to the stage, and in the play he does exactly that. He transforms Bottom and manipulates the lovers, so the audience sees its own role in Puck’s double position, watching and acting on what it watches.

The language of the extract makes the same point about perception. Bottom’s ‘Thisbe, the flowers of odious savours sweet’ is a malapropism, and Quince has to correct him: ‘odorous’. The error is small, but it matches the play’s larger pattern. The lovers mistake their own feelings, Titania mistakes Bottom for a beloved, and Puck mistakes Lysander for Demetrius. In a play where words and sights can be wrong, a man who cannot find the right word for a smell is a comic version of the lovers’ confusion.

Bottom’s line, ‘So hath thy breath, my dearest Thisbe dear’, shows the same mechanism at work in the verse. It has the sound of tragic romance, but its words are conventional rather than felt. The audience hears love reduced to formula, and yet Bottom takes the formula seriously and performs it with conviction. That gap between form and feeling is one of the play’s interests, and the lovers, too, speak in the language of romance while their emotions shift around them.

Puck’s judgement, ‘A stranger Pyramus than e’er played here’, closes the extract by turning the performance back on its audience. The line is both an insult and a verdict, and it places the theatre audience in Puck’s position: people who have watched a poor performance and are invited to decide what it means. The play’s form makes this possible. The mechanicals will perform for the court in the final act, and the theatre audience watches both the performers and the court watching them, so the joke is always about looking as much as acting.

Beyond the extract, the same idea runs through the prescribed text. Theseus argues that ‘the best in this kind are but shadows’, and Puck’s epilogue calls the players shadows too, asking the audience to forgive ‘if we shadows have offended’. The central idea is that imagination supplies what performance lacks. The rehearsal shows this in miniature, since the mechanicals plan to present a wall and a moonshine, and the play trusts the audience to see them.

The extract therefore shows Shakespeare at his most self-aware. Its central ideas, that perception can be deceived, that performance depends on its audience, and that imagination gives ‘airy nothing’ a local habitation, are explored through distinctive qualities of the text: the play within the play, verse that breaks down into error, and an intruding fairy who watches and acts. The prescribed text’s argument is that the audience must judge what it has seen, and the extract is one of the clearest demonstrations of that demand.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it reads the extract closely, tying Puck’s double role and Bottom’s malapropism to the central ideas of imagination and perception, and it moves from the extract to the prescribed text with control. The analysis of the distinctive qualities is precise throughout. To lift it, develop the analysis of the verse in Bottom’s Pyramus line, which is the least developed of the extract’s qualities.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The extract is a rehearsal in the wood, and Puck watches it and comments on it. The mechanicals are rehearsing a play called Pyramus and Thisbe, and Bottom gets a word wrong, saying odious when he means odorous. Quince corrects him. Puck says he might be an audience and perhaps an actor too, and then he says that Pyramus is stranger than any before. Puck’s words also show that he decides when a performance is worth watching, which gives him power over the mechanicals before he acts. This shows that the play is funny and that it is interested in performance. The extract is short, but it contains a lot of the play’s comedy.

The central ideas of the play include imagination and the way people see things. Puck is the fairy who carries out Oberon’s plans for the lovers, so when he watches the mechanicals he is like a member of the audience who could change what happens next. The mechanicals are silly, but their mistakes are similar to the lovers’ mistakes, so the scene links to the main plot. Shakespeare uses a play within a play, which makes the audience think about the difference between acting and watching. The audience sees the mechanicals making mistakes, and it knows that the lovers are making similar ones.

The extract also uses language for comedy. Bottom’s verse is broken by his errors, and this shows he does not understand what he is saying. Quince has to correct him, which shows that the mechanicals depend on each other. The mix-up of words also matters, because the lovers mistake who they love in much the same way. The prescribed text as a whole is about dreams, magic and confusion, and this scene is an example of those ideas. The rehearsal in the wood is also where Bottom is turned into an ass, so the extract leads straight into that. Overall the extract is an interesting part of the play and it shows several important ideas about performance and imagination.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it identifies the play within the play and Puck’s role as onlooker, which is a sound starting point. The reading explains what happens in the extract rather than analysing how the effect is created, and it relies on few quotations. To lift it, quote Puck’s ‘I’ll be an auditor’ and show exactly what it does to the audience’s position.

sampleAnswers.answer: The extract is a scene where some people are doing a play in the wood. Bottom plays Pyramus and gets a word wrong, and Quince tells him the right word. Puck watches them from behind and says he might be in the play too. At the end Puck says that Pyramus is stranger than anyone who has played it before. It is a play within a play, and the extract is a clear example of that. The prescribed text is about lovers and fairies, and this part of it shows how the play is put together. The people in the scene are not very good at acting, so the audience laughs at them. Shakespeare uses the mechanicals to make the audience laugh, and he uses Puck to watch them. The extract is short, but it shows the play’s humour and its interest in plays.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the rehearsal and notes that the play is a play within a play, but it does not analyse how the extract conveys ideas. Its strength is that it recognises Bottom’s error and Puck’s comment as moments of comedy. To lift it, explain one device precisely, such as Puck’s double role, and say what it makes the audience think about imagination.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The extract shows Stasiland at its most reflective. In a few sentences Funder moves from an interviewee's claim about childhood to her own argument about why people joined the Stasi, and then to a question about how the past is handled once the regime has gone. The central ideas explored here are the moral choices people make inside a divided society, the self-justification that follows those choices, and the difficulty of reckoning with them afterwards. Funder explores these ideas through the distinctive qualities of nonfiction: a narrator who questions the person she interviews, a rhetorical method that turns reported speech into argument, and an image that carries the book's concern with how the past is made to look.

The passage opens with the interviewee telling Funder that she cannot see why anyone would join the Stasi without understanding his childhood. The claim is also a complaint about Funder's understanding, and it makes sympathy the condition of comprehension. Funder rejects it in a single sentence: “This isn’t quite true.” The brevity is deliberate. It refuses the idea that understanding a perpetrator requires personal sympathy with him, and it insists that the reasons are open to argument. This self-correction is a distinctive quality of the form, because nonfiction allows the author to stage a disagreement with her subject in front of the reader, so the interview becomes a contest over meaning rather than a simple record.

Funder then argues the question herself, and her reasoning is the centre of the passage. She has thought about motive, and she describes a divided society in which an ambitious young person might want to be one of “the group in the know”. The phrase “riven into ‘us’ and ‘them’” places the decision inside a social structure rather than in individual psychology. Her rhetorical question, asking why a person would not choose “a peaceful life and a satisfying career” when there was no way out, makes the reader consider how a choice can be reasonable within constraints and still carry a moral cost. This is the book's central move on complicity: it is produced by ordinary desires for safety and advancement, not only by cruelty.

The final sentences move from motive to aftermath. Funder says that what interests her is “the process of dealing with that decision”, which states the book's subject directly. The pearl metaphor extends that concern. She asks whether a person can take “the grit that rubs in you” and make it “shiny and smooth as a pearl”. A pearl forms around an irritant, so the image holds both the wound and the beauty that conceals it. The question is therefore whether reworking the past is honest, or whether it is a polish that hides what it covers. The image does this without a lecture, which is one of the distinctive qualities of Funder's prose: a single figure carries an argument about memory.

Stasiland gives the passage its wider context, and the prescribed text tests the extract's question. Julia's career is blocked, and a Stasi major pressures her to inform on her former boyfriend. She refuses, and it is only after she threatens to write to Honecker that he finds her work, so her choice has a cost but also a result. Frau Paul makes a sharper choice, refusing to trap Hinze even when offered a reunion with her son. Both women face real constraints and both choose at a price, which tests the extract's suggestion that the easier path is the natural one. By contrast, Herr Winz, a former agent who monitored thousands, still believes communism was the only just system. His rationalisation shows that the past has not been reworked into anything the book would call honest, and it is the reader who must weigh the polish against the grit.

The passage's question is not answered in the passage, and the book as a whole does not settle it either. Funder shows ordinary people making constrained choices, then shows their afterlives, and leaves the reader to judge how much of the past has been polished and how much remains grit. The first-person narrator, who argues with a source in print and then leaves the argument open, makes the passage a model of the book's method. In that sense the extract is not an aside. It states, in miniature, the question Stasiland asks about how a divided society remembers the choices that divided it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how the extract's ideas of choice, complicity and aftermath are developed through the narrator's rebuttal, the rhetorical question and the pearl image, and it connects these to Julia, Frau Paul and Herr Winz. The quotations are short and precise. The move that would lift it further is to test the pearl image more closely against one specific episode in the prescribed text, rather than asserting the connection.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In this extract Funder responds to a man who says that she cannot understand why people joined the Stasi unless she knows his childhood. She says this is not quite true, and she gives her own explanation. She describes a society divided into us and them, where an ambitious young person might want to be part of the group that knows what is happening and is not persecuted. She then asks why someone would not choose a peaceful life and a satisfying career when there was no way to leave the country.

These ideas are central to Stasiland. The book is about people who were in the Stasi and people who were not, and Funder interviews both groups about the choices they made. Many of the people she meets had to choose under pressure, and Funder records their choices without simple judgement. The passage shows her thinking about motive, and it links to the rest of the book in a clear way.

The last part of the extract asks about dealing with the past now that it is over. Funder uses an image of grit that becomes a pearl. A pearl grows around something bad, so this shows how people might make their past look nice. Funder's question is whether they should do this, and it is an interesting idea. The pearl is a strong image because it is something beautiful that has grown from pain, which is exactly the process Funder is asking about.

In the rest of the book, Julia is an example of someone whose career was damaged by the Stasi. She refused to inform on her boyfriend. Frau Paul also refused to help the Stasi, even though they offered her time with her son. These women show that choices were difficult. The book also has former agents who still defend the old system, which shows that the past is not always dealt with honestly.

So the extract connects to the book's main ideas about choice and memory. The narrator is a personal voice, and this helps the reader understand the interviews. Funder uses the first person and asks questions, which is a feature of nonfiction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the extract's ideas accurately, but its treatment of the pearl metaphor is brief and its links to the prescribed text are general. Its strength is the clear point that Funder's question is about choice under constraint. To move up, it needs to analyse one device closely, such as the rhetorical question, and use one specific episode from Stasiland to test the extract's claim.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this extract, a man tells Funder that she cannot understand why anyone would join the Stasi unless she knows about his childhood. She says that isn't quite true. She thinks people joined because the country was split into us and them, and because a person who wanted a peaceful life might choose the safe group. Then she talks about the process of dealing with the decision now that it is all over. She uses a pearl as a picture of this, and asks whether a person can make the grit in them into something shiny. This connects to Stasiland because the book is about the Stasi and about people who lived with it, and about how they deal with the past now. Funder writes well and the extract is interesting to read. The narrator is in the passage, asking questions, so the reader can see her thinking as well as the interviewee's words.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the extract in its own words, with minimal reference to the prescribed text and little analysis of Funder's techniques. Its strength is an accurate sense that the passage concerns the Stasi and the past. The lift would come from quoting one phrase, naming the device it uses, such as the metaphor of grit becoming a pearl, and explaining what that device shows.

prompts.scenario: Extract: ‘Just a moment,’ he says. ‘It is hard for you to understand. Without understanding my childhood, you can’t see why anyone would want to join the Stasi.’ This isn’t quite true. I have given a lot of thought to why people would want to join. In a society riven into ‘us’ and ‘them’, an ambitious young person might well want to be one of the group in the know, one of the unmolested. If there was never going to be an end to your country, and you could never leave, why wouldn’t you opt for a peaceful life and a satisfying career? What interests me is the process of dealing with that decision now that it is all over. Can you rework your past, the grit that rubs in you, until it is shiny and smooth as a pearl? prompts.question: Analyse how the central ideas of Frank Hurley: The Man Who Made History are explored through the distinctive qualities of the text. In your response, make detailed reference to the extracts below and your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The stem asks for central ideas explored through distinctive qualities, so each paragraph should name a quality, such as the juxtaposition of stills or the voice-over, and say what idea it carries.
The extracts are the stimulus for detailed reference. Strong answers move between the composite, the second still and the two captions rather than paraphrasing the captions in order.
The central idea is contested, not settled. The best answers show the film keeping drama and documentary truth in tension, and say which way the viewer is pushed.
Use the prescribed text beyond the extracts: the blizzard overlay and the interviews with Burton and Affleck show how the film argues, and that is what lifts an answer to the top.
commonStudentErrors: Paraphrasing the two captions in sequence without analysing how the voice-over frames the composite.
Treating the composite as simply fake, without explaining Hurley’s argument that a war could not be caught in one negative.
Describing the plate of biplanes as a second composite, without comparing its effect with the first extract.
Naming the curator in the extract as a specific person without a source, when the question does not name them.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The central ideas of Frank Hurley: The Man Who Made History are the tension between drama and documentary truth, and the question of who gets to decide what a photograph of war is worth. The film explores both through its distinctive qualities: archival stills and film, voice-over that frames each image, interviews with curators and other experts, and the extracts below, which set a composite photograph beside a plate of biplanes over a landscape.

The first extract shows the composite, soldiers in trenches beneath biplanes, and its voice-over sets up the film’s central dilemma. The voice-over presents Hurley’s response as creative: he used his “darkroom skills” to combine photos in a single dramatic picture. The next sentence begins with “But”, and this time his manipulations “would lead to bitter conflict”. The structure is simple, but it matters. The film does not present the composite as either an achievement or a fraud in isolation; it places the image inside a sequence of cause and consequence, so the viewer reads the picture as the start of an argument. Each caption is a line of voice-over, so the audience hears the case before it looks closely at the image, and that order shapes how the image is judged.

The second extract, a plate of biplanes over a landscape, sits beside the composite and invites comparison. Its caption says that others are not so impressed, and the curator’s view that the manipulations have “undermined their historic value” turns the argument from one photographer’s method into a question about the archive. Here the film’s distinctive qualities of juxtaposition and authority do the work: the viewer sees two images and a judgement on them, and is asked to decide which claim to trust.

Beyond the extracts, the film develops the idea that drama and documentary truth pull against each other. Australian Screen notes say that Hurley combined elements from different photographs, planes, exploding bombs, trenches and soldiers “going over the top”, and that there was no question of his “orchestrating or manipulating actual events”. The composite is therefore a claim about what war looked like, not a record of one moment, and the film asks whether an image of that kind can still count as history. Hurley argued that a war on such a vast scale could not be caught in one negative, and the film gives that case a hearing alongside Bean’s.

The film supports this idea with method as well as argument. Stephen Burton of the Australian War Memorial shows how Hurley’s colour plates were aligned by hand, using a transparency and a viewing screen, until the colour appeared. Such a demonstration does not settle whether the composite is true, but it makes clear how much of Hurley’s image-making was manual and deliberate, which is the point the extracts press on the viewer.

The prescribed text’s distinctive qualities also shape the meaning. Archival footage from the Mawson expedition is silent when shot, yet the film overlays it with the sound of a blizzard, so a sensory claim is added to material that never had one. Hurley’s own words are read by an actor, and two Australian War Memorial interviewees show the method and Hurley’s dilemma. The film’s techniques are not neutral: they make the composite seem both a bold response to war and a distortion of it, and the viewer has to hold both ideas together.

The central idea, then, is that a photograph of war can be both dramatic and historically valuable, and the film refuses to say which quality should win. The extracts show the case in miniature: a dramatic composite, a second image for comparison, and a curator’s judgement that its historic value has been undermined. Read together, the two captions move from method to consequence and then to judgement, and the extracts follow the same path. The prescribed text makes that judgement the audience’s own, which is the film’s most distinctive quality as a documentary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it treats the central ideas as a tension between drama and documentary truth, works through both extracts in sequence, and ties each technique to a specific effect on the viewer. The strongest move is the cause-and-consequence reading of the voice-over captions. To lift it, the closing paragraph could weigh the film’s sound overlay against the curator’s judgement rather than summarising both.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Frank Hurley: The Man Who Made History explores the central ideas of drama and truth through its distinctive qualities. The film uses stills, film and voice-over, and the extracts show a composite photograph of soldiers and aircraft next to another photograph of biplanes over a landscape. The voice-over says Hurley used his darkroom skills to combine photos, and it says this led to conflict.

The first extract’s voice-over explains that Hurley combined photos into a dramatic picture, and then says his manipulations caused trouble. This shows that the composite was controversial. The voice-over is important because it tells the viewer how to read the composite before the viewer forms a view. The second extract has a caption saying others are not impressed, and the curator says the manipulations have damaged the historic value of the photographs. These captions make the reader think about whether the photographs are true or not.

The film also includes interviews with experts from the Australian War Memorial, who explain the method. Charles Bean, the official historian, said that the composites were fakes. Hurley thought that war could not be shown in one photograph, so he made composites. The film shows his reasons, and these are its central ideas, which makes the film a study of whether drama can be history.

The film is a documentary that uses archival footage with an added blizzard sound. This is one of its distinctive qualities because the sound makes the footage more dramatic. The film also uses an actor to read Hurley’s words, which means the audience hears his voice as well as seeing the pictures. Together these techniques make the audience feel close to Hurley and to the war, and the audience also learns about the controversy around the photographs.

The film’s techniques help it make an argument as well as a record. The sound added to the Antarctic footage makes the earlier material feel dramatic, and Burton’s demonstration shows that the colour in Hurley’s pictures depended on manual alignment. These choices let the viewer see both the work and the argument about it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the extracts and the film’s techniques, but it tends to paraphrase the captions and to state the central ideas rather than analyse them. To lift it, quote the first caption directly, then test how the composite and the plate work together as evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Frank Hurley: The Man Who Made History is a film about a photographer. In the extracts there is a photo of soldiers in trenches with planes overhead, and another photo of planes over a landscape. The first caption says Hurley used his darkroom skills to combine photos. The second caption says others are not impressed. The curator says the manipulations have undermined the value of the photos. This is about whether the photos are real or fake. The film has interviews and voice-over and shows Hurley’s life. The film also uses an actor to read his words, so the audience hears his voice as well as seeing the pictures. The composite is a big idea in the film, and it shows that Hurley was controversial, which is the main thing the question asks about.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the extracts and the film, with minimal reference to the prescribed text and no analysis of how the central ideas are explored. To lift it, choose one technique, such as the voice-over caption, and explain what it makes the viewer believe about Hurley’s photographs.

prompts.scenario: Stimulus: Two film stills (a composite photograph of soldiers in trenches with biplanes overhead, and a photographic plate of biplanes over a landscape), each captioned with a line of the voice-over. The captions read: VOICE OVER: Hurley’s response was to use his darkroom skills to combine photos in a single dramatic picture. But this time his manipulations would lead to bitter conflict. VOICE OVER: But others aren’t so impressed. The curator of Australia’s war time photo archives believes Hurley’s manipulations have undermined their historic value.
