I used to lie in that shade and think about how he had planted it for a future he would never see. At first it seemed a sad thing to do, planting something for people you will never meet.

He died the winter I turned fifteen, and I did not expect the tree to matter so much after that. In spring its leaves came back, and I found myself watering it on the mornings I could not sleep, as if the can were a way of talking to him.

Now I am the one who kneels in the grass. Some mornings I look up at the shadow and imagine a child reaching for the red fruit long after I am gone, and I understand what he meant. The passage of time is not something you can watch happen. You can only keep showing up with the can, and trust that the shade will one day be there for someone else.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the competent descriptor: it explores patience and the passage of time through a clear narrative anchored in the stimulus image. It leans on familiar phrasing and a closing moral the piece tells rather than shows, and the movement between sections is uneven. Tightening the final section and replacing stock phrases would move it toward the effective descriptor.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mum said to water the plant, so Jess went outside after breakfast. It was a small green thing in a pot near the fence. She poured the water on it and some of it went everywhere. Then she went to school and did maths and forgot about it. When she came back it was still small. She supposed it might get bigger one day. The tree at the end of the street was big. Maybe this one would be too, but Jess was not sure and did not really mind. It was a plant, and that was all she could think to say about it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 4-6 descriptor: it attempts to engage with the stimulus through the seedling and the watering, but the narrative is brief, the idea is not developed, and the shadow and the future figure are absent. Developing one idea, such as patience, through a sustained image would move it toward the sound descriptor.

prompts.scenario: Stimulus: a minimal illustration by Sergio Dulce, drawn in black line and flat grey with a single accent of red. In the foreground a small figure bends to water a tiny seedling with a watering can. Cast up the hillside from the seedling and the figure is a pale grey shadow: the shadow of a large tree in full leaf, and within it the shadow of a woman reaching up to pick red fruit, with a basket of red fruit at her side. Only the fruit is coloured. Ideas the image may suggest include patience, the passage of time, care for beginnings, imagining a future, and the reward of long effort. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks in all; part (a) is worth 15). Allow about 40 minutes for the whole question.

prompts.question: Using the stimulus above, craft an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that captures the richness of a fond memory.
markerNotes: The stimulus idea should shape the first lines, and the strongest pieces open inside the sensation rather than describing it from a distance.
Sensory detail works best when one or two images carry the emotion, not when every sense is listed in turn.
A clear form, such as a return to the memory at the end, gives the piece control and a sense of an ending that the reader feels.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the five senses in turn, so the imagery is catalogued rather than felt.
Writing about a memory in general terms (a holiday, a family dinner) without one specific object or moment to hold it.
Ending with a summary sentence that explains the feeling the piece has already shown.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Composes a highly engaging imaginative or discursive piece of writing that effectively uses the stimulus; Crafts language skilfully to capture the richness of a fond memory; Demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
13-16 marks: Composes an engaging imaginative or discursive piece of writing that effectively uses the stimulus; Crafts language effectively to capture the richness of a fond memory; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
9-12 marks: Composes an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that uses the stimulus; Uses language competently to capture the richness of a fond memory; Demonstrates sound control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
5-8 marks: Composes a piece of writing that attempts to respond to the stimulus; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure
1-4 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing with some relevance to the question

sampleAnswers.answer:
A fond memory brings you a wave of comfort and ignites the senses, and mine always arrives through the screen door of my grandmother's kitchen. I can still hear it: a thin metallic complaint, a spring stretched too tight, then the soft slap of the frame settling against its catch. Everything inside that house ran a little slower than the world outside, as though the clocks had agreed among themselves to keep a gentler time.

The room smelt of lemon peel and scorched sugar. A tin of shortbread sat on the bench beside a cutting board stained the colour of weak tea, and my grandmother stood at the sink with her sleeves pushed past her elbows. Her forearms were freckled and strong. She moved with the unhurried certainty of someone who had never once needed to check a recipe. Water ran over her hands, and the tap made a low, thick sound, like a note held too long, while the refrigerator hummed its own tuneless song beneath it.

I was nine, and I had been given the job of stirring. The wooden spoon was worn pale where other hands had gripped it for decades. At first the mixture resisted, then it loosened into something glossy, and I felt the grit of sugar between my fingers as I worked. The light came through the lace curtain and lay in squares across the floor. I remember that the squares were warm. I remember wanting nothing more than to stay exactly where I was.

My grandmother hummed as she worked, always the same three notes, and she never finished the tune. I used to believe she had forgotten the rest. Years later I understood that she stopped at the part she loved best and left the ending for whoever was listening. She was like that with stories, too. She would begin one about the drought year or the cousin who rode a borrowed horse into the creek, then glance at the window as if the rest had wandered off without her.

Nothing dramatic happened that afternoon. We ate the shortbread while it was still too hot to hold, crumbs catching at our lips, and she told me to wipe my face on the tea towel with the faded rooster on it. A fly circled the fruit bowl. Somewhere down the street a dog barked twice and then forgot why. These small things return to me most vividly, and I have come to think memory keeps them because they hold the whole afternoon, the way a single mouthful of something sweet can carry an entire summer.

I have tried to explain to friends why this memory matters more than the birthdays that are better documented. The honest answer is that I can enter it. I can walk through the screen door in my mind, feel the step that always gave a little under my sandal, and find every object exactly where it was. I can smell the lemon and the scorched sugar before I reach the bench. A fond memory is not a photograph. It is a room, and it stays open for as long as I keep returning to it.

The house has changed. The screen door has been replaced with a heavier one that closes without a sound, and the lemon tree by the side fence came down in a storm. Yet when I stand in the doorway the old kitchen is still there, folded inside the new one like a letter inside its envelope. I bake nothing and stir nothing. I simply breathe in, and for a moment the clocks agree to run slowly again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This piece meets the top row of the craft criteria: it opens on the stimulus idea, builds a single sensory world, and uses concrete objects (the spoon, the lace curtain, the tea towel) to carry the emotion. The structure is controlled, with a return to the present that gives the memory a clear shape. To lift it further, the middle section could take one more risk in voice, so that the reader hears the writer's own rhythm rather than a steady, even pace.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A fond memory brings you a wave of comfort and ignites the senses, and mine begins with the smell of lemon peel. I am nine again, standing at my grandmother's bench with a wooden spoon in my hand. The spoon is worn pale where other hands have held it for years. Sugar grits between my fingers, and the mixture thickens slowly into something glossy.

My grandmother stands at the sink with her sleeves pushed past her elbows. She hums three notes over and over and never finishes the tune. Water runs over her hands, and the tap makes a low sound like a note held too long. The light comes through the lace curtain and lies in warm squares across the floor. I remember wanting nothing more than to stay exactly where I was.

Later we eat the shortbread while it is still too hot to hold. Crumbs catch at our lips. She tells me to wipe my face on the tea towel with the faded rooster on it. Somewhere outside a dog barks twice and then goes quiet.

I have tried to explain to friends why this memory matters more than the birthdays I can barely recall. The answer is that I can walk back into it. I can feel the step that always gave a little under my sandal and find every object where it was. A fond memory is a room, and it stays open for as long as I keep returning to it.

The house has changed since then. The old screen door has been replaced, and the lemon tree is gone. Still, when I stand in the doorway, the kitchen is there inside the new one. I do not bake or stir. I simply breathe in, and for a moment the afternoon is mine again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This piece sits in the middle row: it engages with the stimulus and uses language competently to recall the kitchen, but the sensory images are mostly described rather than developed. The structure is sound, with a clear opening and a return at the end. To lift it, choose fewer images and let each one do more work, and let the closing lines turn the memory into something the writer now understands.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some memories arrive without asking. The screen door sighs and I am nine again, standing in my grandmother's kitchen. Lemon peel and scorched sugar hang in the air. She hums three notes and never finishes the tune, and the light falls through the lace in warm squares. I stir the mixture until it turns glossy. Later we eat shortbread too hot to hold, and she tells me to wipe my face. Nothing important happens that afternoon, and that is the good part. I want to stay there. I still can, when the house is quiet enough to let me back in.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This piece attempts the task and draws on the stimulus, but the imagery is brief and the form is not yet fully controlled. The ending simply restates a wish to return rather than showing what the memory means now. To lift it, develop one sensory moment at length and give the closing lines a clear turn.

prompts.scenario: Stimulus: ‘A fond memory brings you a wave of comfort and ignites the senses. It’s the kind of memory you can visualise and describe in rich detail.’ (This article was originally published as ‘How to live like an Epicurean’ on Psyche.) Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

prompts.question: Create a piece of imaginative, discursive or persuasive writing that ENDS with the provided image.
markerNotes: The strongest pieces commit to one controlling idea and let the stimulus carry it, so the laneway becomes a statement about what a city keeps rather than a list of what is painted on its walls.
The ending has to return to the image without a moral. The final paragraph should work through the painted face, the murals on both walls, the grey lane, the white centre line and the pink splashes.
Control shows in repetition and in sentence length chosen on purpose; a run of and-clauses reads as drafting rather than craft.
Colour matters in this stimulus. The pink splashes against the grey pavement should do a job in the story, not just be named.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the laneway from one end to the other with no story, so the piece reads as a caption for the photograph.
Ending on a general point about art or the city rather than on the image itself.
Ignoring the white centre line and the pink splashes, which are the details that make this stimulus specific.
Keeping one flat tone and pace from start to finish, so there is no visible control of language or structure.
prompts.markingCriteria:
10-12 marks: Effectively composes a piece of writing that concludes with the stimulus; Effectively crafts a range of language devices or stylistic features to create an engaging piece of writing; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
7-9 marks: Competently composes a piece of writing that concludes with the stimulus; Competently crafts a range of language devices or stylistic features to create an engaging piece of writing; Demonstrates competent control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
4-6 marks: Composes a piece of writing that concludes with the stimulus; Uses some language devices or stylistic features to create a piece of writing; Demonstrates some control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
1-3 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing that has some relevance to the question; Demonstrates limited control of language

sampleAnswers.answer:
The council crew never comes in daylight. They arrive before the bakeries open, two men in hi-vis and a van that smells of thinners, and by the time I reach the laneway the first roller is already dripping grey. I stand by the bins with my coffee going cold and watch the wall I know best disappear. Nobody asked me to watch. I came anyway, the way you go back to a room after the furniture has gone.

Two summers ago my brother Tom and I borrowed a ladder from the hardware yard behind the station and climbed the left-hand wall after midnight. We were painting our grandmother. Nan had taught me to hold a brush the way she held a pen, and that is how I drew her eyes: half closed, as though she were still deciding whether to forgive us. Tom knocked a tin of pink off the top rung. It burst across the pavement in a fan of splashes, and we left them there. They were the only part of that night that nobody planned.

By nine the roller has reached the right-hand wall. The murals there go under one at a time: a blue bird with a broken wing, a row of raised hands, a city skyline that somebody spent a month on. The grey climbs over them like a tide over sand, slow at the edges and then all at once. I count the seconds between strokes because counting is easier than watching. Twelve. Eleven. The roller hums, soft and almost kind, and that is the part I cannot forgive.

Street art is never the last word on a wall. The council will be back next winter, and the winter after that, and every surface in this city has been scraped and written on again. The laneway is simply more honest about it. It does not pretend to be finished.

By ten both walls are grey, all except her. The older man stops in front of the face and looks up for a long moment. Then he wipes his brush on a rag and walks back to the van without touching her. She looks as if she has been left standing in the rain.

By six the artists have come, as they always do. A girl with a bucket of silver paint and a boy with a box of stencils arrive together. Nobody asks permission. The bird returns in blue and then in a brighter blue, the hands gather around it, and the skyline climbs out of the grey one building at a time.

Tonight the lane looks the way it always does. A painted face watches from the left-hand wall, eyes half closed, still deciding. Murals cover both walls, layered so thickly that no single colour wins. Near the bins the pink splashes have faded to a blush on the pavement, but they have outlasted two summers of rain and three rounds of paint. Down the middle of the grey pavement, a white centre line runs straight past the bins towards the street, unbroken.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 10-12 row: it has a controlling idea (a lane that renews itself while one accident survives every repaint), a structure that runs from dawn to night and returns to the stimulus, and controlled imagery such as the grey climbing over the murals like a tide over sand. The move that would lift it further is to cut the fourth paragraph, which states the idea that the images already carry, so the final image does all the work.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The council trucks come early on Saturdays. I hear them from my bed before I see them, the engine and then the beeping as the van reverses into the lane. My name is Nell and I have been coming to this lane since I was small, so I know what is going to happen. They are going to paint over the murals. I go down anyway with a coffee in my hand and stand by the bins to watch.

I feel angry and sad at the same time. Two years ago my brother Tom and I painted our nan on the left wall. It was a big face and it took us all night. Tom knocked over a tin of pink paint and it splashed on the ground, which made Mum cross, but I think it looks nice now. I wanted the lane to stay the same forever.

The men start with the right wall. The bird that Tom liked goes first, then the hands, then the skyline. The roller goes up and down and the grey covers everything. It is quite quick. I did not expect it to be so quick, which made me upset.

By lunchtime the artists come back and paint new pictures, so I know the lane will change again. I suppose this is how it works. Nan’s face is still there, looking down the lane with her eyes half shut. The walls are full of colour again and the white line is still in the middle of the grey pavement, where it has always been. The pink splashes are still there too.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 7-9 row: it is a competent narrative with a clear setting that returns to the lane at the end, but the narrator tells feelings directly (I feel angry and sad) and some sentences flatten into plain statements such as it is quite quick. The move that would lift it is to replace one piece of telling with a concrete image, such as the grey reaching the bird’s broken wing.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I went to the lane this morning to look at the painting. There is a big face on one wall and there are murals on both sides. The ground is grey and there is a white line down the middle. Some pink paint is on the ground too, from when somebody spilt it. I like the street art because it makes the city look more interesting.

It is a good place to think about things. The lane is narrow, so it feels a bit like a tunnel, and the face looks sad to me. I think the artists want people to come and look at their work. The white line goes all the way down the lane, so I walked along it to the end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 1-3 row: it attempts the task and names several details from the stimulus, but it is a list of observations with no story, no controlling idea and little control of language. The move that would lift it is to give the narrator a problem in the lane and let the final sentence return to the image.

prompts.scenario: Stimulus: Colour photograph of a narrow city laneway covered in street art: a large painted face on the left, murals on both walls and a grey paved lane with a white centre line and pink paint splashes (photograph by Brittany Kulick). Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks in all; this part is worth 12). Allow about 40 minutes for the whole question.

prompts.question: Compose a piece of imaginative writing that is set in a significant place. Begin with the words: ‘This is my world now, and it can be yours too, if you like. A place can soak through your skin like sweat, and ooze into your heart and soul. Breathe it in, and let me tell you a story.’
markerNotes: The strongest pieces treat the given opening as a voice to continue. The second person and the invitation to a story should carry into the first line, not be copied out.
A significant place works when the setting does a job in the plot: the pan's colour rules, its dangers and its loss shape what the narrator does and what she learns.
Control of structure shows in movement: an instruction, a turn, a return, and an ending that stays with the image rather than explaining what the place means.
A limited piece usually describes a place without changing it. The move from setting to story is what separates the top bands from the bottom.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a general description of a beach, forest or city that could begin anywhere, so the place is named but never felt.
Abandoning the extract's voice and starting with a new narrator and tone, so the piece does not continue the extract.
Ending on a lesson about why places matter, rather than letting the story carry the meaning.
Summarising years of events in a few sentences, so the reader never stands in the place with the narrator.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Composes an engaging piece of imaginative writing that creates a significant sense of place and continues the extract effectively; Crafts language effectively to compose an imaginative piece of writing; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and form
13-16 marks: Composes a developed piece of imaginative writing that creates a clear sense of place and continues the extract competently; Crafts language competently to compose an imaginative piece of writing; Demonstrates competent control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and form
9-12 marks: Composes a sound piece of imaginative writing that creates some sense of place and has some continuity with the extract; Uses language adequately to compose an imaginative piece of writing; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and form
5-8 marks: Composes a limited piece of imaginative writing that uses setting and attempts to continue the extract; Uses language variably to compose a piece of imaginative writing; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure
1-4 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing with some relevance to the question; Demonstrates minimal control of language

sampleAnswers.answer:
The pan lies two hours past the last fence post, a white floor so flat that a car can come towards you across it for most of an hour before it seems to move. Nothing grows out there. The wind has nothing to hold on to, so it pushes the heat straight into your face and leaves salt in the creases of your skin. The pan is the most significant place I have known, and I have spent half my life trying to decide whether that is a compliment.

My father raked salt on that pan for twenty-six years. He taught me to read the water before I could read a book. Clear meant the brine was still too thin. Pink meant it was ready. A dark patch, almost black in the middle of the white, meant the ground was wet underneath, and wet salt would take a leg to the knee before you knew it had changed its mind. Walk on the ridges, he said. Walk where the crust sings.

The rake was taller than I was. He gave it to me on my seventh birthday without ceremony, the way other fathers hand over a bicycle, and showed me how to drag the salt into low white rows that caught the sun. My arms burned by eleven. He did not stop for me. He raked a long straight line, leaned on the handle at the end of it, and looked back at the marks we had made. Nobody else would ever see those lines, and I thought that was the point of them.

I was nine the summer the rain came. It fell for eleven days on a country that had forgotten what rain was, and by the second week the pan had turned from white to a sheet of brown water the colour of weak tea. The company sent a letter. My father read it at the kitchen table with his hands flat on either side of the page, and he did not say a word for the rest of the night.

In town the mothers at the bakery said the company had been cruel, and the men at the pub said my father should have fought it. He did not fight. For six weeks after the letter, when there was nothing left to rake, he drove out to the pan every morning and stood at the edge with his boots in the mud. I followed him once. He did not see me, and I did not go any closer.

In March we drove out of town with everything we owned tied to the roof. I watched the pumphouse shrink in the back window until it was a single white mark, like a full stop at the end of a sentence I had not finished reading. Years later I came back on a Tuesday in autumn, alone. Nobody else wanted to see it. The water had gone and left a crust so bright I had to squint through my fingers. The pumphouse stood with its door open like a gate with no fence around it, and a tin sign on the shed had rusted to the colour of old blood. The wind kept knocking it against the post, the same flat knock I had fallen asleep to as a child.

I walked out on the ridges, as I had been taught, and the crust sang under my boots in the same thin note I remembered. I had changed. The pan had not noticed. The crust held, as it always had in the places he taught me to trust, and I stood there longer than I meant to, listening to the sound of it, as if the pan were still reading me the rules. I knelt where the dark patch had been and pressed my palm flat to the salt. It was warm, and when I lifted my hand it was dusted white, the way his hands had been every evening of my childhood.

I put a finger to my tongue, as he used to, and tasted the whole place at once: the rain, the rake, the years of brine, and something sharper that might have been me. It is already in my skin, and by now, I suspect, it is in yours.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it builds a significant sense of place from the flat pan, the father's rules and the salt on the skin, and it continues the extract's second-person invitation in a voice that stays steady throughout. One strength is the structure, which moves from instruction to loss to return without announcing each shift. The move that would lift it is to cut the final sentence, since the salt on the tongue already carries the idea.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The salt pan is a place I think about often, and I want to tell you about it. It sits out past the fence line, a long flat white space that goes on for a long way. My father worked on it for many years. He taught me how to rake the salt and how to read the water, because the colour told you when it was ready. I learned that the dark patches were dangerous, which was an important lesson for a child to learn.

When I was nine, it rained for a long time. The pan filled with water and turned brown, and the work stopped. The company wrote a letter and my father was very sad about it. We left the town in autumn, and I remember looking back at the pumphouse, which got smaller and smaller until I could not see it any more. It made me feel upset, and I still think about that day a great deal. The mothers at the bakery talked about it for weeks, and I did not know what to say to them. Many things changed for my family after that.

Years later I went back on my own. Nobody else wanted to go with me, so I drove out by myself. The pan was white again and very bright. I walked on the crust where my father had said it was safe, and it made a sound like something breaking softly. I felt the place had been waiting for me, although I know that is not really true. The sky was very big and the heat was strong, and I had forgotten how much I liked it. I knelt down and touched the salt, and it was warm and it stuck to my hand.

I tasted it, like he used to do, and it reminded me of all the things we did together when I was young. The pan is important to me because it is where I learned about my father and about myself. It is always going to be part of who I am. I hope that you will remember it too, because a place like that deserves to be remembered by people. I still have a jar of salt from that day on the shelf in my kitchen, and I look at it sometimes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it creates some sense of place and keeps a loose link to the extract's invitation, but it reports events in summary and tells the reader what to feel, so control of language varies. One strength is the rule about the dark patches, which gives the pan a real danger. The move that would lift it is to dramatise one moment in full, such as the day the water rose, rather than summarising the years.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Let me tell you about the salt lake out past the fence. It is a big white place and there is salt everywhere. My dad worked there when I was little. He had a rake and he used it on the salt. We walked on the salt and it was hard and white and bright. Sometimes it was wet in the middle, and you had to be careful where you stood.

One year it rained a lot and the lake filled up with water, so we had to leave the town. I remember the lake going small in the back window of the car. Now I have gone back and it is still there, white and flat, just like before. It is a special place for me and I think about it a lot. The lake is full of memories, and that is why it is important to me.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it uses setting and attempts to continue the extract, but it is a limited sequence of statements with few images and little variety in language. One strength is the clear setting of the salt lake and the rake. The move that would lift it is to replace general statements with two or three specific sensory details, such as the sound the crust makes underfoot.

prompts.scenario: You are not required to write out the opening words as part of your response. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

prompts.question: Craft an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that explores the power of the senses. In your composition, you should emphasise ONE of the five senses (sight, smell, sound, taste OR touch).
markerNotes: The strongest pieces commit to smell from the first line and let its absence drive the structure, so the sense is shown to be powerful rather than announced as important.
Control shows in the choices. The list of remembered smells is short on purpose, the photograph image is extended into one comparison, and the eight days give the piece its shape.
The ending works because it stays with the house arriving, not with a lesson about the senses. A closing sentence that explains the theme is the most common way strong pieces lose ground.
Form and voice should be deliberate: one first-person narrator, a steady past tense and a wry tone that makes the frustration believable.
commonStudentErrors: Listing all five senses in turn, which breaks the instruction to emphasise ONE of them.
Piling up smells without a controlling idea, so the piece reads as an inventory rather than a composition.
Ending with a statement that smell is important, which tells the reader the theme instead of letting the image carry it.
Explaining how smell works in scientific terms in place of showing what it does to the narrator.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Composes an engaging imaginative or discursive piece of writing that effectively responds to the question; Crafts language effectively to explore the power of ONE of the five senses; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
10-12 marks: Composes a competent imaginative or discursive piece of writing that responds to the question; Crafts language competently to explore the power of ONE of the five senses; Demonstrates competent control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
7-9 marks: Composes an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that responds to the question; Uses language adequately to explore the power of ONE of the five senses; Demonstrates sound control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
4-6 marks: Composes a piece of writing that attempts to respond to the question; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
1-3 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing with some relevance to the question

sampleAnswers.answer:
The doctor said the smell would return in a month, perhaps two, so I stopped trying to smell things and started trying to remember them instead.

I began with the easy ones. Toast burnt at the edges. The orange peel my father left drying on the windowsill. Wet wool on a winter morning, and the warm dust on the bookshelves in the hall. I said each one aloud in the kitchen, the way you check a list of names before a roll call, and each one came back to me as a sentence rather than a place. I could describe them. I could not stand inside them.

That was what the illness had taken. Not the pleasure of a smell, which I had always assumed was a small bonus, but its power to pull me somewhere without asking. Smell had never waited for me. It crept under the door of every room I entered and clung to every coat I hung on a hook. Now everything had to be fetched, and I fetched it badly.

Each morning I stood at the back door before school and breathed in slowly, the way I had as a child, when the wind came up from the creek with cut grass and woodsmoke in it. Nothing came. The air was only air, cool and flat, like water left overnight in a glass. My mother said the brain was patient. She said it in the voice she used for splinters. But I had waited at that door all my life without knowing I was waiting, and now I waited at it like someone expecting a letter that might never arrive.

I tried other things. Chlorine at the pool. The wax on the school floors. Petrol on the forecourt. Each one returned as a word and nothing more, a label stuck to an empty jar.

By the fifth day I had stopped trusting memory. The smells I recalled were like photographs printed in grey. The outlines were there, the lemon tree and the washing line and the shed door, but whatever made them live had drained away. When I tried to summon sawdust, I got the word sawdust.

On the eighth day it rained. I was at the back door when the first drops struck the path and made dark coins in the dust, and I thought, with a bitterness I am not proud of, that the rain was only putting on a show. I watched the path darken instead, the dust gathering itself into small craters, and I stopped waiting for anything.

Then the smell came, and not the way I expected. It did not rush. It arrived slowly, as if the ground were lifting its breath for me: the cold iron of the downpipe, the wet earth opening, hot tar cooling in the gutter, and under everything something green and sour that I had forgotten was the smell of my own childhood. The scientists have a name for it, petrichor. The name is a label too. The smell was never the label.

I went inside. The kettle had been left on, and when I stepped into the hallway the whole house arrived at once: toast and peel, wet wool, the dust warm on the shelves, my father’s coat with its faint trace of machine oil. I did not have to fetch any of it. It came to me the way a room lights up when someone opens the door, and I stood in the hallway with my eyes shut and let the house fill me.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 13-15 row: smell is sustained from the first paragraph to the last, the absence of smell is used to test its power, and the closing image of the house arriving at once shows the power of the sense rather than stating it. To lift it further, the middle section could cut one of the remembered smells so that the others do more work.

sampleAnswers.answer:
When I lost my sense of smell, I realised how much I had taken it for granted. The doctor said it might come back in a month or two, so I tried to carry on as normal. I still remembered the smells of my life, but they were not the same as the real thing.

The first thing I missed was toast. Every morning Mum made toast and it burnt a little on the edges, and I could smell it from my bedroom. Now it was just bread. I also missed the orange peel my dad left on the windowsill and the smell of the laundry in winter. I tried to think about these things, but it was hard to get them back.

Smell is very powerful because it is linked to memory. A smell can bring back a memory suddenly, without you trying. This is why I missed it so much. Without it, my memories felt flat and far away, like photos rather than real places.

Every morning I went to the back door and tried to smell the air, the way I used to when I was little. Nothing happened. Mum kept saying it would come back, and I kept saying I knew. On the eighth day it rained. I was at the back door, and the rain made the path wet and dark. I could not smell anything, but I could see it. After a while the smell came back, and it was the smell of rain on the ground. It was amazing. I went inside, and the whole house smelled of home again.

I realised from this experience that smell is one of the most important senses because it can make you feel something without even trying. I will never take it for granted again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 7-9 row: the narrator explores smell and memory with a clear sequence, but the power of smell is explained in general statements rather than shown through imagery, and the days are retold in order. Replacing the explanation with one carefully chosen smell, developed through a sustained image, would move it toward the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Smell is a sense that everybody has, and I never thought about it until today. I woke up and I could not smell anything. I went downstairs and Mum had made breakfast, but I could not smell it. I ate my toast anyway. It was just bread. At school my friends were talking about the pizza at lunch and I could not smell it either, and it was a bit annoying. I thought about how smell is important and how we should be grateful for our noses. I was sad all afternoon. When I got home it was raining and I could smell the rain, so my nose came back. It was good, and I was happy again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 4-6 row: it responds to the stem with a simple narrator and a sequence of events, but smell is named more than it is crafted and the piece closes by stating a lesson. Developing one sense through specific images, and ending on an image rather than on the lesson, would move it toward the 7-9 row.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks in all; this part is worth 15). Allow about 40 minutes for the whole question.

dotPoints.description: Use appropriate metalanguage to assess and reflect on the ways meaning is made in their own writing and the writing of others

prompts.question: Define THREE items of metalanguage used to assess the meaning made in your own writing, giving ONE example of each from your draft.
markerNotes: Metalanguage is the vocabulary of the craft. Define each term precisely, so the definition could be used to check the writer's own draft.
The example should come from the writer's own draft, showing that the term applies to something the writer actually did.
commonStudentErrors: Defining a term loosely, such as saying a metaphor is 'a fancy comparison' without saying what it does.
Giving an example that is not from the draft or that does not fit the term.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines three metalanguage terms accurately and gives a specific example of each from the draft
2 marks: Defines two terms accurately, or three with a general or missing example
1 mark: Defines one term accurately, or names terms without definition

sampleAnswers.answer: Metalanguage helps a writer describe meaning precisely. A metaphor describes one thing as another, so the town as a sleeping dog suggests something quiet that could wake. An example from the draft is the sleeping dog comparison that opens the story. A tricolon is three parallel elements, such as the list of three short sentences in the middle section. A rhetorical question is asked for effect, like the closing question about where the town's children will go.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three items of metalanguage are defined accurately, and each is matched to a specific example from the draft that fits the definition. This is the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: A metaphor is when one thing is described as another, like the town being a sleeping dog. A rhetorical question is a question that does not need an answer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two terms are defined accurately, and the metaphor is matched to the draft, but no third term is defined, which matches the 2-mark line.

sampleAnswers.answer: A metaphor is a comparison.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One term is defined only partially, without the detail that would make it usable for assessing the writer's meaning, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing a reflective commentary to accompany a short story in a folio. The teacher has asked for accurate metalanguage rather than general comments such as 'the writing is good'. The invented story's opening paragraph uses a metaphor that compares the town to a sleeping dog, its middle section uses a list of three short sentences, and its final paragraph ends with a rhetorical question. The question asks where the town's children will go.

prompts.question: Assess how well the metalanguage in the peer feedback reflects the meaning made in the writer's story, with reference to TWO examples.
markerNotes: Assess the metalanguage against what it is supposed to do: make the meaning of the writing visible to the writer. Precision is the test.
Use two examples from the feedback and test each one. A strong answer shows why a term is too vague to help a revision, and what a more precise term would do.
commonStudentErrors: Judging the feedback as kind or unkind rather than as metalanguage that reflects meaning.
Quoting the feedback terms without testing whether each one is precise.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses how well the metalanguage reflects the meaning made, judging each example against precise evidence from the story, and reaches a clear view on the feedback's usefulness to the writer
5 marks: Assesses the metalanguage with clear reference to two examples and a view on its usefulness, but the analysis of meaning is brief
4 marks: Assesses the metalanguage with some reference to examples, and a general view on how well it reflects meaning
3 marks: Describes the terms used in the feedback and notes whether they are precise, with limited judgement
2 marks: Makes a general statement about the feedback with little reference to the terms
1 mark: Quotes a term from the feedback without assessing it

sampleAnswers.answer: The metalanguage in the peer feedback is only partly effective, because some terms are precise and others are too general to help the writer. 'Strong imagery' names a category of language, which is correct, but it does not say which images are strong or what they do, so the writer cannot tell whether the imagery is working on the reader. The meaning made by the imagery remains unassessed. 'Nice tone' is a value judgement rather than metalanguage: nice describes the reader's pleasure, not the tone itself, which could be wry, anxious or detached. 'The ending works well' is less a term than an endorsement, and it withholds the reasons that would let the writer repeat the effect. Assessed against the writer's need, the feedback reflects some meaning but never shows how that meaning is made. On balance it is useful as encouragement, not as a guide to revision, because its metalanguage stops at description.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The metalanguage is assessed against what it should do, with its examples tested in detail, and the answer reaches a clear view that the peer feedback is useful for encouragement but not for revision. This is the full-mark assessment.

sampleAnswers.answer: The peer feedback uses strong imagery and nice tone, which are general terms. Strong imagery is a category of language, but it does not say what the images are or what they do. Nice tone is a judgement, not a term about the tone itself. The feedback is useful for encouragement but not for helping the writer see how meaning is made.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The metalanguage is assessed with some reference to two examples and a general view on how well it reflects meaning, but the analysis of meaning is brief and the examples are not tested in depth. This is the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The peer feedback says the ending works well.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A term is quoted from the feedback without any assessment of its precision or usefulness, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: A peer's invented feedback sheet on a classmate's 400-word short story uses terms such as 'strong imagery', 'nice tone' and 'the ending works well'. It gives no reference to the story's language features, and the writer is asking whether the feedback is useful for revision.

prompts.question: Explain how ONE stylistic device you have used in part (a) was inspired by ONE of the prescribed texts in Module C.
markerNotes: Name the device precisely, then trace it through the piece rather than describing the piece in general.
The link to Bradbury needs a concrete textual reference: a character, a setting or a moment from The Pedestrian, not a general claim that it is about loneliness.
Explain what the device does differently in your own piece. The strongest answers show the inspiration and the adaptation together.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a device without showing where it appears in the part (a) piece.
Summarising the plot of The Pedestrian in place of explaining how one element of it shaped the writing.
Choosing a device the piece does not use, such as dialogue, when the piece is written as a single narrated voice.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains effectively the use of ONE stylistic device in part (a) and how ONE prescribed text from Module C inspired it, using relevant textual references and demonstrating effective control of language
4 marks: Explains competently the use of ONE stylistic device in part (a) and how ONE prescribed text from Module C inspired it, using relevant textual references and demonstrating competent control of language
3 marks: Explains the use of ONE stylistic device in part (a) and how ONE prescribed text from Module C inspired it, using some textual references and demonstrating sound control of language
2 marks: Attempts to explain the use of ONE stylistic device in part (a) and how ONE prescribed text from Module C inspired it
1 mark: Attempts to respond to the question

sampleAnswers.answer: In part (a), the device I worked hardest on is the shadow. It is cast up the hillside from the seedling, so it points forward to the future, and it recurs in each section, lengthening and shrinking with the sun to measure the passing of time. This was inspired by Ray Bradbury’s short story The Pedestrian, in which Leonard Mead walks an empty city in 2053 and sees only the shadows of people moving behind lit windows. Bradbury’s shadows show people shut away from one another and from the world outside, whereas my shadow shows the future that present care is still making. The recurring image is how I connect the patient gardener to the reward of long effort.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the highest descriptor: it names one device, the sustained shadow image, traces it through the piece, and explains its inspiration from The Pedestrian with a concrete textual reference to Leonard Mead's walk through the empty city of 2053. To lift it further, it could show more precisely how the device changes meaning between the two texts, from isolation to hope.

sampleAnswers.answer: In my part (a) piece, the shadow of the tree is a repeated image. It grows and shrinks across the hill as the day passes, which shows time moving. Ray Bradbury’s The Pedestrian also uses shadows: Leonard Mead walks an empty city in 2053 and sees the shadows of people shut inside their houses. My shadow is more hopeful, because it shows the tree still growing and the future still coming.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the sound descriptor: it identifies the shadow as a repeated image and links it to The Pedestrian with some textual reference, but the explanation of why the device was chosen is brief. Developing the comparison of what the shadow signals in each text would move it toward the competent descriptor.

sampleAnswers.answer: My story has a shadow that moves across the hill as the day goes on. Ray Bradbury’s The Pedestrian also has shadows in an empty city.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the lowest descriptor: it attempts to respond to the question by naming a shadow and a text, but it does not explain how one inspired the other. Explaining what the shadow does in the piece, and how it relates to Bradbury's use of shadow, would move it toward the sound descriptor.

prompts.scenario: Refer to the piece you crafted for part (a). The sample answers below respond to a model part (a) piece, which is a present-tense story in which Ilse waters a seedling each morning while a shadow cast up the hillside shows a tree in full leaf and a woman picking red fruit. Its central image is that shadow, which lengthens and shrinks with the sun and carries the future, and the piece uses this recurring motif, with deliberate repetition, to explore patience, the passage of time and the reward of long effort. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (5 marks).

prompts.question: Explain how your study of the craft of writing has enabled you to create an engaging piece of writing. In your response, make detailed reference to your use of language in part (a).
markerNotes: The strongest reflections name a choice, trace it to a specific moment in the part (a) piece, and explain what that choice does for the reader.
Quote the piece accurately and briefly. A reflection that paraphrases its own images loses the detail the question asks for.
Connect the craft of writing to the piece with precision: controlling idea, structure and point of view are stronger terms than general words such as good or interesting.
The explanation of engagement matters more than the list of devices. The best answers say how the reader is kept moving through the piece.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the part (a) piece in order instead of explaining the choices that made it engaging.
Listing several devices without linking any of them to a specific effect on the reader.
Describing the craft of writing in general terms, without showing how it changed a particular decision in the writing.
Quoting the part (a) piece inaccurately, or at a length that replaces the explanation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Explains in a detailed and relevant manner how the study of the craft of writing has enabled the creation of a piece of imaginative, discursive or persuasive writing; Explains in a detailed and relevant manner how language has been used to create an engaging response in part (a); Demonstrates effective control of language
5-6 marks: Explains how the study of the craft of writing has enabled the creation of a piece of imaginative, discursive or persuasive writing; Explains how language has been used to create an engaging response in part (a); Demonstrates competent control of language
3-4 marks: Describes some aspects of the craft of writing; Makes some reference to the piece of writing in part (a); Demonstrates some control of language
1-2 marks: Provides some relevant information about the piece of writing in part (a) and/or their study of the craft of writing

sampleAnswers.answer:
My study of the craft of writing taught me how to create an engaging piece of writing, and the first lesson was to fix a controlling idea before drafting. For part (a) the idea was that a laneway renews itself while one small accident survives every repaint, so each image had to serve that idea or go. I cut the paragraphs where I was only describing the lane, because a description without a job does not hold a reader.

The structure is circular, and the study of how a text closes shaped the ending most of all. The piece opens at dawn with a council crew and finishes at night with the same walls, so the last image has to echo the opening without copying it. My use of language does that work. The grey “climbs over them like a tide over sand”, a simile that makes the paint behave like weather, and the skyline that climbs back out of the grey gives the lane a second life.

Sensory detail was the device I trusted most. The roller hums, soft and almost kind, and the smell of thinners fixes the scene in the reader’s body before any idea is stated. The line “that is the part I cannot forgive” is deliberately plain, because a plain sentence makes the feeling harder to dismiss.

The study also taught me to distrust my first ending. The version I wrote first explained what the lane meant, and I replaced it with the white centre line, which runs past the bins and does not need a sentence of comment. A reader who finishes the piece looking at the lane has been given the idea without being told it.

The piece is engaging because it withholds. The pink splashes outlast three coats, and the reader only works that out in the last paragraph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 7-8 row: it explains how specific craft choices, including the circular structure, the simile and the plain sentence, shaped the piece, and it supports each with an exact quotation from the part (a) piece. The move that would lift it is to explain the effect of one device at more length, since the answer names four in a short space.

sampleAnswers.answer: In my study of the craft of writing I learned that a piece needs a clear idea and a shape, and I tried to use both. For part (a) I wanted the lane to change but also to stay the same, so I made the piece run from morning to night. I used a simile, “like a tide over sand”, to show the paint covering the murals, because a simile helps the reader see the paint. I also used the sound of the roller and the white centre line at the end. The roller hums, which makes the crew seem gentle while they erase the murals, and I wanted the reader to notice that. In class we looked at how writers finish a piece, and that helped me decide to end where I started. I think these choices make the piece engaging because I used them on purpose, and the study showed me how.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-6 row: it explains the shape of the piece and one simile and shows that the study of craft informed the writing, but the explanation stays general and only one reference is used. The move that would lift it is to link two or three devices to the particular effect each has on the reader, rather than naming them.

sampleAnswers.answer: My piece is about a laneway in the city where people paint on the walls and then the council paints over them. I used a lot of description, like the pink splashes and the white line, and I think the ending is good. The study of craft helped me think about how to write it and what to put in, and I tried to make the lane come alive for the reader.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 1-2 row: it gives some relevant information about the piece and about the study of craft, but it describes the piece rather than explaining how it became engaging. The move that would lift it is to choose one device, quote its exact wording and say what it does to the reader.

prompts.scenario: Refer to the piece you crafted for part (a). The sample answers below respond to a model part (a) piece, which is a first-person story told mostly in the present tense: a narrator watches a council crew paint over a city laneway at dawn, and by night the walls have been repainted. The piece ends on the stimulus, with a painted face, murals on both walls and a white centre line, and its pink splashes outlast every repaint. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: craft language to address the demands of the question; use language appropriate to audience, purpose and form to shape meaning.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks in all; this part is worth 8). Allow about 40 minutes for the whole question.

dotPoints.description: Draft, reflect, edit, refine, revise and present texts for a range of purposes and audiences

prompts.question: Recommend revisions to the draft so that it better suits its audience of Year 9 students, explaining why each revision matters.
markerNotes: A recommendation names a specific change, says where it goes and gives a reason tied to the audience. Vague advice such as make it better scores in the bottom band.
The top band recognises the order of revisions, because some changes make others possible, and reflects on that sequence.
Keep the speech's purpose in view. A revision that makes the speech clearer but less persuasive does not serve the task.
commonStudentErrors: Recommending that the student make the speech more interesting without naming a change.
Suggesting a revision that suits the writer rather than the Year 9 audience.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Recommends specific revisions that suit the Year 9 audience and the speech's purpose, each explained with a clear reason linked to how the audience will respond, and reflects on the order of the revisions
5 marks: Recommends specific revisions suited to the audience and purpose, each with a reason
4 marks: Recommends revisions with reasons, but some are general or not clearly linked to the audience
3 marks: Recommends two or three revisions with limited reasons
2 marks: Makes general suggestions about the draft without specific revisions
1 mark: Comments on the draft without making a recommendation

sampleAnswers.answer:
I recommend three revisions, made in this order because each prepares the next. First, the long introduction should be cut to two sentences that name the problem. Year 9 students will judge the speech in its opening lines, so a short opening that connects to their school day keeps them listening. Second, 'biodegradable polymer' should be replaced with plain language, such as 'plastic that breaks down slowly', so that the audience does not stop to decode the argument. Third, the summary should become a clear call to action, such as asking each class to pick one plastic item to remove from their lunch. A summary repeats what has been said, whereas a call to action gives the audience a purpose for the next day.

The order matters: once the introduction is cut, I would reflect on the draft, because the plainer language may change the rhythm of the middle section. A final edit should check every sentence against the audience's likely response before the speech is presented.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three specific revisions are recommended, each with a reason tied to how Year 9 students will respond, and the order of the revisions is justified. The reflection on the sequence is what earns the top band. This is the full-mark recommendation.

sampleAnswers.answer: I would cut the long introduction so the speech starts quickly. I would also replace the technical term with plain words, because students may not know it. The ending could be a call to action so students do something. These changes would help the audience understand the speech better.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Revisions are recommended with reasons, but the reasons are general and the link to the Year 9 audience and to the speech's purpose is only partly made. This is the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The draft could be improved in a few places.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The draft is commented on without any specific recommendation, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: A Year 10 student has drafted an invented short persuasive speech for a Year 9 assembly on reducing plastic at school. The draft has a long introduction, uses technical terms such as 'biodegradable polymer' without explanation, and ends with a summary rather than a call to action. The teacher has asked for revisions before the speech is presented.

prompts.question: Explain how drafting, reflecting and editing work together to refine a text for a range of purposes and audiences.
markerNotes: Explain the dependence. Show what each process produces that the next one needs, rather than treating the three as a list.
The top band ties each process to purpose or audience, so the explanation shows how the text is refined for its readers.
commonStudentErrors: Describing drafting, reflecting and editing as three separate steps with no link between them.
Treating reflecting as a general opinion about the draft rather than as a judgement against purpose and audience.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how the three processes depend on one another to refine the text, with specific examples of how each affects purpose and audience
3 marks: Explains the three processes and their role in refining the text, with some link to purpose or audience
2 marks: Describes each process with limited explanation of how they work together
1 mark: Names one or more processes without explaining their role

sampleAnswers.answer: Drafting, reflecting and editing work together as a cycle in which each process produces what the next one needs. Drafting gets ideas onto the page: the first draft of the plastic speech was long and technical because the student was still working out what to say. Reflecting examines that draft against its purposes and audiences, and the peer discussion showed the technical language would not reach a Year 9 audience. Editing carries out those decisions, replacing the technical term with plain language and turning the ending into a call to action. Each stage helps the student refine the speech, so the final version suits its purposes and audiences.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The three processes are shown to depend on one another, with each producing what the next needs, and each is tied to purpose or audience through the specific changes made to the speech. This is the full-mark explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Drafting produces the first version. Reflecting looks at the draft and editing changes it. Together they make the speech better for the students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each process is described, but the answer does not explain how the processes work together or how they affect purpose and audience, which matches the 2-mark line.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student did drafting, reflecting and editing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The processes are named without any explanation of their role, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: A student is describing how an invented speech about plastic was produced for a Year 9 audience. The student drafted the speech, reflected on it with a peer, and then edited it for its purpose and audience before it was presented in assembly. The first draft was long and used technical terms, and editing turned its ending into a call to action.

prompts.question: Describe the stages the student moved through between the first draft and the final presented version of the speech.
markerNotes: Describe asks for the sequence and what happens at each point. Keep the stages in order, and name one concrete action for each.
The strongest answers show the stages as a progression from draft to presentation, so the reader can see how the speech changed along the way.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the final result without describing the stages that led to it.
Describing the stages out of order, so the progression is lost.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the stages in order from the first draft to the presented version, with a specific change or action at each stage
2 marks: Describes the stages in general terms, or describes some stages with specific actions
1 mark: Names the first draft and the presented version without describing the stages between them

sampleAnswers.answer: The stages ran from the first draft to the presented version. The first draft had a long introduction and the technical term 'biodegradable polymer'. In reflection with a peer, the student saw that these would lose the audience. In editing, the introduction was cut to two sentences, the technical language was made plain and the ending became a call to action. In rehearsal, the speech was read aloud before the presented version.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The stages are described in order from the first draft to the presented version, with a specific change or action at each one. This is the full-mark description.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student wrote a first draft and then edited it. Then the speech was presented in assembly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The stages are described only in general terms, with no specific change at any stage, which matches the 2-mark line.

sampleAnswers.answer: The speech was changed before it was presented.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The stages between the first draft and the presented version are not described, which matches the 1-mark line.

prompts.scenario: An invented student speech on reducing plastic at school went through several stages between its first draft and the final presented version. The student reflected on the first draft with a peer, edited the technical language and the ending, and then rehearsed the speech aloud before presenting it in assembly. The first draft had a long introduction and used terms such as 'biodegradable polymer', and the introduction was later cut to two sentences.
